sources.ARC-AGI-2: MARC2 — description that passed description-only solver validation

_meta.validated: true for larc, marc2 (independent human or solver reconstruction) and conceptarc_rules_csv (the dataset authors' rule); false for drafts, generator docstrings and program descriptions
_meta.parc_note: All 50 P-ARC rules reviewed 2026-09-18. Ten written from scratch for tasks that had no rule; 38 redrafted from each task's transform function and reviewed; t11 and t12 carried over as harvested.

007bbfb7.rule:
In the input, you should see...a 3x3 grid of black cells and cells of another color.
The output grid size...is 9x9.
To make the output, you have to...consider the 9x9 output grid as a 3x3 grid of 3x3 blocks. Each cell of the input (3x3 cells) thus corresponds to an output block (3x3 blocks). For each input cell, if the cell is black, then leave its corresponding block black as well ; else copy the whole input grid into the block.
007bbfb7.author: Adrien

00d62c1b.rule:
In the input, you should see...a design with lines and empty squares.

The output grid size...stays the same.

To make the output, you have to...look at the color that form the design in the input.Find any empty areas of blocks that are enclosed  by the lines that form the main design, fill them yellow.You should end with the same original design from the input, but with the empty areas filled yellow.

017c7c7b.rule:
In the input, you should see...a grid that is 3x6 with black and blue.

The output grid size...add 3 rows to the bottom.

To make the output, you have to...keep the original pattern, change the blue to red, and then continue the pattern in the new 3 rows.

025d127b.rule: The input contains one or more colored outline shapes on a black background. Each shape has a lower-right L-shaped part made from its bottom horizontal row and the cell directly above the right end.  The output grid size stays the same. Keep this lower-right L in place. Move every other colored cell in each shape one square to the right.
025d127b.author: Philipp

045e512c.rule:
In the input, you should see...a prototype (largest) shape and a couple of isolated colored shapes or cells around it on a unicolored background.

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid size.

To make the output, you have to...turn the surrounding colored shapes or cells into copies of the prototype (retaining their color), then, copy the offset from the original prototype (shortest path, diagonal is fine) to make more copies of the new shapes until the border is hit (partial shapes at the border are fine). The offset is copied at each new copy.
045e512c.author: Claas

0520fde7.rule:
In the input, you should see...a grid with a gray line down the center

The output grid size...should be 3x3

To make the output, you have to... look at both the left and right parts of the input grid. You will notice that the left and right parts are 3x3. For each square that is colored on both the left and right parts, color the output grid with red on the new 3x3.

05269061.rule:
In the input, you should see...7 by 7 grid being different colored on black background

The output grid size...should be same as input size

To make the output, you have to...fill the black grid with same pattern of row color, next row need to replace the same pattern of first row one column move shifted left

05f2a901.rule:
In the input, you should see...a light blue cube and a red shape.

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid.

To make the output, you have to...keep the light blue cube in the same exact location. Then copy and move the other shape directly towards the blue cube, until it is touching it. At the end you'll have the light blue cube in the same exact spot as in the input grid and the the other shape will be the same but moved directly towards and touching the blue cube.

06df4c85.rule:
In the input, you should see... different color pattern on black background

The output grid size...should be same as input size

To make the output, you have to...fill the black 2x2 square grid with same color in between the two same color of 2x2 grid and connect

08ed6ac7.rule:
In the input, you should see...a few bars that are gray

The output grid size...does not change

To make the output, you have to...change the color of the tallest to blue, then second talest to red,third tallest to green,then finally shortest to yellow for both pairs.

09629e4f.rule: The input and outbut are each an 11x11 grid with two grey rows and two grey columns partitioning the grid into a 3x3 arrangement of subgrids. Each of these subgrids is itself 3x3 cells. Each subgrid in the input contains the same number of uniquely colored cells, using the same palette, except for one. Use this subgrid as the template for the output, where each subgrid in the output is fully filled with the color of the corresponding cell in the input's  odd subgrid. In all demonstrations here, each subgrid contains exactly five cells of different non-background colors—red, green, yellow, magenta, and cyan—except for the single odd subgrid, which omits cyan.
09629e4f.author: Ryan

0962bcdd.rule:
In the input, you should see...two plus sign shapes with a different center color

The output grid size... is the same as input

To make the output, you have to...extend the plus sign one square in every direction and then make a 5x5 'X' of the center color through the center square. You should result in nine squares the color of the center and eight the color of the original plus sign.

0a938d79.rule:
In the input, you should see...either a long or tall black grid with 2 different colored pixels

The output grid size... remains the same.

To make the output, you have to... create a pattern of short stripes alternating between the 2 colors. Start from the first colored pixel and create a line that goes to the opposite side using that color. Then go to the second colored pixel and do the same. Continue the pattern of stripes to the RIGHT for a long grid or go DOWN for a tall grid all the way to the end.

0b148d64.rule:
In the input, you should see...a rectangular pattern in each corner, one a different color than the others.

The output grid size...becomes the size of the pattern that is a different color.

To make the output, you have to...copy the pattern that is a different color

0ca9ddb6.rule:
In the input, you should see...grid with single pixel colored squares

The output grid size...same as input

To make the output, you have to...copy image exactly.  Where there's a red square, put yellow squares at it's corners (4 total).  Where there's a dark blue square, put orange squares directly above and below it (4 total). Do nothing with light blue or magenta squares

0d3d703e.rule:
In the input, you should see...a 3 by 3 grid with three different colored column.

The output grid size...is also 3 by 3.

To make the output, you have to...change the column color to a specific other color. If the original color is dark red, change it to pink. If it is green, change it to yellow. If dark blue, change to grey. If light blue, change to dark red. The opposite is also true (for example if it is light blue, change to dark red).

0dfd9992.rule:
In the input, you should see...a mostly filled in grid with a few black holes.

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid.

To make the output, you have to...start by copying the input grid exactly. Fill in all of the black boxes to complete the pattern until there are no more black boxes. To do this notice the pattern of the colored boxes. For example the top row might repeat every 4th row (or 5 rows or whatever the number of rows is before it repeats).  Once you've figured out the pattern just fill in the black boxes with the correct colored boxes. In the end you should see repeating patterns of colored boxes and there should be no black boxes in the grid.

0e206a2e.rule:
In the input, you should see...a fully colored object and unfulfilled 3 color boxes with black backround.

The output grid size...is same as given

To make the output, you have to...try to fill up the empty space between the three color boxes as the original object given.

10fcaaa3.rule:
In the input, you should see... 1 or 2 squares filled in with the same color on a black background.

The output grid size... is double the height and width of the input grid.

To make the output, you have to... resize the output grid to be double the width and height of the input grid. Then, copy and paste each colored square in the input grid 4 times -- once in each "quadrant" (if, in the input, the square is in the uppermost and leftmost corner, then it should be in the uppermost and leftmost corner in the output, as well as in the uppermost and leftmost corner of each "quadrant"). Then, for every single colored square, do the following: put a light blue square on each adjacent corner, forming a cross with 4 light-blue squares and the colored square in the middle.

11852cab.rule:
In the input, you should see...shapes with one color that is not complete the pattern

The output grid size...is the same as input

To make the output, you have to...complete the pattern that is not there by color each side with the color that is not there to complete the pattern

1190e5a7.rule:
In the input, you should see...colored grid

The output grid size...number of size

To make the output, you have to...successfully

137eaa0f.rule:
In the input, you should see...single object fill grid

The output grid size...In the input, you should see...single object fill grid

To make the output, you have to...In the input, you should see...single object fill grid

150deff5.rule:
In the input, you should see... a black 9x9 grid with a gray pattern.

The output grid size... is the same for input and output

To make the output, you have to... copy pattern and change 2x2 areas to light blue and 1x3 to red.

178fcbfb.rule:
In the input, you should see...a grid with red, blue, and green squares

The output grid size...is the same as the input

To make the output, you have to...draw a vertical red line through any red squares.  Then draw lines, left to right, for the green and blue squares.  Go over any red squares from before.

1a07d186.rule:
In the input, you should see...one or two main colors with a third that is different than the rest.

The output grid size...remains the same

To make the output, you have to...remove the different color that does not match the rest. move the single squares so they are in the same horizontal or vertical place depending if it is a vertical or horizontal line and have them touch the same side the single squares were on.

1b2d62fb.rule:
In the input, you should see... two red pattern and a blue line in the middle.

The output grid size... is 3 wide and 5 up and down

To make the output, you have to... put both pattern together, if it is red in either pattern make it red in the output. Then turn the black light blue and the red black.

1b60fb0c.rule:
In the input, you should see...a three-part blue pattern against a black background.

The output grid size...should match the input.

To make the output, you have to... recreate the blue pattern then add another part on the left, in red.

1bfc4729.rule:
In the input, you should see...two colors, one at the top and the other at the bottom

The output grid size...is the same size

To make the output, you have to...use the top color to fill in the entire first row, the first and last blocks of the second row, the entire third row, and the first and last blocks of the 4th and 5th rows. Then use the bottom color to fill in the first and last blocks of the 6th and 7th rows, fill in the entire 8th row, the first and last blocks of the 9th row, and the entire bottom (10th) row

1c786137.rule:
In the input, you should see... a complex color pattern with a distinctive rectangle of a single color

The output grid size...will be the size of the area inside the rectangle

To make the output, you have to...copy the grid inside the rectangle

1caeab9d.rule:
In the input, you should see... 3 shapes of blue, red, and yellow colors.

The output grid size...is the same size as the input grid

To make the output, you have to...keep the blue shape where it is, and move the red and yellow shapes up or down so that they are at the same level as the blue-colored shape.

1cf80156.rule:
In the input, you should see...a colored image on a black grid.

The output grid size...it becomes the size of the colored image.

To make the output, you have to...you just need to make sure the colored image is exactly (top, bottom, left, right) in the new grid. No color change.

1e0a9b12.rule:
In the input, you should see... grids of squares with colored square scattered.

The output grid size... doesn't change from the input.

To make the output, you have to... think of the grid as a black field and as the colored squares as being objects floating in space. Gravity is suddenly turned on and all of the block fall vertically to the bottom.  That produces the correct output grid.

1e32b0e9.rule:
In the input, you should see...a 17x17 grid that is split into 9 5x5 squares. Inside of these 9 blocks you should see blocks of the same color.

The output grid size...is the same

To make the output, you have to...replicate what is inside of the top left 5x5 grid throughout the rest of the 8 grid left. The color of these additional blocks should match the color of the block cut line.

1f0c79e5.rule:
In the input, you should see a 2*2 square placed anywhere in the grid.
The output grid size stays the same.
To make the output, you have to look at the red cells in the square in the input grid. There can be a maximum of 3 red cells. You have to recolor these cells in the other color present in the square (the square will only be of two colors maximum - red and some other color) and then extend the square in the direction that each red cell pointed to. Extending the square means extending each cell of the square diagonally till it hits an edge.
1f0c79e5.author: Navya

1f642eb9.rule:
In the input, you should see...a large blue area with colored squares around the edge.

The output grid size...keep the same

To make the output, you have to...make a copy of each of the colored small squares and put those copy into the blue shape into the same line near to the same block.

1f85a75f.rule:
In the input, you should see...a dense color block inside the big back ground

The output grid size...is the size of the small dense part

To make the output, you have to...copy the small dense part

1f876c06.rule:
In the input, you should see...various pairs of colored blocks in a black grid.

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid size.

To make the output, you have to...copy the input grid. Then, form a diagonal line by connecting the two of the same color blocks. The diagonal line between each set of matching color blocks should be the same color as the two blocks you are connecting. Do this for each set of matching blocks.

1fad071e.rule:
In the input, you should see...multiple  2x2 blue grids and other colors on black background

The output grid size... 5x1 grid

To make the output, you have to...fill single blue grid from the left for every 2x2 blue grids available

2013d3e2.rule:
In the input, you should see... a colored shape on a black background

The output grid size... is 3x3

To make the output, you have to... fill the grid with the upper left corner of the colored shape. The output should look like the top left corner of the colored shape.

2204b7a8.rule:
In the input, you should see...two colored sides of the grid, with some colored blocks in the middle.

The output grid size...same as input

To make the output, you have to...change the color of the block in the middle of the grid to match the color of the side they are closest to.

22168020.rule:
In the input, you should see...a box of color with colored shapes up from each side.

The output grid size...should be the same as the input

To make the output, you have to...fill in the area above the four square base until you get to the top of the colored area

22233c11.rule:
In the input, you should see...green pattern or patterns

The output grid size...same size

To make the output, you have to...on each of the center line direction of the green pattern, draw blue color pattern, and the blue color pattern is half of the green pattern

2281f1f4.rule:
In the input, you should see...a mostly black grid with grey cells scattered on the edges.

The output grid size...stays the same as the input.

To make the output, you have to...mark those cells red where a grey cell is at two orthogonal borders, in the same column (for example at the top) and in the same row (for example on the right).
2281f1f4.author: Claas

228f6490.rule:
In the input, you should see...same grid

The output grid size...10x10

To make the output, you have to...fill in the shapes within the gray area with the color shapes that represent the space.

22eb0ac0.rule:
In the input, you should see...single pixels of different colors in two horizontal lines along the left and right sides of the grid.

The output grid size...stays the same size as the input.

To make the output, you have to....copy the input. If two blocks across from each other are the same color, fill in the rest of that horizontal row with that color. Don't do anything with the blocks across from each other that are different colors

234bbc79.rule:
In the input, you should see...three shapes, all of which have a main color with some grey boxes.

The output grid size...changes in length by removed any black columns that separate the shapes

To make the output, you have to...make any grey boxes the same color as the blocks to which it is connected. Remove columns of black boxes. Align the middle and right shapes so that the former grey squares are connected.

23581191.rule:
In the input, you should see... two colored squares

The output grid size... is the same

To make the output, you have to... continue both lines in their color both left to right and up and down. where the two lines cross each other make that square red

239be575.rule:
In the input, you should see...Blue grid and two red squares with the random Black grid.

The output grid size...1 grid square.

To make the output, you have to...make the color of the square the same color as the square that is five down and three across of the input.

23b5c85d.rule:
In the input, you should see...different colored objects in the grid.

The output grid size...should be the one colored object with the smallest area.

To make the output, you have to...change the grid size with the colored object with the smallest area and fill the same color.

253bf280.rule:
In the input, you should see...light blue dots

The output grid size...is the same as the old one

To make the output, you have to...use green lines to connect blue dots that are in the same line

25d487eb.rule:
In the input, you should see...a single pattern

The output grid size...does not change

To make the output, you have to...take the smaller color and shoot it out the top

25d8a9c8.rule:
In the input, you should see...colored pattern in the grids.

The output grid size...same as the input grid size.

To make the output, you have to...fill the row with grey if the row has the same colors in the input. color the row with black if the row contain different colors.

25ff71a9.rule:
In the input, you should see...3 by 3 grid blue color grid on black background

The output grid size...same as input size

To make the output, you have to...move all the blue color move down  by one grid

264363fd.rule:
In the input, you should see...large grid

The output grid size...input size grid

To make the output, you have to...blocks tall and touch

272f95fa.rule:
In the input, you should see...four lines - two horizontal, two vertical - in a single color on a black background.

The output grid size...same as input

To make the output, you have to...copy the input. Fill the top row middle shape (between the lines) in red. For the second (center) row, fill the first shape with yellow, the middle with pink, and the last (right) in green. Then fill the middle shape of the bottom row with blue. The four corner shapes will still be black.

27a28665.rule:
In the input, you should see...a 3 by 3 grid filled with different colored squares.

The output grid size...will change to a 1 by 1 square.

To make the output, you have to...see which design you have. if you have two black lines that are 2 squares long, one coming down from the top left, and one going left from the bottom right, your output will be a green square.If you have a grey cross that is filled in, your output is a magenta square. If you have a black cross, with the middle square filled in with a different color, your output will be an orangey red. If you have a cross of a different color, with the middle square black, and the upper left square filled in with the color as well, then your output will be a blue square.

28bf18c6.rule:
In the input, you should see...a figure on a big grid.

The output grid size...3 up and 6 to the sides.

To make the output, you have to...copy the figure two times in that grid size.

28e73c20.rule:
In the input, you should see...a black background.

The output grid size...is the same as the input.

To make the output, you have to...make a green "spiral." Begin in the upper left corner and work clockwise around the outer edges of the grid. Turn clockwise one cell short of making a complete border of green. Continue coloring green until you reach the center of the grid.

29623171.rule:
In the input, you should see...9 black boxes with colored blocks inside them

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid size

To make the output, you have to...find the black box or boxes with the highest number of colored blocks in the input grid. The corresponding box or boxes in the output grid should be colored entirely that color. The rest of the boxes should be all black

29c11459.rule:
In the input, you should see...5x11 grid

The output grid size...stays the same

To make the output, you have to...add four more blocks of the same color to the right of the block on the left side of the grid. Add a gray block. Then add four blocks of the same color of the block on the right side of the grid to connect the line.

29ec7d0e.rule:
In the input, you should see...fill with create colors

The output grid size...same size

To make the output, you have to...fill with bottom

2bcee788.rule:
In the input, you should see...an object on a black background with red blocks.

The output grid size...stays the same.

To make the output, you have to...change the background to green. The object should have 2 colors red and some other color. From the input, take the color that is not red and copy it exactly as it is. You want to make another copy of that color but make it a mirrored image in the direction of the red block.

2bee17df.rule:
In the input, you should see...two different colors of squares around the edges of the grid.

The output grid size...stays the same.

To make the output, you have to...Copy the input grid into the output. Around the outside of the grid, you will notice some squares are only one square deep around. Take note of these squares. Using green, draw straight lines horizontally and vertically from these squares that are only one deep around the outside, connecting them ONLY to squares on the other side of the grid that also are only one square deep.

2c608aff.rule:
In the input, you should see...a pattern with a central square and colored dots.

The output grid size...is the same as input

To make the output, you have to...If the dots could connect to the central square with a straight line, connect it with the same color as the dot

2dc579da.rule:
In the input, you should see... a grid broken up into 4 sections by a cross, where 1 section has an off-color single square in it.

The output grid size... is the size of 1 of the 4 sections.

To make the output, you have to... "zoom in" on the section with an off-color square.

2dd70a9a.rule:
In the input, you should see...red and green dots

The output grid size...is the same as the old one

To make the output, you have to...use green line to connect the red and green parts in straight lines

2dee498d.rule:
In the input, you should see... A repeating pattern (usually repeats three times)

The output grid size... should be set to the equivalent grid size that the singular pattern takes up

To make the output, you have to... fill the grid up with the singular identified pattern

31aa019c.rule:
In the input, you should see...large grid with many colored blocks.

The output grid size...same as the input.

To make the output, you have to....make the entire output black. Then, you need to locate a block that is the only color in the input and place it in the same position. Surround the block with red blocks until it forms a square.

321b1fc6.rule:
In the input, you should see...a black grid with four different structures. Three are the same color and one is multi-colored.

The output grid size...stays the same.

To make the output, you have to...change the colors of all the single-colored structures to the multi-colors. Then change the original multi-colored structure to all black.

32597951.rule:
In the input, you should see... an incomplete rectangle or square

The output grid size...same as the input size

To make the output, you have to...replace the blue squares with green squares to complete a square of a rectangle with the light blue blocks

3345333e.rule:
In the input, you should see...a grid of black cells and other cells colored with up to two different colors. One of the colors composes some kind of object supposed to have a vertical symmetry axis, but the other color makes a rectangle that partially overlaps that object.
The output grid size...stays the same.
To make the output, you have to...remove entirely the colored rectangle and restore the vertical symmetry of the occluded object, by filling in with its color or black cells the cells where the rectangle was.
3345333e.author: Adrien

3428a4f5.rule: The input is a 5×13 grid. It contains two 5×6 red-and-black patterns separated by a horizontal yellow line. Create a 5×6 output by comparing the two patterns cell by cell. Make a cell green when exactly one of the two matching cells is red. Make it black when both matching cells are the same (either both black or both red).
3428a4f5.author: Philipp

3618c87e.rule:
In the input, you should see... two blue colored grids on top of the grey grids, a black grid is between the two blue grids

The output grid size...the two blue grids have been moved two steps downwards

To make the output, you have to...change blue grids to black background, count two steps below each grid's initial placement and fill with blue

3631a71a.rule:
In the input, you should see...a large grid with a multicolored pattern. Notice that the pattern is mirrored horizontally and vertically.

The output grid size...stays the same.

To make the output, you have to...Copy the input grid to the output grid. You will see boxes where the pattern is missing. In these boxes, mirror the pattern from the opposite side of the grid, exactly. Use the same colors.

363442ee.rule:
In the input, you should see... a pattern on the left, a grey bar and blue squares on the right

The output grid size... is the same as the input

To make the output, you have to... copy the pattern on the left and recreate the same pattern over each blue square on the right side, such that the center of the pattern is where the blue square was

36d67576.rule:
In the input, you should see...Yellow patterns with a single red square on each and one yellow shape with blue and green squares.

The output grid size...Copy grid size

To make the output, you have to...Repeat pattern shown on single yellow pattern onto others

36fdfd69.rule:
In the input, you should see... a grid with many squares in one color and a smaller number of squares in red.

The output grid size... is the same as the input grid

To make the output, you have to... copy the input grid. Connect the red squares with yellow to create yellow and red rectangles or squares. Only connect red squares that are close together. Do not turn any black squares yellow - only connect red squares that you can connect by making the other color in the grid yellow. The output grid will have more than one yellow and red rectangle or square.

3906de3d.rule:
In the input, you should see...a black grid with a blue pattern across the top and red at the bottom

The output grid size...same as the input

To make the output, you have to...imagine the blue is a vacuum and sucks the red up into the open spaces.  Move all red straight up.

39a8645d.rule:
In the input, you should see... a few different kinds of 3x3 shape. Each kind should have a unique shape and color. There may be multiple copies of each kind.

The output grid size... is 3x3

To make the output, you have to... count the number of copies of each shape. Zoom in on the shape with the most copies.

39e1d7f9.rule:
In the input, you should see...a grid of pixel lines within the overall grid.

The output grid size...same as the same

To make the output, you have to...copy the input grid, replicate the main pixel placement within the grid and replicate half at the top right corner.

3aa6fb7a.rule:
In the input, you should see...three incomplete squares that are each missing a corner.

The output grid size...is identical

To make the output, you have to...fill in the missing corners with a blue square.

3ac3eb23.rule:
In the input, you should see...a grid with a unicolored background and a few single colored cells.

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid size.

To make the output, you have to...expand the colored shapes into a predefined pattern, which is 0-C-0, C-0-C, 0-C-0 and so forth until the border, where C is the relevant color and the first row is 0-C-0.
3ac3eb23.author: Claas

3af2c5a8.rule:
In the input, you should see...pattern of color squares.

The output grid size...change to 8x6.

To make the output, you have to...imagine grid is cut in half vertical. Copy pattern to top and below left half. Mirror pattern to right half of grid to top and below.

3bd67248.rule:
In the input, you should see... a colored line on the left side of the grid.

The output grid size... is the same as the input grid.

To make the output, you have to... copy the input grid. Fill in all of the squares on the bottom row of the grid with yellow. Then draw a red line diagonal from the black square in the bottom left up to the top right of the grid. Do not change the bottom left color when you draw the yellow and red lines; the yellow and red lines each begin in the second column of the grid.

3bdb4ada.rule:
In the input, you should see...large rectangle shapes.

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid size.

First, a 45-degree diagonal line is drawn, bisecting the grid (and forming the grid's axis of symmetry); then, diagonal lines of slopes 2 and 1/2 are drawn using a different color and the area between them filled with that color (without overwriting any previously colored cells); then, diagonal lines of slopes 3 and 1/3 are drawn with a different color and the uncolored area between them filled with that color; and so on, until the entire grid has been colored this way, leaving no blank areas left. Finally, several "holes" are cut in the grid using black, interrupting the pattern and making it incomplete. The output grid shows the completed grid with the black "holes" filled in according to the original pattern.

00dbd492.rule:
The input grid contains one or more rectangles outlined entirely in red (R) cells. Each rectangle's border is a complete, axis-aligned loop of R cells. The interior of each rectangle (the cells enclosed by the red border) is filled with black (.) cells except for exactly one red (R) cell somewhere inside, which serves as a marker. The rest of the grid outside the rectangles is black (.) background.

For each red-bordered rectangle in the grid: (1) Measure the interior dimensions — that is, the width and height of the space enclosed by the red border, not counting the border itself. (2) Based on the interior size, choose a fill color: 3×3 interior → azure (A), 5×5 interior → yellow (Y), 7×7 interior → green (G). (3) Replace every black (.) cell inside the rectangle's border with the chosen fill color. (4) Leave the single red (R) marker cell inside the rectangle unchanged. (5) Leave the red border itself and all cells outside rectangles unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly. The background is black (.). All rectangles have square interiors with odd side lengths (3, 5, or 7). Red (R) cells form the borders and interior markers and remain unchanged in the output. The only change is that interior black cells become azure, yellow, or green depending on the rectangle's interior size.

03560426.rule:
The input grid contains several colored rectangular blocks arranged along the bottom rows, ordered from left to right with single-column gaps of black (.) cells between them. Each block is a solid rectangle of a single color. The rest of the grid above the blocks is entirely black (.).

1. Identify all distinct colored rectangular blocks in the input, ordered from left to right by their horizontal position. Note each block's width and height. 2. Place the blocks in a diagonal chain starting from the top-left corner of the grid (row 0, column 0). 3. Place the first block so its top-left corner is at (row 0, col 0). 4. For each subsequent block, position its top-left corner at the bottom-right corner of the previous block. The bottom-right corner is defined as (top_row + height - 1, left_col + width - 1) of the previous block — the next block's top-left goes exactly there. 5. Where two blocks share a cell (the overlap at the junction point), the later block's color overwrites the earlier one. 6. Fill all remaining cells with black (.).

The grid dimensions remain the same as the input (10x10). The background is black (.). Blocks are repositioned but retain their original shape and color.

05a7bcf2.rule:
The input grid (30x30, black background) contains three colored elements: (1) A continuous azure (A) line that spans the full width or height of the grid, dividing it into two halves — it can be vertical or horizontal. (2) On one side of the A line, a continuous red (R) line runs parallel to A, also spanning full width or height. Additional R cells extend from this R base line toward the A line, forming a jagged profile — the number of R cells varies per row (if lines are vertical) or per column (if lines are horizontal). (3) On the opposite side of the A line from R, scattered yellow (Y) shapes of various sizes and positions appear against the black background.

For each row (if the A/R lines are vertical) or column (if the A/R lines are horizontal) that contains any yellow (Y) cell, apply this transformation to that entire row or column:

1. Replace every Y cell with green (G), keeping each G at its original Y position.
2. Fill yellow (Y) into every empty cell between the G cells and the A line (the gap between the nearest G and the A line position, exclusive of G, inclusive up to and not including A).
3. Count the total number of R cells on that same row/column in the input (this includes the R base line cell plus any extension cells toward A). Place that same number of R cells at the far grid edge on the R side of A (i.e., push the R profile to the boundary of the grid).
4. Fill azure (A) into all cells between the repositioned R cells and the A line position (inclusive of the A line position itself, filling the entire gap between R at the edge and the original A line).
5. Cells beyond the G positions (on the side away from A) remain unchanged.

Rows or columns that contain no Y cells are left completely unchanged.

30x30 grid with black (.) background. The azure (A) and red (R) lines are always parallel to each other — both vertical or both horizontal. The A line is always exactly one cell thick and spans the full dimension. The R line is also one cell thick spanning the full dimension, with variable-length extensions protruding toward A. Yellow shapes appear only on the opposite side of A from R. Green does not appear in the input; it is produced only by the transformation.

0692e18c.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid containing some cells filled with a single foreground color and the remaining cells black (empty).

First, create the inverse of the input grid: swap every foreground-colored cell to black and every black cell to the foreground color. This produces a 3×3 'stamp' pattern. Next, construct a 9×9 output grid initialized to all black. For each cell in the original input that contains the foreground color, place a copy of the stamp pattern into the corresponding 3×3 block of the output grid. The output is a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks; the block at row r, column c corresponds to input cell (r, c). Blocks corresponding to black input cells remain all black.

The input grid is always 3×3. The output grid is always 9×9, composed of a 3×3 tiling of 3×3 blocks. The background color is black (.). Only one foreground color appears in any given puzzle.

070dd51e.rule:
The input is a grid containing empty cells and colored cells, two per color present in the grid. The cells sharing a color are either on the same row or in the same column in the grid, with a variable number of only empty cells between them.
To produce the output grid, first copy the input grid. Then, for each pair of cells sharing the same color and aligned in the same row, fill in the cells between them with that same color, in order to connect them with a line. Finally, proceed in the same way for the pairs aligned in the same column, overwriting any color that may already be present.
070dd51e.author: Adrien

0b17323b.rule:
The input grid contains a small number of blue (B) dots placed on a black (.) background. These blue dots form a diagonal line with a constant step size: each consecutive blue dot is offset from the previous one by the same number of rows down and the same number of columns to the right.

1. Identify all blue (B) cells and sort them by row (or equivalently by column, since they lie on a diagonal). 2. Compute the constant step between consecutive blue dots: Δrow = row difference, Δcol = column difference. 3. Starting from the last blue dot, repeatedly add (Δrow, Δcol) to generate new positions. 4. For each new position that falls within the grid boundaries, place a red (R) dot. Continue until the next position would fall outside the grid. 5. Leave all existing blue dots and the black background unchanged.

The grid is 15 rows by 15 columns with a black (.) background. Blue dots appear at regular diagonal intervals. The grid uses a 0-indexed coordinate system with (0,0) at the top-left corner.

0bb8deee.rule:
The input grid is divided into four quadrants by a vertical line and a horizontal line of the same color (e.g., blue, red, or green). These divider lines span the full width and height of the grid and intersect at one point, forming a cross. Each of the four quadrants (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) contains exactly one small shape composed of a unique color, set against a black background. Each shape fits within a 3×3 bounding box.

1. Identify the two divider lines: one vertical column and one horizontal row, both filled with the same color. These lines partition the grid into four quadrants. 2. In each quadrant, locate the single non-black, non-divider-colored shape. 3. Extract each shape by cropping it to its minimal 3×3 bounding box. 4. Construct a 6×6 output grid by tiling the four 3×3 extracted shapes: place the top-left quadrant's shape in the top-left 3×3 block, the top-right quadrant's shape in the top-right 3×3 block, the bottom-left quadrant's shape in the bottom-left 3×3 block, and the bottom-right quadrant's shape in the bottom-right 3×3 block.

The input grid is rectangular with a single-color vertical line and a single-color horizontal line acting as dividers that span the full grid, intersecting to create four quadrants. The background is black (color 0). The output grid is always 6 rows by 6 columns, composed of the four 3×3 shape bounding boxes tiled in a 2×2 arrangement matching the spatial layout of the quadrants.

0c786b71.rule:
The input is a small rectangular grid (R rows × C columns) filled with colored cells. There are no special regions or background — every cell carries a meaningful color value.

Create an output grid of size (2R) × (2C) by tiling four transformed copies of the input in a 2×2 arrangement: (1) Top-left quadrant: rotate the input 180° (reverse both row order and column order). (2) Top-right quadrant: flip the input vertically (reverse the row order, keeping columns intact). (3) Bottom-left quadrant: flip the input horizontally (reverse the column order, keeping row order intact). (4) Bottom-right quadrant: place the original input unchanged. Equivalently, the output is the input reflected across both its bottom edge and its right edge to produce a point-symmetric 2×2 tiling.

The input grid has dimensions R × C (in the observed instances, 3 × 4). The output grid has dimensions 2R × 2C (6 × 8). The output is partitioned into exactly four quadrants, each the same size as the input. The center of the output is the point of 180° rotational symmetry.

0c9aba6e.rule:
The input grid is divided into three vertical sections by a horizontal row of orange (O) cells. Above the orange separator is a 6-row binary mask using red (R) cells and black (.) cells. Below the orange separator is a 6-row binary mask of the same dimensions using magenta (M) cells and black (.) cells. Both masks share the same width (4 columns) and height (6 rows).

Remove the orange separator row. Compare the red mask and the magenta mask cell by cell, position by position. For each cell: if the cell is empty (black/dot) in BOTH the red mask AND the magenta mask, place an azure (A) cell at that position in the output. Otherwise, place a black (.) cell. The output grid has the same dimensions as either individual mask (6 rows by 4 columns).

The input grid is 13 rows by 4 columns: 6 rows for the red mask, 1 row of orange separator, and 6 rows for the magenta mask. The output grid is 6 rows by 4 columns, containing only azure (A) and black (.) cells.

0d87d2a6.rule: The input contains red rectangles and single-marker blue cells placed along the outer edges of the grid. When a blue cell is placed on one edge of the grid, there is also a blue cell at the corresponding position on the opposite edge. The output grid size stays the same.  Connect blue cells on opposite edges. Connect left and right cells with a horizontal blue line, and top and bottom cells with a vertical blue line. Any red rectangle crossed by one of these lines becomes blue. Everything else stays unchanged.
0d87d2a6.author: Philipp

0e671a1a.rule:
The input grid contains exactly three colored cells on a black background: one yellow (Y), one red (R), and one green (G). These three points form the vertices of an axis-aligned rectangle (with sides parallel to the grid edges). Yellow always occupies one corner of this implied rectangle, while red and green occupy two other corners — specifically, one shares yellow's row and the other shares yellow's column (or equivalently, red and green each share exactly one coordinate with yellow).

Draw two L-shaped paths of grey (X) cells connecting yellow to each of the other two colored points, routed through the corner of the implied rectangle diagonally opposite yellow. Specifically: (1) Identify the fourth corner of the axis-aligned rectangle defined by the three colored points — this is the intersection of the row/column of R and G that yellow does not occupy. (2) From yellow to green: draw grey cells along the row from yellow toward green's column (stopping at green's column), then along that column from yellow's row toward green (stopping at green). (3) From yellow to red: draw grey cells along the column from yellow toward red's row (stopping at red's row), then along that row from yellow's column toward red (stopping at red). Both L-shaped paths share the segment from yellow to the opposite corner, forming a cross or T-junction at that corner. The three original colored cells (Y, R, G) remain unchanged and are not overwritten. Only black cells along the paths become grey.

The grid is 13 columns by 13 rows. The background is black (.). The grid dimensions and background remain unchanged in the output. Coordinates can be referenced as (row, column) starting from (0,0) at the top-left.

0f63c0b9.rule:
The input is a 15x15 grid with a black background containing several single colored pixels (dots) scattered at various positions. Each dot is a different color. The dots' row positions determine how the output grid is partitioned into horizontal bands.

1. Identify all colored dots in the input grid and record each dot's color and row index. Ignore column positions.
2. Sort the dots by row index from top to bottom.
3. Partition the 15 rows into consecutive bands by computing midpoints between adjacent dots' row indices. The boundary between two adjacent dots at rows r1 and r2 is floor((r1 + r2) / 2) + 1, meaning the first band ends at row floor((r1+r2)/2) and the next band starts at floor((r1+r2)/2)+1. The topmost band starts at row 0 and the bottommost band ends at row 14.
4. For each band, fill it with its dot's color as follows:
   a. The row where the dot originally sat becomes a full solid horizontal line (all 15 cells filled with the dot's color).
   b. The first and last rows of the entire grid (row 0 and row 14), if they fall within this band, also become full solid horizontal lines of the dot's color.
   c. All other rows in the band become border rows: only the leftmost cell (column 0) and rightmost cell (column 14) are filled with the dot's color; the interior cells (columns 1-13) remain black.

Both input and output grids are 15x15. The background color is black (.). The input contains exactly N single-colored pixels (N varies per puzzle instance) placed at distinct positions. The output uses the full 15x15 grid, partitioned into N horizontal bands with no gaps or overlaps, each rendered as a rectangular frame segment in the corresponding dot's color.

11e1fe23.rule:
a few scattered colored cells on a unicolored background.

there is a unique center of the colored cells, to which each colored cell has a diagonal offset. move diagonally from each colored cell until you are one cell away from the unique center cell. This cell is colored in the color of the starting cell. The unique center cell is colored grey.

The input and output grid have the same shape.
11e1fe23.author: Claas

137f0df0.rule:
The input is a 10×10 grid with black (.) background containing several 2×2 grey (X) blocks arranged in a semi-regular grid pattern. The blocks are separated by gap rows and gap columns of black cells. Some gaps appear between adjacent blocks (interior gaps), while other gaps appear at the edges of the grid beyond the outermost blocks (edge gaps). The blocks always come in 2×2 squares, and the gaps between them are either 1 or 2 cells wide. The arrangement varies per instance — blocks may be shifted, and edge gaps may appear on different sides.

1. Identify all 2×2 grey (X) blocks and determine which rows and columns they occupy (block rows and block columns). 2. Identify interior gap rows: rows that lie between two groups of block rows (i.e., rows that separate vertically adjacent blocks). Similarly identify interior gap columns: columns that lie between two groups of block columns. 3. Identify edge gap rows: rows that are outside the span of all block rows (above the topmost or below the bottommost blocks). Similarly identify edge gap columns. 4. Fill with red (R) every cell that is at the intersection of: (a) an interior gap row and any block column or interior gap column, OR (b) a block row and an interior gap column, OR (c) an interior gap row and an interior gap column. In short, fill all interior gaps — both between blocks and at gap-line crossings — with red. 5. Fill with blue (B) every cell that is at the intersection of an edge gap row/column with an interior gap column/row. Specifically: if a cell is on an edge gap row AND on an interior gap column, make it blue; if a cell is on an edge gap column AND on an interior gap row, make it blue. 6. All remaining cells (edge×edge intersections, edge×block intersections, and original X cells) stay unchanged.

The grid is always 10×10. The background color is black (.). Grey (X) blocks are always exactly 2×2. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. Two new colors are introduced in the output: red (R) for interior gap fills and blue (B) for edge extensions of interior gap lines. The original grey blocks remain unchanged in place.

13f06aa5.rule:
The input grid has a uniform background color filling most cells. Embedded in the grid are one or more small cross-shaped or T-shaped figures composed of a secondary color. Each figure contains exactly one cell of a unique 'special' color (different from both the background and the figure's main color). The special color cell is positioned at one edge of its figure — top, bottom, left, or right — indicating a direction pointing outward from the figure toward the nearest grid border.

For each figure: (1) Identify the special color cell and determine which edge of the figure it occupies — this gives the direction the special color 'fires' toward the nearest border. (2) Starting from the special color cell, place a dot of that special color every 2 cells along the firing direction (skipping one cell, coloring the next, repeating) until reaching the grid border. (3) Fill the entire border wall that the ray hits with the special color (the full row if firing up/down, or the full column if firing left/right). (4) Where two colored border walls meet at a corner cell, set that corner cell to black (.). All other cells remain unchanged.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. The background and all embedded figures remain in place. The only additions are: colored border walls along edges where rays terminate, ray dots every 2 cells between figures and their target borders, and black corner cells where two colored borders intersect.

140c817e.rule:
The input grid has a uniform background color with several blue (B) cells scattered at various positions. These blue cells serve as seed points for a cross-based transformation.

For each blue (B) cell in the input: (1) Extend a full cross from that cell — fill its entire row and entire column with blue (B). (2) Replace the original B cell itself with red (R). (3) Place green (G) on the four diagonal neighbors of the original B position (one step up-left, up-right, down-left, down-right), but only if that diagonal cell falls within grid bounds. When a cell would receive both a green (G) marking and lies on a blue cross line from another seed, blue takes priority — blue crosses override green. Red and green never conflict since green is placed on diagonals while red sits at cross intersections. All cells not affected by any of these rules remain the background color.

The grid dimensions are the same in input and output. The background is a single uniform color (whichever non-blue color fills the input). The coordinate system is row-column with (0,0) at top-left. Grids can be any rectangular size. Blue seed points can appear anywhere in the grid.

15663ba9.rule: The input grid contains one or more hollow shapes composed of straight lines and 90-degree bends. In the output grid, bends in the interior of the hollow outlines are colored red, and bends on the exterior are colored yellow. Formulated another way, imagine moving along each hollow border as a closed loop, traveling clockwise, by following each straight segment and making 90-degree turns left or right. For each cell where you must turn left as you circumnavigate clockwise, color that cell in the output red; for each cell where you must turn right, color that cell in the output yellow. Do so for all closed loops in the grid.
15663ba9.author: Ryan

15696249.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid. Exactly one row or one column is filled with a single uniform color (all three cells are the same color). The remaining cells contain a mix of other colors.

1. Identify the uniform line: find the row or column where all three cells share the same color. Note whether it is a row (top=0, middle=1, bottom=2) or a column (left=0, middle=1, right=2). 2. Create a 9×9 output grid filled entirely with black (.). 3. If the uniform line is a row at position R (0, 1, or 2): copy the entire 3×3 input into the output three times side by side, placing them in output rows R×3 through R×3+2, spanning all 9 columns. 4. If the uniform line is a column at position C (0, 1, or 2): copy the entire 3×3 input into the output three times stacked vertically, placing them in output columns C×3 through C×3+2, spanning all 9 rows.

The input grid is always 3×3. The output grid is always 9×9 (a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks). The background fill is black (.). The 3×3 input is tiled three times along the axis indicated by the uniform row or column, placed in the corresponding strip of the 9×9 grid.

17b80ad2.rule:
The input grid contains a row near the bottom that has one or more X (grey) cells. These X cells mark specific columns as 'anchor columns.' Within each anchor column, scattered above the X cell, there are zero or more colored (non-black, non-X) cells at various row positions. The X cell itself sits at or near the bottom of the grid. All other cells in the grid (those not in anchor columns) contain various colored cells that are unrelated to the transformation.

1. Identify all X cells in the grid. They will appear in a single row near the bottom. Note which columns contain an X — these are the 'anchor columns,' and the row containing X is the 'anchor row.' 2. For each anchor column, collect every non-black cell in that column, including the X cell itself. Record each cell's color and row position. 3. Sort these colored cells by row position from bottom to top. The bottommost will be the X cell. 4. Fill the anchor column as follows: Starting from the X cell's row, fill downward to the last row of the grid with X. Then, working upward through the sorted list of colored markers, each color fills from its own original row upward to one row below the next color above it. The topmost colored marker extends upward from its original row all the way to row 0 (the top of the grid). 5. All cells outside of anchor columns remain exactly as they are in the input.

The grid dimensions match the input (variable size, up to 30x30). The background color is black (.). The coordinate system is row-column with row 0 at the top. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. Only the anchor columns (those containing X in the anchor row) are modified; all other columns are copied unchanged from input to output. The anchor row is typically the second-to-last or last row, identifiable by containing one or more X cells in a horizontal line.

17cae0c1.rule:
The input is a 3-row by 9-column grid divided into three 3×3 sections (left, middle, right). Each section contains a distinct pattern made of grey (X) pixels on a black (.) background. The five possible patterns are: (1) a full border frame with an empty center (8 grey cells: all cells except the center), (2) a single grey cell in the center position only, (3) a full top row of three grey cells with the rest black, (4) a full bottom row of three grey cells with the rest black, and (5) an anti-diagonal line of three grey cells running from top-right to bottom-left.

Divide the input grid into three 3×3 sections (columns 0-2, 3-5, 6-8). For each section, identify which of the five grey-pixel patterns it contains, then replace the entire 3×3 section with a solid block of the corresponding color: full border frame (8 cells) → green (G), single center cell (1 cell) → yellow (Y), top row filled (3 cells across the top) → magenta (M), bottom row filled (3 cells across the bottom) → blue (B), anti-diagonal (top-right, center, bottom-left) → maroon (W). The output grid has the same 3×9 dimensions with each 3×3 section uniformly filled with its mapped color.

Both input and output grids are 3 rows by 9 columns. The grid is logically partitioned into three equally sized 3×3 blocks arranged horizontally. The input uses only grey (X) and black (.) pixels. The output uses only solid-color 3×3 blocks drawn from the set {green, yellow, magenta, blue, maroon}, with each block's color determined by the shape pattern in the corresponding input block.

195ba7dc.rule:
The input is a rectangular grid composed of three colors: orange (O), black (.), and a single vertical column of red (R) that divides the grid into a left half and a right half of equal dimensions.

Remove the red divider column to obtain two equally-sized subgrids (left and right). Combine them cell by cell using a logical OR: if a cell is orange in the left subgrid, the right subgrid, or both, output blue (B). If the cell is black (.) in both subgrids, output black (.).

The input grid has dimensions R rows by (2C+1) columns, where the middle column is entirely red. The output grid has dimensions R rows by C columns, containing only blue (B) and black (.).

1990f7a8.rule:
The input is a large grid with a black (.) background containing exactly four small red (R) shapes, each fitting within a 3×3 bounding box. The four shapes are spatially distributed across the grid so that two appear in the upper portion and two in the lower portion, and within each vertical half, one is to the left and one is to the right. This gives four quadrant-based positions: upper-left, upper-right, lower-left, and lower-right. Each 3×3 shape is a distinct pattern of red and black cells.

1. Identify the four 3×3 red shapes in the input grid. Determine each shape's quadrant position (upper-left, upper-right, lower-left, lower-right) based on its relative location compared to the other shapes. 2. Extract each shape as a 3×3 subgrid of R and . cells. 3. Construct a 7×7 output grid by placing the four 3×3 shapes in a 2×2 arrangement: upper-left shape goes in rows 0-2, columns 0-2; upper-right shape goes in rows 0-2, columns 4-6; lower-left shape goes in rows 4-6, columns 0-2; lower-right shape goes in rows 4-6, columns 4-6. 4. Fill the separator row (row 3) entirely with black (.) and the separator column (column 3) entirely with black (.).

The output grid is always 7 columns wide and 7 rows tall. It consists of four 3×3 blocks arranged in a 2×2 layout, separated by a single-cell-wide black divider: column 3 is all black and row 3 is all black. The background color is black (.).

1a2e2828.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background with several colored stripes running across it. Each stripe is either a full row or a full column of a single non-black color. These stripes intersect each other, and at each intersection point, one stripe's color overwrites the other's — meaning one stripe passes through unbroken while the other is interrupted at that crossing.

Identify all colored stripes (complete rows or columns of a single color). For each stripe, check whether it is completely uninterrupted across its entire span — that is, every cell along that row or column contains that stripe's color with no exceptions. Most stripes will be interrupted at one or more intersection points where another stripe's color has overwritten theirs. Exactly one stripe will be fully intact, passing through every intersection without yielding its color. Output that stripe's color as a single cell.

The input is a rectangular grid of variable dimensions with black (.) as the background color. Non-black colors appear only as full-row or full-column stripes. The output is a single 1x1 cell containing the color of the one uninterrupted stripe.

1c56ad9f.rule:
The input grid has a black background with a single colored rectangle drawn in one non-black color. The rectangle is defined by solid border rows at the top and bottom, and solid border columns at the left and right, forming a grid-like structure. The interior is divided into cells by internal horizontal and vertical lines of the same color, with black cells filling the spaces between the lines. The rectangle can vary in size, position, number of internal divisions, and color.

Identify the rectangular structure and its top and bottom border rows. Let the bottom border row have distance d=0. For each row of the rectangle, compute d = (bottom_row - current_row). Shift the entire row's colored content horizontally according to d mod 4: if d mod 4 is 0, no shift; if d mod 4 is 1, shift left by 1; if d mod 4 is 2, no shift; if d mod 4 is 3, shift right by 1. Shifting means moving every cell in that row (both colored and the black cells between colored cells) by 1 position in the indicated direction. Vacated positions become black and content that moves fills its new position. All rows outside the rectangle remain unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly. The background is black (.). The colored rectangle occupies a contiguous region and is always axis-aligned. The grid is large enough that horizontal shifts of ±1 do not push content outside the grid boundaries.

1d398264.rule:
The input grid has a black background with a single 3x3 block of non-black colored cells. The block consists of nine distinct cells arranged in three rows: a top row, a middle row, and a bottom row, each containing three colored cells.

1. Locate the 3x3 block of non-black cells. Label its cells as: top-left (TL), top-center (TC), top-right (TR), mid-left (ML), center (C), mid-right (MR), bottom-left (BL), bottom-center (BC), bottom-right (BR).
2. The middle row becomes a horizontal axis spanning the full width of the grid. Fill every cell to the left of ML in that row with ML's color. Fill every cell to the right of MR in that row with MR's color. The center cell C remains unchanged.
3. From TC, draw a vertical ray upward (same column) using TC's color, extending to the top edge of the grid.
4. From TL, draw a diagonal ray going up-and-left (one step up, one step left per cell) using TL's color, until hitting a grid edge.
5. From TR, draw a diagonal ray going up-and-right (one step up, one step right per cell) using TR's color, until hitting a grid edge.
6. From BC, draw a vertical ray downward (same column) using BC's color, extending to the bottom edge of the grid.
7. From BL, draw a diagonal ray going down-and-left (one step down, one step left per cell) using BL's color, until hitting a grid edge.
8. From BR, draw a diagonal ray going down-and-right (one step down, one step right per cell) using BR's color, until hitting a grid edge.
9. The original 3x3 block cells remain in place. All other cells stay black.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. The background is black (.). The 3x3 block remains at its original position, with six rays emanating from the top and bottom rows and the middle row extended horizontally across the full grid width.

2072aba6.rule:
The input is a 3x3 grid containing grey (X) cells and black (.) cells. The grey cells form a pattern against the black background.

Create an output grid that is exactly twice the size of the input in both dimensions (so a 3x3 input becomes 6x6). Replace each cell in the input with a 2x2 block: each grey (X) cell becomes the 2x2 checkerboard pattern B R / R B (blue top-left, red top-right, red bottom-left, blue bottom-right). Each black (.) cell becomes a 2x2 block of all black (. . / . .).

The input is a 3x3 grid. The output is a 6x6 grid (2x the input dimensions in each direction). The background color is black (.). The output is composed entirely of 2x2 blocks, each corresponding to one cell of the input.

20981f0e.rule:
The grid contains a lattice of red (R) markers that form a regular grid of intersection points. These R markers divide the space into rectangular cells, each with a 4×4 interior region. Within each cell's interior, there is a small blue (B) shape consisting of 3 or 4 pixels, always fitting within a 2×2 bounding box (e.g., an L-shape, a full 2×2 square, etc.). The blue shapes appear at various positions within their respective cells — sometimes flush against an edge or corner, sometimes already centered. The rest of the grid is black (dot) background.

1. Identify all red (R) marker positions. They form a regular lattice of rows and columns, defining a grid of rectangular cells.
2. Determine the interior region of each cell: the 4×4 block of pixels strictly between adjacent R rows and adjacent R columns.
3. For each cell, locate the blue (B) pixels inside it. Extract the shape defined by those blue pixels (its 2×2 bounding box and the pattern of filled/empty pixels within that box).
4. Clear all blue pixels from the cell interior.
5. Place the extracted blue shape back into the cell, centered within the 4×4 interior. Specifically, position the shape's 2×2 bounding box at rows 1–2 and columns 1–2 of the cell's local 4×4 coordinate system (0-indexed). The shape's internal pattern (which corners are filled vs empty) is preserved exactly.
6. Leave all red markers and black background unchanged.

The grid dimensions vary but are always structured by a regular lattice of red (R) markers. R markers appear at evenly spaced rows and columns, creating a uniform tiling of cells. Each cell's interior is exactly 4×4 pixels. The background is black (.). Blue (B) pixels appear only inside cell interiors, never on or adjacent to the R lattice lines. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input.

20fb2937.rule:
The input grid has three sections. (1) A color palette in the top three rows: three 3x3 colored blocks positioned at column groups 0-2, 4-6, and 8-10, separated by orange (O) columns. (2) A key row (row 4) containing exactly three single-cell symbols, each positioned at the center column of one of the three color block zones (columns 1, 5, and 9). These symbols establish a mapping from symbol to color block. (3) A magenta (M) divider spanning the full width at row 6. Below the divider (rows 7 onward) is a canvas of orange (O) cells with scattered single-cell symbols — the same symbols that appear in the key row.

Step 1: Read the key row (row 4) to build a symbol-to-color mapping. The symbol at column 1 maps to the 3x3 color block at columns 0-2 (left block). The symbol at column 5 maps to the block at columns 4-6 (center block). The symbol at column 9 maps to the block at columns 8-10 (right block). Step 2: Extract the canvas region below the magenta divider — rows 7 through the last row. This becomes the basis for the output. Subtract 7 from each row index to get output row coordinates. Step 3: For each symbol found on the canvas, look up its mapped 3x3 color block. Place that 3x3 block centered on the symbol's position — meaning the symbol's (row, col) becomes the center cell, and the block fills a 3x3 area from (row-1, col-1) to (row+1, col+1) in output coordinates. Step 4: All non-symbol cells remain orange (O). Where 3x3 blocks overlap (if ever), later placements overwrite earlier ones.

The input grid is always 20 rows tall and 11 columns wide. The output grid is 13 rows tall (the canvas portion: input rows 7-19) and 11 columns wide. The background color is orange (O). The top section (rows 0-5) and divider (row 6) are consumed by the transformation and do not appear in the output. Column 3 and column 7 act as orange separators between the three color block zones in the palette.

21f83797.rule:
The input grid contains exactly two red cells on a black background. These two red cells define two distinct row positions and two distinct column positions, forming the corners of an implicit rectangle.

1. Locate the two red cells and note their row and column positions (r1, c1) and (r2, c2), where r1 < r2 and c1 < c2. 2. Draw full-width red horizontal lines across the entire grid at rows r1 and r2 (every cell in those rows becomes red). 3. Draw full-height red vertical lines down the entire grid at columns c1 and c2 (every cell in those columns becomes red). 4. Fill the interior rectangle — all cells with row strictly between r1 and r2 AND column strictly between c1 and c2 — with blue.

The grid dimensions remain the same as the input (13 columns by 13 rows). The background is black. The coordinate system is zero-indexed with row 0 at the top and column 0 at the left.

25e02866.rule:
The input grid has a uniform background color. Embedded in the background are several same-sized rectangles, all filled with a single shared border/fill color (distinct from the background). Each rectangle contains a small 'mark' — one or more cells of a unique color that differ from both the background and the rectangle fill color. The marks occupy different positions within their respective rectangles, and no two rectangles' marks overlap in relative position.

1. Identify the background color (the most common color in the grid). 2. Identify all rectangles of uniform non-background color; they will all be the same dimensions. 3. For each rectangle, find the cells whose color differs from the rectangle's fill color. Record each mark's color and its position relative to the rectangle's top-left corner. 4. Create an output grid matching the dimensions of one rectangle, filled entirely with the rectangle fill color. 5. Overlay every mark from every rectangle onto the output grid at its recorded relative position, replacing the fill color with the mark's color.

The output grid has the same dimensions as any one of the embedded rectangles (they are all identical in size). It is filled with the rectangle fill color, with all collected marks composited on top. The input grid is a larger rectangle whose exact dimensions can vary, containing an arbitrary number of same-sized sub-rectangles at arbitrary positions.

2601afb7.rule:
The grid has an orange (O) background. Vertical bars of a single non-orange color occupy every other column (odd-indexed columns: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …). Each bar is anchored to the bottom row and extends upward for some height. Different bars have different colors and different heights. Even-indexed columns (0, 2, 4, …) are entirely orange and serve as separators.

1. Identify all vertical bars on odd-indexed columns. For each bar, record its color and its height (number of consecutive non-orange cells from the bottom up). 2. List the bars in order from left to right. 3. Rotate the sequence of colors one position to the RIGHT (the rightmost bar's color wraps around to become the leftmost bar's color). 4. Simultaneously rotate the sequence of heights one position to the LEFT (the leftmost bar's height wraps around to become the rightmost bar's height). 5. Redraw the grid: assign each bar position its new color and new height, filling from the bottom up, with all remaining cells orange.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly (same number of rows and columns). The background color is orange (O). Bars exist only on odd-indexed columns (1, 3, 5, …), and even-indexed columns remain entirely orange. Each bar is a contiguous vertical stripe of one color anchored to the bottom edge.

2685904e.rule:
The input is a 10-row by 10-column grid with three key regions. Row 0 contains some number N of azure (A) cells starting from the left, with the rest black. Rows 1-5 are entirely black (empty canvas). Row 6 is a solid horizontal barrier of grey (X) cells spanning the full width. Row 7 is entirely black. Row 8 contains a sequence of 10 colored cells (various non-black, non-grey colors). Row 9 is entirely black. The colors in row 8 each appear some number of times across the 10 columns.

1. Count N, the number of azure (A) cells in row 0. 2. Examine the 10 colors in row 8. For each distinct color, count how many times it appears across the 10 columns. 3. Identify which colors appear exactly N times. 4. For each color that appears exactly N times, find every column where that color occurs in row 8. In each of those columns, fill that color into the N rows immediately above the grey barrier — that is, rows (6-N) through (6-1). 5. All other cells in rows 1-5 remain black. Rows 0, 6, 7, 8, and 9 are unchanged.

The grid is always 10 rows by 10 columns. The background color is black (.). Row 6 is always a full-width grey (X) barrier dividing the grid into an upper region (rows 0-5) and a lower region (rows 7-9). Row 0 holds the azure count indicator. Row 8 holds the color pattern. Rows 1-5 are the working area where selected colors get projected upward from row 8, filling downward from row 5 toward row (6-N).

2753e76c.rule:
The input grid has a black background with several colored rectangles scattered across it. Each rectangle is a solid block of a single color (e.g., green, yellow, azure, red, blue) and can be any size (2×2, 3×3, 4×4, 2×3, etc.). Multiple rectangles may share the same color but appear as separate, non-touching blocks at different positions in the grid.

1. Identify every distinct contiguous rectangle of non-black color in the input grid. Two blocks of the same color that do not touch are separate rectangles. 2. Count how many rectangles exist for each color. 3. Rank the colors from most rectangles to fewest. 4. Determine the output width as the maximum rectangle count across all colors. The output height equals the number of distinct colors present. 5. Build the output grid as a right-aligned staircase: the top row corresponds to the color with the most rectangles and is fully filled (width cells of that color). Each subsequent row corresponds to the next color in descending count order, with that many cells of its color right-justified in the row (padded with black on the left). The result is a staircase descending from upper-right to lower-left.

The output grid has width equal to the largest rectangle count among all colors and height equal to the number of distinct colors. The background is black (.). Each row contains one color, right-aligned, with the number of colored cells equal to that color's rectangle count. Rows are ordered top-to-bottom from highest count to lowest count.

27a77e38.rule:
The input grid has an odd number of cells and is a square. The top half of the square will be colored completely with different non-grey colors. The center row of the square will be colored completely in grey.
Create an exact copy of the input grid. Then identify the color that appears the most number of times in the top half of the input grid, and color the center cell of the bottommost row in the copy (the output) in that color.
The output grid will be the exact same size as the input. Every cell except the center cell of the bottommost row, which is colored according to the frequency rule, will be the exact same as the input grid.
27a77e38.author: Navya

27f8ce4f.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid containing cells of various colors. One color appears more frequently than all others — this is the dominant color. The positions of the dominant color within the 3×3 grid serve as a placement map.

1. Count the occurrences of each color in the 3×3 input grid and identify the most frequent color (the dominant color). 2. Create a 9×9 output grid filled entirely with black (dot) cells. Conceptually divide this output into a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks, where block (r, c) occupies rows r*3 through r*3+2 and columns c*3 through c*3+2. 3. For each cell in the input grid that contains the dominant color, place a full copy of the original 3×3 input into the corresponding block position in the output. All other blocks remain black.

The input is always a 3×3 grid with colors from the ARC palette (values 0–9). The output is always a 9×9 grid (3× the input dimensions in each direction), with black (.) as the background fill. The output is conceptually a 3×3 tiling of 3×3 blocks, where each block either contains a copy of the input or is entirely black.

281123b4.rule:
The input grid consists of four 4×4 panels arranged side by side, separated by single green (G) columns. Each panel is associated with a distinct color: the first panel uses azure (A), the second uses grey (X), the third uses maroon (W), and the fourth uses yellow (Y). Within each panel, some cells are filled with that panel's color and some are empty (black/.).

Construct a 4×4 output grid. For each cell position (row, column), check which of the four panels have a filled (non-empty) cell at that same position. Among the panels that are filled at that position, select the color with the highest priority according to this fixed ranking: W (maroon) > Y (yellow) > A (azure) > X (grey). Place that color in the output cell. If no panel is filled at that position, output black (.).

The input is a 4×19 grid composed of four 4×4 colored panels separated by three single-column green (G) dividers. The output is a single 4×4 grid. The panels and output share the same row-column coordinate system, so position (r, c) in the output corresponds to position (r, c) within each panel.

29700607.rule:
The input grid has a black background with two key features: (1) A horizontal 'header segment' of exactly 3 consecutive colored pixels in row 0, and (2) scattered 'anchor' pixels elsewhere in the grid, each matching one of the header colors. Each anchor pixel appears at most once per header color. Some header colors may have no corresponding anchor pixel.

For each of the 3 header colors, from left to right occupying columns L, M, R in row 0: (1) Find whether an anchor pixel of that color exists elsewhere in the grid. (2) If an anchor exists at position (row_a, col_a): fill that color's header column from row 0 down through row_a, then fill row_a horizontally from col_a to the header column (inclusive), connecting the anchor to the column. (3) If no anchor exists for that color: extend that color's header column from row 0 all the way down to the last row of the grid. All other cells remain black.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly (no resizing). The background is black (.). Row 0 contains a contiguous 3-pixel colored segment; the rest of the grid is black except for isolated anchor pixels. The coordinate system is row-major with (0,0) at the top-left.

2c737e39.rule:
The input grid contains exactly two grey (X) cells. One X is embedded within a multi-colored pattern of adjacent non-background cells — this is the 'template X.' The other X stands alone with no colored neighbors — this is the 'anchor X.' The template pattern consists of the template X plus all colored (non-black, non-X) cells that form a connected cluster around it.

1. Identify the two X cells. The template X is the one adjacent to or surrounded by other colored cells; the anchor X is the isolated one. 2. For every colored (non-black) cell in the template pattern (excluding the template X itself), compute its row and column offset relative to the template X's position. 3. For each such offset, place the same color at the corresponding offset from the anchor X's position. 4. Replace the anchor X itself with background (black/dot) — do not copy X to the new location. 5. Leave the original template pattern (including its X) unchanged in place.
