The grid dimensions match the input (variable size, rectangular). The background color is black (.). The grid uses a standard row-column coordinate system with (0,0) at the top-left. The copied pattern must fit within the grid boundaries.

310f3251.rule:
The input is a small grid (H rows × W columns) with a black (.) background containing one or more colored cells (non-black, non-red) at various positions.

1. Start with the input grid (H × W). 2. For each colored (non-black) cell at position (r, c), place a red (R) cell at the position one step diagonally up-left, wrapping around the grid edges: ((r−1) mod H, (c−1) mod W). This red cell is added to the grid without removing anything. 3. Tile this modified grid in a 3×3 arrangement to produce the output grid of size 3H × 3W. Each tile is an identical copy of the modified grid, laid out in a regular 3-row by 3-column grid of tiles.

The output grid has dimensions 3H × 3W, where H and W are the height and width of the input grid. The background is black (.). The output consists of 9 identical tiles arranged 3×3, each tile being the input grid augmented with red markers at the wrapped diagonal-up-left neighbor of every colored cell.

31d5ba1a.rule:
The input is a 6-row by 5-column grid divided into two halves. The top half (rows 1-3) contains a pattern of maroon (W) cells on a black (.) background. The bottom half (rows 4-6) contains a pattern of yellow (Y) cells on a black (.) background. Each half acts as a binary mask over the same 3×5 grid positions.

Produce a 3×5 output grid by comparing the top half (W mask) and bottom half (Y mask) cell by cell at each corresponding position. Apply an XOR rule: if exactly one of the two cells is colored (W in the top half or Y in the bottom half) and the other is black, output magenta (M). If both are colored or both are black, output black (.). In other words, M appears only where W and Y disagree.

The output grid is 3 rows by 5 columns, matching the dimensions of each half of the input. It uses only two values: magenta (M) for active cells and black (.) for inactive cells.

32e9702f.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background with one or more horizontal contiguous segments of a single non-black color. Each segment sits in its own row; no row contains more than one segment. The segments vary in length and horizontal position.

1. Replace every black (.) cell in the grid with grey (X). 2. For each horizontal contiguous colored segment, shift it one position to the left. If the segment already touches the left edge (column 0), it loses its rightmost cell (the segment shrinks by one on the right) rather than extending beyond the grid boundary. The colored cells overwrite the grey cells at their new positions.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. The background is grey (X) instead of black. All colored segments remain horizontal and in their original rows, each shifted one column to the left (or clipped on the right if already at the left edge).

332efdb3.rule:
The input is a uniformly black grid of odd width and odd height, filled entirely with black (.) cells.

Replace every cell in the grid with blue (B) if the cell is in an even-numbered row (0-indexed) OR in an even-numbered column. Leave the cell black (.) only when both its row index and column index are odd. Equivalently: fill all even rows entirely with blue, and in odd rows alternate blue and black starting with blue in column 0.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. Both width and height are always odd numbers. The grid uses only two colors: blue (B) and black (.).

342ae2ed.rule:
A grid with a uniform background color and colored shapes. For each color, except for the background color, there should be two shapes.

Connect shapes with the same color using a diagonal line of the same color, starting from the corners.

The output grid has the same size as the input grid.
342ae2ed.author: Claas

3490cc26.rule:
The input is a grid containing empty cells and colored cells. The colored cells form non-adjacent 2x2 colored squares. One is red, all the others are cyan. The red square spans the same two rows or the same two columns as at least one cyan square.
To produce the output grid, first copy the input grid. Then, fill in the cells between the red square and its closest (in the same rows or columns) cyan square, in orange. Repeat the process with that cyan square as new starting point, that is, fill in the cells between it and its closest cyan square (in the same rows or columns) in orange. Iterate until no cyan square spans the same rows or columns as the latest reached cyan square.
3490cc26.author: Adrien

34b99a2b.rule:
The input grid contains a single vertical column of yellow (Y) cells that divides the grid into two equal halves: a left half and a right half. The left half contains azure (A) cells and black (.) background cells. The right half contains grey (X) cells and black (.) background cells.

Remove the yellow divider column and compare the left and right halves cell by cell. For each position, apply an XOR rule: if exactly one of the two sides has a colored cell (A on the left or X on the right) and the other side is black (.), output red (R). If both sides have a colored cell or both sides are black, output black (.). The result is a grid with only red (R) and black (.) cells.

The output grid has the same number of rows as the input and a width equal to half the input width minus the divider column. For example, a 5×9 input with a 1-cell-wide divider produces a 5×4 output. The background is black (.) and the only foreground color is red (R).

37ce87bb.rule:
The grid has an orange (O) background. Vertical bars of azure (A) and red (R) cells grow upward from the bottom row. These bars are always located at odd-numbered columns (0-indexed: columns 1, 3, 5, 7, …). Each bar is a contiguous vertical strip of a single color anchored to the bottom edge of the grid. Some odd columns are empty (all orange). The bars vary in height (number of filled cells counting from the bottom row upward).

1. Identify every odd-numbered column (1, 3, 5, 7, …) that contains a vertical bar of azure (A) or red (R) cells rising from the bottom row. Record each bar's color and height (number of contiguous colored cells from the bottom). 2. Compute the sum of all azure bar heights and the sum of all red bar heights. 3. Calculate the result height: (sum of azure heights) minus (sum of red heights). 4. Find the first odd-numbered column (scanning left to right) that is entirely empty (all orange). 5. Place a grey (X) bar in that column, anchored to the bottom row, with height equal to the result calculated in step 3. All other cells remain unchanged.

The grid dimensions vary (rows and columns differ across instances). The background color is orange (O). Columns are 0-indexed. Bars only appear at odd-indexed columns. The grid is tall enough to accommodate all bars and the resulting grey bar. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid, with the only change being the addition of the grey (X) bar.

37d3e8b2.rule:
The input grid has a black background containing several distinct rectangular blocks made of azure (A) cells. These blocks are separated from each other by black space. Each block is a solid rectangle of azure cells, but with some internal cells that are black (holes or gaps within the block). The blocks vary in size and position across the grid.

For each azure block in the grid, identify all the black cells that are fully enclosed within the block's bounding rectangle (the internal holes). Count the number of connected components among these internal black cells, using 4-connectivity (up, down, left, right — not diagonal). Then recolor all azure cells in that block according to the number of connected hole components: 1 component → blue (B), 2 components → red (R), 3 components → green (G), 4 components → orange (O). The internal black holes remain black. The background remains black.

The grid dimensions vary but the background is always black (.). Azure blocks are axis-aligned rectangles whose outer boundary is entirely azure, with zero or more internal black holes. Blocks do not overlap or touch each other — there is always at least one column or row of black cells separating them.

3979b1a8.rule:
A 5×5 grid containing exactly three colors arranged in a concentric diamond pattern. The four corner cells (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) share one color — call this the 'corner color' (level 0). The central plus-sign shape (center cell plus its 4 orthogonal neighbors) uses a second color — the 'center color' (level 2). All remaining cells use a third color — the 'body color' (level 1). The pattern has 4-fold symmetry.

1. Identify the three colors and assign levels: corner color (the color at position (0,0)) = level 0, body color (the color at position (0,1)) = level 1, center color (the color at position (2,2)) = level 2.
2. Create a 10×10 output grid, divided into four 5×5 quadrants.
3. TOP-LEFT quadrant (rows 0–4, cols 0–4): Copy the original 5×5 input unchanged.
4. Define a 'band sequence' of 5 colors: band[k] is the color whose level equals (−k) mod 3. Concretely: band[0]=corner, band[1]=center, band[2]=body, band[3]=corner, band[4]=center.
5. TOP-RIGHT quadrant (rows 0–4, cols 5–9): Fill each column uniformly with the corresponding band color. Column 5 gets band[0], column 6 gets band[1], column 7 gets band[2], column 8 gets band[3], column 9 gets band[4].
6. BOTTOM-LEFT quadrant (rows 5–9, cols 0–4): Fill each row uniformly with the corresponding band color. Row 5 gets band[0], row 6 gets band[1], row 7 gets band[2], row 8 gets band[3], row 9 gets band[4].
7. BOTTOM-RIGHT quadrant (rows 5–9, cols 5–9): Use local coordinates i′=row−5, j′=col−5 (each 0–4). For off-diagonal cells (i′≠j′), set the color to band[max(i′,j′)]. For diagonal cells (i′=j′=k), set the color to the color whose level is (−k−1) mod 3. This produces a staircase of nested L-shapes using the band colors, with the diagonal shifted one level down.

Input is always a 5×5 grid with exactly three colors in the concentric diamond arrangement described above. Output is always a 10×10 grid (double the input dimensions in both directions). The four 5×5 quadrants tile the output: top-left is the original, top-right and bottom-left are uniform bands, and bottom-right is a staircase pattern. Colors 0–9 from the ARC palette may appear in any three-color combination maintaining the concentric diamond structure.

3d31c5b3.rule:
The input is a 12-row by 6-column grid divided into four equally-sized 3×6 horizontal layers stacked vertically. Each layer uses exactly one non-black color: the top layer (rows 1–3) is grey (X), the second layer (rows 4–6) is yellow (Y), the third layer (rows 7–9) is red (R), and the bottom layer (rows 10–12) is azure (A). Within each layer, some cells are filled with that layer's color and the rest are black (empty). The four layers share the same spatial dimensions and can be thought of as transparent overlays aligned on top of each other.

Produce a 3×6 output grid by compositing the four layers using a fixed priority rule. For each cell position (row, column) in the output: (1) If the grey (X) layer is filled at that position, the output cell is grey (X). (2) If the grey layer is empty at that position, check the remaining three layers in this strict priority order: yellow (Y) first, then azure (A), then red (R). Output the color of the highest-priority layer that is filled at that position. (3) If all four layers are empty at that position, the output cell is black (.). In short, grey always wins; among the remaining colors, yellow overrides azure, which overrides red.

The input grid is always 12 rows by 6 columns, composed of four 3×6 blocks stacked vertically in a fixed order: grey, yellow, red, azure (top to bottom). The output grid is always 3 rows by 6 columns. The background color is black (represented by '.'), and the ten possible ARC colors may appear but each layer uses exactly one non-black color. The coordinate system is row-major, with (0,0) at the top-left corner.

3d6c6e23.rule:
The input grid has a black background with one or more columns containing colored cells. Each such column has colored cells scattered vertically in its upper portion, separated by gaps of black cells, with empty space below. A column may contain cells of a single color or multiple colors. When multiple colors appear in a column, they are grouped contiguously from top to bottom (e.g., all red cells appear above all blue cells). The total number of colored cells in each column is always a perfect square (1, 4, 9, 16, ...).

For each column that contains colored cells, do the following independently: (1) Count the total number of colored cells N in that column. Compute the triangle size as sqrt(N), call it S. (2) Record the colors from top to bottom in the column, preserving their order. (3) Clear the entire column. (4) Build a triangle of S rows at the very bottom of the grid, centered on that column. The bottom row of the triangle sits on the last row of the grid. Row widths from top to bottom are 1, 3, 5, ..., 2S-1 (odd numbers). Each row is horizontally centered on the column. (5) Fill the triangle rows with colors from top (narrowest) to bottom (widest). Assign colors in the same top-to-bottom order as they appeared in the input column: the first color fills cells starting from the top row of the triangle, consuming one cell per triangle position left-to-right, top-to-bottom, until that color's count is exhausted, then continue with the next color. All cells not part of any triangle become black.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. The background is entirely black except for the triangle(s) drawn at the bottom. Multiple columns may each produce their own independent triangle, and these triangles coexist on the grid without overlapping. Triangles are always bottom-aligned (touching the last row) and horizontally centered on their source column.

3f23242b.rule:
The input grid has a black background containing one or more green (G) cells scattered at various positions. Each green cell serves as the seed point for generating a house-shaped structure.

For each green cell at position (r, c), draw a 5-wide, 5-tall house structure centered on it:
1. Roof row (r-2): Place grey (X) cells at columns c-2 through c+2.
2. Upper wall row (r-1): Place red (R) at c-2 and c+2, grey (X) at c, and leave c-1 and c+1 as black.
3. Middle row (r): Keep the green (G) at c. Place red (R) at c-2 and c+2. Leave c-1 and c+1 as black.
4. Lower wall row (r+1): Place red (R) at c-2 and c+2. Leave c-1, c, and c+1 as black.
5. Floor row (r+2): Place azure (A) at columns c-2 through c+2. Fill every other cell in that entire row with red (R), extending from column 0 to the last column of the grid.

Repeat for all green cells. The house interior and roof are local (5 columns wide), but each floor row spans the full width of the grid.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. The background is black. Green cells must be positioned so that the full 5-tall house structure (from r-2 to r+2) and 5-wide body (c-2 to c+2) fits within the grid boundaries. Floor rows extend wall-to-wall across the grid width.

414297c0.rule: The input contains one large solid-colored rectangle with several differently colored marker cells inside it. Outside the rectangle are small red patterns, each containing a colored marker that might match one inside the large rectangle. It is possible that there exist a red pattern with a marker that does not match any of the markers inside the solid-colored rectangle. However, all markers inside the solid-colored rectangle are covered by exactly one red pattern. The output is cropped to the size of the large rectangle.  Place each small red pattern onto the large rectangle so that its colored marker sits exactly on the matching colored marker in the rectangle. Keep the red parts of each pattern around it.
414297c0.author: Philipp

42a15761.rule:
The grid consists of vertical strips, each 3 cells wide, separated by single columns of black (.) cells. Every strip is filled with red (R) cells, except that some strips have 'holes' — positions in odd-numbered rows (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ...) where the center cell of the 3-wide strip is black (.) instead of red. Each strip has a distinct number and pattern of holes.

1. Identify each 3-wide vertical strip separated by the black dot columns. 2. For each strip, count the number of holes (rows where the center cell is black instead of red). 3. Sort the strips from left to right in ascending order by their hole count (fewest holes on the left, most holes on the right). 4. Reassemble the grid with the sorted strips, keeping the single black dot columns as separators between them. Each strip retains its original hole pattern — only the left-to-right ordering changes.

The grid has an odd number of columns following the pattern (3 × N) + (N − 1) where N is the number of strips, and an odd number of rows. Every 4th column (columns 3, 7, 11, ...) is a separator column filled entirely with black (.) cells. The remaining columns form 3-wide strips. All non-hole cells are red (R). The number of rows and number of strips can vary across instances.

45737921.rule:
The input grid contains one or more distinct shapes on a black background. Each shape is a connected rectangular region composed of exactly two non-black colors. Within each shape, the two colors form a pattern where one color appears more frequently (the majority color) and the other appears less frequently (the minority color).

For each shape in the grid, identify the two non-black colors it contains. Swap every occurrence of those two colors within that shape: every cell that was color A becomes color B, and every cell that was color B becomes color A. Leave all black background cells unchanged. Each shape is processed independently.

The grid dimensions remain unchanged from input to output. The background is black (.). Shapes are isolated rectangular clusters of non-black cells separated from each other by black cells. The positions and sizes of all shapes remain the same; only the colors within them change.

45bbe264.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background with two or more isolated colored pixels scattered at different positions. Each colored pixel is a distinct non-black color and no two pixels share the same color.

For each colored pixel in the input, extend its color across its entire row and its entire column, filling every cell in that row and column with the pixel's color. Where two lines from different-colored pixels intersect (i.e., a cell that lies on both the row of one colored pixel and the column of another, or on the column of one and the row of another), place red (R) instead of either color. Each pixel's own original position retains its original color (it sits on its own row and column, so no conflict occurs there).

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. The background remains black (.) except where overwritten by the projected color lines. The grid uses a standard row-column coordinate system with no special boundary behavior.

470c91de.rule:
The input grid contains several distinctly colored rectangular shapes on an orange (O) background. Each shape is an almost-complete rectangle — it is missing exactly one corner cell. That missing corner is filled with an azure (A) cell instead of the shape's own color. The azure cell thus sits at one corner of what would be the shape's full bounding rectangle, indicating a direction.

For each colored shape (ignoring orange background and azure markers): 1. Identify the shape's bounding rectangle by finding the minimal rectangle that contains all cells of that color plus the adjacent azure (A) cell that completes the rectangle's missing corner. 2. Determine which corner of the bounding rectangle the azure cell occupies (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, or bottom-right). 3. Complete the shape into a full rectangle by replacing the azure cell with the shape's color. 4. Shift the entire completed rectangle by exactly 1 cell in the direction indicated by the azure corner: top-left corner means shift up 1 and left 1; top-right means shift up 1 and right 1; bottom-left means shift down 1 and left 1; bottom-right means shift down 1 and right 1. 5. Place the shifted rectangle on a blank orange background. Repeat for all shapes. The original positions are cleared to orange.

The grid dimensions are the same for input and output. The background color is orange (O). All colored shapes remain fully within grid bounds after shifting. Shapes do not overlap.

48131b3c.rule:
The input is a rectangular grid containing exactly two cell types: one non-black color (e.g., blue, orange, azure, yellow) and black (.). Together they form a binary pattern.

1. Create an inverted copy of the input grid by swapping every colored cell to black and every black cell to the colored value. 2. Tile this inverted grid in a 2×2 arrangement: place the inverted grid in the top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right quadrants. The output dimensions are exactly twice the input height and twice the input width.

The input grid can be any height H and width W. The output grid is always 2H × 2W. The output consists of four identical copies of the color-inverted input arranged in a 2×2 tile pattern.

48f8583b.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid containing cells of various colors. Each color appears with a certain frequency. One color appears less often than all others — this is the rarest color. The positions of this rarest color within the 3×3 grid serve as placement markers.

1. Count the frequency of each color in the 3×3 input grid. 2. Identify the rarest color (the color with the lowest count). 3. Create a 9×9 output grid filled entirely with black (.). 4. Treat the 9×9 output as a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks (block row 0–2, block column 0–2). 5. For every cell in the input grid where the rarest color appears, place a full copy of the original 3×3 input into the corresponding 3×3 block in the output. All other blocks remain black.

The input grid is always 3×3 with cells colored from the ARC palette (values 0–9). The output grid is always 9×9, conceptually divided into a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks. Each block is either an exact copy of the input or entirely black (.), depending on where the rarest color appeared in the input.

494ef9d7.rule:
The grid contains scattered single-color cells on a black background. Among the colors present, two special pairs exist: orange (O) paired with yellow (Y), and azure (A) paired with blue (B). In some rows, both members of a pair appear, separated by one or more empty (black) cells. Other colors (red, green, magenta, maroon, grey, white) may also appear but are not part of any active pair.

For each row of the grid, check whether it contains both members of either special pair: {O, Y} or {A, B}. If a row contains both members of a pair, identify which one is farther left (the anchor) and which is farther right (the mobile element). Move the mobile element from its current position to the cell immediately to the right of the anchor. The mobile element's original cell becomes black (empty). All other cells in the grid remain unchanged. Process each row independently.

The grid can be any rectangular dimensions. The background color is black (.). Colored cells are sparse, with at most one of each color per row. The grid dimensions and all cell positions not involved in a pair operation are preserved exactly from input to output.

4a1cacc2.rule:
The input grid has an azure (A) background with exactly one non-azure colored pixel located somewhere in the grid.

Find the single non-azure pixel and note its color and position (row, column). Determine which of the four grid corners is closest to that pixel (using the shortest distance in rows and columns; if equidistant, the corner toward which the pixel is offset applies). Fill the entire rectangle defined by the pixel's position and that nearest corner with the pixel's color. All other cells remain azure.

The grid is rectangular with variable dimensions. The background color is azure (A). The grid uses a coordinate system where (0,0) is the top-left corner. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input.

4cd1b7b2.rule:
The input is a 4×4 grid filled with four colors — blue (B), green (G), red (R), and yellow (Y) — plus black dots (.) representing empty cells. Each row and each column contains some subset of these four colors, with no color repeated within any single row or column.

Complete the grid as a Latin square: replace every black dot (.) with the unique color from the set {B, G, R, Y} that is missing from both its row and its column. Each row and each column in the finished grid must contain all four colors exactly once.

The grid is always 4×4. Exactly four colors are used: B, G, R, Y. Black (.) marks empty cells to be filled. The completed grid is a 4×4 Latin square — every row and every column is a permutation of the four colors.

506d28a5.rule:
The input grid consists of two equally-sized rectangular grids stacked vertically, separated by a single horizontal row of yellow (Y) cells that acts as a divider. The top grid contains red (R) cells and black (.) cells. The bottom grid contains blue (B) cells and black (.) cells.

Remove the yellow divider row to isolate the top grid and bottom grid. Create an output grid of the same dimensions as either half. For each cell position, if the top grid has red (R) at that position OR the bottom grid has blue (B) at that position (or both), set the output cell to green (G). If neither grid has a colored cell at that position (both are black), set the output cell to black (.). This is a logical OR operation across the two grids.

The input grid has dimensions (2n+1) rows by m columns, where the middle row is entirely yellow. The output grid has dimensions n rows by m columns. In the examples, n=4 and m=5, producing a 9×5 input and a 4×5 output.

50a16a69.rule:
The input grid contains two regions: (1) a rectangular region filled with a repeating tile pattern made of two or more colors, and (2) an L-shaped border region along the right side and/or bottom, filled entirely with a single uniform color. The border color is distinct from the colors used in the repeating pattern. The repeating pattern tiles perfectly across its region with a small period in both the horizontal and vertical directions.

1. Identify the border color — the single color that fills the L-shaped region along the right and/or bottom edges of the grid. 2. Identify the repeating tile pattern in the non-border region by finding its horizontal and vertical period. 3. Extend the repeating tile pattern to fill the entire grid (same dimensions as the input), completely replacing the border region. 4. Shift the entire tiled result one position to the left (cyclically within the pattern period). Equivalently, for each row, take the repeating sequence that row follows and advance it by one step, so the color that was at column 1 is now at column 0, column 2 moves to column 1, and so on, wrapping the pattern cyclically.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. Every cell is filled with colors from the repeating pattern; the border color does not appear in the output. The tiling covers the full grid uniformly with no background or empty regions.

50c07299.rule:
The input is a 16×16 grid with an orange background. On it sits a diagonal line segment of N red cells running from upper-right to lower-left (i.e., each successive cell is one row down and one column left). The line's length N can be 1, 2, 3, 4, or more cells.

1. Locate the diagonal line of red cells and count them: call that count N. 2. Identify the top-right endpoint of the line (the cell with the smallest row index and largest column index). Call its position (r, c). 3. Compute the new length: N_new = N + 1. 4. Compute the new top-right endpoint: (r_new, c_new) = (r - (N+1), c + (N+1)). This shifts the top-right corner up by N+1 rows and right by N+1 columns. 5. Erase all existing red cells (set them to orange). 6. Draw a new diagonal line of N_new red cells starting at (r_new, c_new), extending down-left: place red at (r_new + i, c_new - i) for i = 0, 1, …, N_new − 1.

The grid is 16×16. The background color is orange (O). The only non-background elements are red (R) cells forming a single diagonal segment. The coordinate system is row 0 at top, column 0 at left.

551d5bf1.rule:
multiple blue rectangles which can be solid or have a once-cell gap in their outline.

All rectangles are filled with cyan. If there is a gap in their outline the cyan additionally forms a line from that gap to the border of the grid, in the direction of the gap (e.g if the gap is at the top, the line is from the filled interior of their rectangle to the top of the grid.

The output grid size is the same as the input size.
551d5bf1.author: Claas

575b1a71.rule:
The input grid is filled mostly with grey (X) cells, with a small number of black (.) cells scattered across the grid. Each black cell occupies a position in one of exactly four distinct columns. No two black cells appear in more than four unique columns total.

1. Identify every cell containing a black dot (.) in the input grid. 2. Collect the set of unique column indices that contain at least one black dot. There will be exactly four such columns. 3. Sort these four column indices in ascending order (left to right). 4. Assign colors to the sorted columns in this fixed order: first column gets blue (B), second gets red (R), third gets green (G), fourth gets yellow (Y). 5. Replace every black dot (.) with the color assigned to the column it belongs to. 6. All grey (X) cells remain unchanged.

The grid is 10 rows by 10 columns. The background color is grey (X). The grid uses a standard coordinate system with row 0 at the top and column 0 at the left. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input, with all cells identical except that each black (.) cell is replaced by a color determined solely by its column membership.

5783df64.rule:
The input grid has a black background with exactly 9 colored (non-black) cells scattered across it. Each colored cell is a distinct color. The grid dimensions are evenly divisible by 3 in both height and width, allowing the grid to be partitioned into a 3×3 arrangement of equally-sized rectangular sub-regions.

Divide the input grid into a 3×3 arrangement of equal sub-regions (each sub-region has height = total_rows/3 and width = total_cols/3). Each sub-region contains exactly one non-black colored cell. Construct a 3×3 output grid where the cell at position (r, c) takes the color of the single colored cell found in the corresponding sub-region at row-block r, column-block c.

The input grid is square or rectangular with dimensions divisible by 3 (e.g., 6×6, 9×9). The background is black (.). The output grid is always 3×3, with no black cells — each cell holds one of the 9 distinct colors from the input.

58e15b12.rule: The input grid contains two pairs of lines, one cyan pair and one green pair, which define two shapes in the output grid of the same colors that resemble Xs, chromosomes, or hyperbolae. Each line in a pair extends in both directions and away from its partner. The length of the lines in the pair define the slope at which they extend away from the partner; for lines of length n, each arm will have a slope of n or -n; in other words, they will extend as diagonal lines where each segment of the diagonal is n cells long. Anywhere the green and cyan shapes intersect in the output grid is colored magenta instead of green or cyan.
58e15b12.author: Ryan

59341089.rule:
A 3×3 grid of colored cells. Each cell contains one of several colors. There are no special regions or background — every cell is meaningful.

1. Take the input grid and create its horizontal mirror by reversing the order of columns (i.e., reverse each row left-to-right). 2. Construct the output by tiling four copies of the 3×3 grid side by side in this repeating pattern: [mirrored, original, mirrored, original]. Concatenate the corresponding rows from each copy to form each output row. The result is a grid with the same number of rows as the input but four times as many columns.

The input is a 3×3 grid. The output is a 3×12 grid (same height, 4× the width), composed of four 3×3 blocks placed side by side. The blocks alternate between the horizontally mirrored input and the original input: mirror, original, mirror, original.

5ad8a7c0.rule:
The input grid contains red (R) cells on a black (.) background. The red cells form pairs on certain rows, with exactly two R cells per row (one on the left side, one on the right side), creating a symmetric outline. Some rows may have no red cells at all. Each row with red cells defines a 'span' — the horizontal distance between its two R endpoints.

1. Identify all rows that contain exactly two red (R) cells. 2. For each such row, compute its span: the number of columns from the left R to the right R, inclusive (i.e., right_column - left_column + 1). 3. Find the minimum span among all R-bearing rows. 4. For every row whose span equals that minimum: fill all cells between (and including) the two R endpoints with R. 5. Leave all other rows unchanged.

The grid is rectangular (observed as 4 rows by 6 columns, though dimensions may vary). The background color is black (.). Red (R) is the only non-background color. Rows either contain exactly two R cells or no R cells at all. The R pairs are positioned symmetrically about the horizontal center of the grid.

5af49b42.rule:
The grid has a black background with two types of elements: (1) 'palette groups' — short horizontal sequences of distinct colors sitting on the border rows of the grid (top row and/or bottom row), and (2) 'anchor dots' — single colored cells scattered throughout the interior of the grid. Every anchor dot's color appears in exactly one palette group, and each color appears at a specific position (index) within that group.

1. Identify all palette groups: these are contiguous horizontal runs of non-black cells located on the top and bottom border rows. Record each group as an ordered list of colors and note its position.
2. Identify all anchor dots: these are isolated single non-black cells in the interior of the grid (not on the palette rows).
3. For each anchor dot, find the palette group that contains the dot's color. Note the index (0-based, left to right) of that color within the group.
4. Place the entire palette group horizontally on the anchor dot's row, positioned so that the color at the matched index aligns exactly with the anchor dot's column. The group extends to the left and right of that aligned position according to the other colors in the sequence.
5. Leave the original palette groups on the border rows unchanged.
6. All other cells remain black.

The grid is rectangular with variable dimensions. The background is black (.). Palette groups appear only on the topmost and/or bottommost rows. Anchor dots appear only in interior rows (not on the palette rows). The grid uses up to 10 colors (0-9). No palette group overlaps another when placed, and placed groups do not extend beyond grid boundaries.

5b526a93.rule:
The input grid has a black background with identical 3x3 blue hollow squares (blue border with a black center). These squares are arranged in two distinct groups: a 'seed row' — one row of squares that contains multiple squares spread horizontally — and a 'seed column' — one column of squares that contains multiple squares spread vertically. The seed row and seed column share exactly one column position, where they intersect. At the intersection, squares appear in both groups. All other grid positions are empty (black).

1. Identify the seed row: find the horizontal line of 3x3 squares that has the most squares arranged across different column positions. Note all the column positions where squares appear in this row. 2. Identify the seed column: find the vertical line of 3x3 squares that has the most squares arranged across different row positions. Note all the row positions where squares appear in this column. 3. For every combination of (row position from the seed column) × (column position from the seed row), place a 3x3 hollow square at that grid location. 4. Color rule: any square that existed in the original input (i.e., was part of the seed row OR the seed column) remains blue (B). Any newly created square — one that fills a previously empty intersection of a seed-column row and a seed-row column — is colored azure (A). The azure squares have the identical 3x3 hollow shape (azure border, black center).

The grid dimensions match the input exactly (no resizing). The background is black (.). The 3x3 hollow squares are the only non-background elements. Squares are positioned on a regular spacing grid determined by the original seed row and seed column positions, with gaps of varying size between them preserved exactly as in the input.

5b6cbef5.rule:
The input is a small grid (N×N, typically 4×4) containing cells of exactly two types: one non-black color and black (.). The colored cells form a pattern against the black background.

Create an output grid whose dimensions are N² × N² (for an N×N input, the output is N²×N²). Divide the output into an N×N arrangement of N×N blocks. For each cell (r, c) in the input: if the cell is colored (non-black), fill the corresponding block at position (r, c) with a complete copy of the entire input grid. If the cell is black, fill the corresponding block with all black cells. This is a single-level fractal expansion: the input pattern tiles itself wherever a colored cell appears.

The input grid is N×N (4×4 in all examples). The output grid is N²×N² (16×16). The output is composed of N×N blocks arranged in an N×N layout. Each block is either a full copy of the input or an all-black block of the same size. The background color is black (.). Only one non-black color is used per puzzle.

5d2a5c43.rule:
The input grid has N rows and 9 columns. A vertical column of blue (B) cells runs down column 5 (the 5th column), dividing the grid into a left half (columns 1-4) and a right half (columns 6-9), each 4 columns wide. The left and right halves contain a mix of yellow (Y) and black (.) cells.

Remove the blue divider column to split the input into a left 4-column grid and a right 4-column grid. For each cell position, apply a logical OR: if the left half has Y OR the right half has Y (or both), output azure (A). If both halves have black (.), output black (.). The result is a single grid with the same number of rows and 4 columns.

The output grid has the same number of rows as the input and 4 columns (half the input width minus the divider). It contains only azure (A) and black (.) cells.

5d588b4d.rule:
The input is a grid where the top row contains some number N of colored cells (all the same color) packed to the left, followed by black cells. All remaining rows below are entirely black. The grid has width W and a variable number of rows.

1. Count N, the number of colored cells in the top row. Note the color C and the grid width W. 2. Generate a linear sequence of cells by producing runs of C-colored cells with lengths 1, 2, 3, ..., N, ..., 3, 2, 1 (ascending from 1 to N, then descending back to 1). Separate each consecutive pair of runs with exactly one black cell. 3. If the total length of this sequence is not a multiple of W, pad the end with black cells until it is. 4. Wrap this linear sequence into rows of width W. The resulting rows form the output grid.

The output grid has the same width W as the input. The number of output rows equals the total padded sequence length divided by W. The background color is black (.). Only one non-black color appears, matching the color from the input's first row.

60c09cac.rule:
The input is a small grid containing black (background) cells and one or more colored cells forming a pattern.

Scale the entire grid by a factor of 2 in both dimensions. Replace every single cell in the input with a 2×2 block of the same color in the output.

The output grid has exactly twice the width and twice the height of the input grid. The background color is black.

60d73be6.rule:
The input grid contains two perpendicular divider lines made of the same color that span the full width and height of the grid, forming a cross. These dividers split the grid into four quadrants. Exactly one quadrant (typically the top-left) contains non-background colored cells scattered among the orange background, while the other three quadrants are entirely filled with the background color (orange). The divider lines themselves are a single consistent color (e.g., blue, magenta, green, or yellow).

1. Identify the two perpendicular divider lines: one full row and one full column, both the same color. Note the divider row index (H) and divider column index (V). 2. Identify which quadrant contains non-background content (colored cells other than orange and the divider color). 3. Reflect that quadrant's content across the vertical divider to fill the horizontally adjacent quadrant. For each non-background cell at (r, c) in the content quadrant, place the same color at (r, 2*V - c) if that position is within the grid bounds and not on a divider line. 4. Reflect the content quadrant across the horizontal divider to fill the vertically adjacent quadrant. For each non-background cell at (r, c), place the same color at (2*H - r, c) if within bounds and not on a divider. 5. Reflect the content quadrant across both dividers (diagonal reflection) to fill the opposite quadrant. For each non-background cell at (r, c), place the same color at (2*H - r, 2*V - c) if within bounds and not on a divider. 6. Leave the divider lines unchanged. Leave any cells that fall outside the grid boundary unfilled. Cells in the reflected quadrants that have no reflected content remain as the background color.

The grid is rectangular and may be non-square. The background color is orange (O). One full row and one full column share the same non-background, non-orange color and act as perpendicular dividers, creating four quadrants of potentially unequal size. The dividers remain fixed and are not modified. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input.

62b74c02.rule:
The input grid has a rectangular pattern of colored cells on the left side, followed by a region of black (.) cells extending to the right. The pattern has a key property: in each row, the first and last cells of the pattern share the same color, forming a 'border' color for that row. The interior cells between these matching border cells may be different colors.

1. Identify the pattern block on the left side of the grid (all columns before the black/dot region). Note its width W and the total grid width T. 2. For each row, identify the border color, which is the color of the first (and last) cell of the pattern block. 3. Construct the output row as follows: place the original pattern block at the left edge, place a mirrored copy of the pattern block at the right edge (so columns T-W through T-1 are the same as columns 0 through W-1), and fill all cells in between with that row's border color. 4. Repeat for every row.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid (same number of rows and columns). The height equals the height of the input pattern. The width equals the full grid width including the dot region. No black cells remain in the output; they are all replaced by either the repeated border color or the mirrored pattern.

642248e4.rule:
The grid has colored bars along two opposing edges (which may be the top and bottom rows, or the left and right columns). These bars are solid lines of a single non-black color spanning the full edge. The interior of the grid is mostly black (empty) with scattered blue (B) dots.

For each blue dot in the grid, determine which of the two colored edge bars is closer (measuring the perpendicular distance from the blue dot to each bar). Then place one cell of that nearest bar's color in the cell immediately between the blue dot and that bar — i.e., one step closer to the nearer bar along the perpendicular axis. The blue dot itself remains unchanged. If a blue dot is equidistant from both bars, no marker is placed (this case does not arise in practice). All other cells remain unchanged.

The grid is rectangular with a black (.) background. Two opposite edges each contain a solid row or column of a single color, forming boundary bars. The interior contains only black cells and blue (B) dots. Grid dimensions vary but the two colored bars always span the full length of their respective edges.

668eec9a.rule:
The input is a 16×16 grid with an orange (O) background. Several non-orange colors appear, each forming either a diagonal line (extending down-right or down-left across the grid) or a horizontal line spanning most of a row (typically the bottom row). Each color's line begins at a different row, so the colors are vertically staggered. The diagonal lines are exactly one cell wide and advance one column per row. No two colors share the same starting row.

1. Identify every distinct non-background (non-orange) color present in the input grid. 2. For each color, find the topmost row in which it first appears — this is its rank. 3. Sort the colors by their first-appearance row, from top (earliest) to bottom (latest). 4. The output grid has exactly 5 rows and 3 columns. Each row is filled entirely with one color. Place the sorted colors into the output rows from top to bottom. 5. If there are fewer than 5 colors, pad the top of the output with rows of orange (O) so the total is 5 rows. The colored rows occupy the bottom positions in order.

The input grid is always 16×16 with an orange (O) background. The output grid is always 5 rows by 3 columns. Each output row is a uniform solid color. Orange rows in the output serve as padding when fewer than 5 non-background colors are present.

66e6c45b.rule:
A 4×4 grid with a black background. Four non-black colored cells form a 2×2 block at the center of the grid (rows 1–2, columns 1–2).

Move each of the four colored cells from the central 2×2 block outward to the corresponding corner of the grid: top-left cell moves to corner (0,0), top-right cell moves to corner (0,3), bottom-left cell moves to corner (3,0), bottom-right cell moves to corner (3,3). Set all other cells to black.

The grid is 4×4. The background color is black. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input.

66f2d22f.rule:
The input is a 4×14 grid containing green (G) cells, red (R) cells, and black (.) cells. The grid is divided into two equal halves: a left half (columns 0–6) and a right half (columns 7–13). Green cells appear only in the left half and red cells appear only in the right half. Each half is 4 rows by 7 columns.

1. Split the input grid vertically into two 4×7 halves: the left half (columns 0–6) and the right half (columns 7–13). 2. For each cell position (row, col) in the 4×7 output grid, check whether that position is occupied by green (G) in the left half OR by a non-black color (R) in the corresponding position of the right half (i.e., column col of the right half, which is column col+7 in the input). 3. If neither half has a colored cell at that position (both are black/dot), mark the output cell as grey (X). 4. Otherwise, mark the output cell as black (dot).

The output grid is 4 rows by 7 columns — half the width of the input and the same height. The background is black (.). Grey (X) marks positions where neither the green pattern nor the red pattern had a colored cell. Only two colors appear in the output: black (.) and grey (X).

68b67ca3.rule:
The input is a 6x6 grid where colored (non-black) cells appear only at even-indexed row and column positions (rows 0, 2, 4 and columns 0, 2, 4). All odd-indexed rows and columns are entirely black, serving as spacers between the meaningful cells.

Remove all odd-indexed rows (rows 1, 3, 5) and all odd-indexed columns (columns 1, 3, 5) from the input grid. Keep only the cells at even row and even column intersections, preserving their original values and relative positions. This compresses the 6x6 grid down to a 3x3 grid.

The input grid is always 6x6. The output grid is always 3x3. The background color is black (.). The input grid uses odd rows and columns as empty black spacers; the output grid is the input with those spacers stripped away.

695367ec.rule:
The input is an NxN square grid filled entirely with a single non-black color C.

Create a 15x15 output grid. Let N be the side length of the input grid and let C be the color filling it. Compute the spacing S = N + 1. For every cell (r, c) in the output (0-indexed), set it to color C if r mod S equals N or c mod S equals N; otherwise set it to black. This produces a regular grid pattern where full rows and columns of color C appear at intervals of S, with NxN black cells filling each compartment between the colored lines.

The output grid is always 15x15. The background is black. The colored lines form a cross-hatch or lattice pattern whose spacing is determined by the input grid size N, with colored lines at every (N+1)th position starting at index N.

6a11f6da.rule:
The input is a tall grid consisting of three equally-sized square layers stacked vertically. Each layer is 5 rows by 5 columns. The top layer contains cells that are either blue (B) or black (.). The middle layer contains cells that are either azure (A) or black (.). The bottom layer contains cells that are either magenta (M) or black (.). Each layer acts as a binary mask for its respective color, where the colored cells are 'present' and black cells are 'absent.'

Divide the input into three equal layers from top to bottom: the B-layer (blue), the A-layer (azure), and the M-layer (magenta). Each layer has the same dimensions. Create an output grid of the same dimensions as one layer. For each cell position, apply a priority rule to determine the output color: if the M-layer has a colored cell at that position, the output is M (magenta); otherwise, if the B-layer has a colored cell at that position, the output is B (blue); otherwise, if the A-layer has a colored cell at that position, the output is A (azure); otherwise, the output is black (.). In short, the priority order is M > B > A > black.

The input grid is 15 rows by 5 columns, composed of three stacked 5×5 layers. The output grid is 5 rows by 5 columns. The background color is black (.). The three colors used are blue (B), azure (A), and magenta (M), each exclusive to its respective layer in the input but potentially co-occurring at the same position in the output resolution.

6d1d5c90.rule:
The input grid has N rows and 7 columns. The first column (column 0) is filled entirely with the color magenta (M), except for exactly one cell which is red (R). The remaining 6 columns contain a pattern of colored regions.

1. Note the row index of the single red (R) cell in column 0. Call this row index r. 2. Remove column 0 entirely, leaving a grid of N rows and 6 columns. 3. Cyclically rotate the rows of this reduced grid upward by (N - r) positions. Equivalently, the new row order starts at row (N - r) mod N and wraps around. In other words, the output row order is: row (N-r) mod N, row (N-r+1) mod N, ..., row (N-r-1) mod N.

The input grid is N rows by 7 columns. The output grid is N rows by 6 columns (one column narrower, since column 0 is removed). Colors use values 0-9. There is no fixed background color; the grid contains irregularly shaped colored regions filling all cells.

6ea4a07e.rule:
The input grid contains cells of exactly two types: black (.) cells and cells of a single non-black color (one of grey X, azure A, or green G). The colored cells form a sparse pattern against the black background.

Invert the grid so that every colored cell becomes black (.) and every black cell becomes colored. The new color is determined by the original color using this fixed mapping: grey (X) becomes yellow (Y), azure (A) becomes red (R), green (G) becomes blue (B). Each color has exactly one complement partner.

The grid dimensions remain the same as the input (typically 3×3). Every cell is filled — there are no empty or undefined cells. The output grid has the same dimensions and uses exactly two values: black (.) and the mapped complement color.

6ffe8f07.rule:
The input grid has a black background containing one azure (A) filled rectangle, several blue (B) filled rectangles, and several red (R) filled rectangles scattered around the grid. The azure rectangle serves as the central anchor. The blue and red rectangles vary in size and position.

1. Identify the azure rectangle and note the rows and columns it spans. 2. From each edge of the azure rectangle, project yellow rays outward along every row and column the rectangle occupies, in all four cardinal directions (up, down, left, right). Specifically: for each column the azure rectangle spans, extend yellow upward from the top edge and downward from the bottom edge; for each row the azure rectangle spans, extend yellow leftward from the left edge and rightward from the right edge. 3. Each ray travels cell by cell in its direction. If a cell is black (.) or red (R), replace it with yellow (Y). If a cell is blue (B), STOP that ray immediately — do not overwrite the blue cell and do not continue past it. If a ray reaches the grid boundary, it stops. 4. Azure cells are never changed. Blue cells are never changed. Red cells that are NOT in the path of a ray remain unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input (no resizing). The background is black (.). The coordinate system is row-major with (0,0) at top-left. The azure rectangle is always axis-aligned and filled. Blue and red rectangles are also axis-aligned and filled. No cells outside of the yellow ray paths are modified.

705a3229.rule:
The input grid will have an even number of cells. There will be a few isolated, distinctly colored cells in the input.
Create an exact copy of the input grid. Then, for each colored cell, extend it in the horizontal direction to the nearest edge (left or right) and extend it in the vertical direction to the nearest edge (top or bottom) of the grid. These extensions will create L-shapes from each colored cell.
The output grid will be the exact same size as the input.
705a3229.author: Navya

712bf12e.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background scattered with grey (X) marks and a single special bottom row that contains red (R) marks at certain positions. The rest of the grid above the bottom row contains only black (.) and grey (X) cells. The R marks in the bottom row serve as launch points for upward-propagating paths.

For each R in the bottom row, propagate a path straight upward through the grid: (1) Move up one row in the same column. If that cell is empty (.), fill it with R and continue upward. If that cell is X, do NOT move into it; instead, shift one column to the RIGHT in the current row, placing an R there as a diagonal connector. Then continue upward from that new column. (2) If the rightward-shifted cell is also X or falls outside the grid boundary, the path terminates — stop tracing that path entirely. (3) Continue this process until the path reaches the top of the grid or terminates due to a double block. All original X cells and R cells remain unchanged. Multiple paths from different bottom-row R positions are traced independently and may coexist on the grid.

Rectangular grid of variable dimensions. Background color is black (.). Grey (X) cells act as static obstacles. Red (R) cells appear only in the bottom row of the input and mark the starting columns for upward paths. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input, with R cells added along the traced paths while all other cells remain unchanged.

72207abc.rule:
The input is a 3-row grid where the top and bottom rows are entirely black. The middle row contains a short seed sequence of two or three distinct colored cells clustered near the left edge, with the rest of the row black. The seed colors appear at positions that already follow the start of an increasing-gap pattern: the first color is at column 0, the second at column 1 (gap of 1), and if a third seed color exists, it is at column 3 (gap of 2).

Extract the ordered sequence of non-black colors from the middle row, reading left to right — call these the seed colors. These colors cycle repeatedly. Place them along the middle row at positions given by triangular numbers: position 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, ... (where the nth position equals n*(n+1)/2, zero-indexed). At each successive position, assign the next color in the cycling seed sequence. The gap between consecutive placements increases by one each time (gap 1, then 2, then 3, ...). Continue until the next position would exceed the grid width. All other cells remain black. The top and bottom rows are unchanged.

The grid has exactly 3 rows. The width varies across instances but is always wide enough to accommodate several repetitions of the pattern. The background color is black (.). Only the middle row (row 1) contains non-black cells. The coordinate system is zero-indexed with columns numbered left to right.

72a961c9.rule:
The input grid contains a single horizontal bar made of blue (B) cells spanning one full row, with one or more non-blue colored marker cells (such as azure A or red R) embedded at specific positions within that bar. The rest of the grid is black (.) empty space. The bar can appear at any row in the grid.

For each non-blue marker cell in the horizontal bar, grow a vertical column upward from that marker's position. The column's height (including the marker copy at the top) depends on the marker's color: azure (A) produces a column of height 3 (the top cell is A, followed by 2 blue B cells below it, connecting down to the bar), and red (R) produces a column of height 4 (the top cell is R, followed by 3 blue B cells below it, connecting down to the bar). The marker cell in the original bar remains unchanged. All other cells remain black.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly and do not change. The background is black (.). The horizontal bar occupies exactly one row. Columns grow strictly upward from the bar; no cells are modified below the bar or beyond the grid boundaries.

73182012.rule:
The input is a 12x12 grid with a black (.) background. Somewhere on the grid there is a single colored pattern that exhibits 4-fold symmetry — it is symmetric across both a horizontal and a vertical axis of reflection. The pattern is composed of concentric layers of colored cells arranged around a central point. The axes of symmetry pass between two adjacent rows and between two adjacent columns (i.e., the center of symmetry falls at the intersection of four cells, not on a single cell).

1. Identify the bounding box of all non-black cells in the input grid. 2. Find the center of symmetry of this pattern: it lies at the exact midpoint of the bounding box, between the two middle rows and two middle columns. 3. Extract the top-left quadrant of the pattern — from the top-left corner of the bounding box to the center point (inclusive of the rows and columns just above and to the left of the center). This quadrant has half the height and half the width of the full pattern. 4. Output this extracted quadrant as the result.

The input grid is 12x12 with a black (.) background. The output grid dimensions are half the height and half the width of the bounding box of the colored pattern in the input. For example, if the pattern occupies an 8x8 region, the output is 4x4.

73c3b0d8.rule:
The input grid contains a horizontal red line spanning the full width of the grid, a set of yellow dots scattered on the black background (some above the red line, some below it), and otherwise empty black cells.

1. Shift every yellow dot down by exactly one row. The red line remains fixed in place.
2. After shifting, check each yellow dot that is now positioned exactly one row above the red line. For each such dot, generate a V-shaped bounce pattern: place additional yellow dots along two diagonal paths extending upward from that dot's position — one going up-left (row-1, col-1 per step) and one going up-right (row-1, col+1 per step). Continue each diagonal path until it exits the grid boundary.
3. Yellow dots that are not exactly one row above the red line after shifting (whether above or below the red line) simply remain at their new shifted position with no bounce effect.
4. All other cells remain unchanged.

The grid dimensions and the position of the red horizontal line vary across instances. The background is black (.). The red line always spans the full width of the grid. Yellow dots may appear anywhere above or below the red line. The coordinate system is row-column with row 0 at the top.

758abdf0.rule:
The input grid has a background of orange (O) cells. One entire edge (a full row or column) is filled with black (.) cells, forming a border wall. Adjacent to this border, within the first two layers of cells perpendicular to it, there are azure (A) cells scattered among the orange. Some positions have a single A cell (only in the layer immediately next to the border), while other positions have a double A (A cells in both the first and second layers from the border). The rest of the grid is entirely orange.

1. Identify the border edge: the complete row or column of black (.) cells. 2. For each line perpendicular to the border, examine the two cells closest to the border (depth 1 and depth 2). 3. If a line has a single azure (A) at depth 1 only: extend it by also placing an A at depth 2, creating a double-A. 4. If a line has azure (A) at both depth 1 and depth 2 (a double-A): remove both A cells (replace with orange O), then place black (.) cells at the two positions farthest from the border in that line (i.e., at the maximum depth and maximum depth minus one). 5. All other cells remain unchanged.

Rectangular grid of arbitrary dimensions. One complete edge (row or column) consists of black (.) cells serving as a fixed border wall. The background color is orange (O). Azure (A) is the only signal color and appears only in the two layers adjacent to the border. The border edge and grid dimensions are preserved in the output.

759f3fd3.rule:
The input grid contains a green cross: one full horizontal line of green cells and one full vertical line of green cells that span the entire grid and intersect at a single point. All other cells are black. The green lines divide the grid into four rectangular quadrants.

Keep all green cells unchanged. For every non-green cell at position (row, col), compute its distance to the horizontal green line as dr = |row - row_h| and its distance to the vertical green line as dc = |col - col_v|, where row_h is the row index of the horizontal green line and col_v is the column index of the vertical green line. Then compute max(dr, dc). If this value is even (including zero), color the cell yellow. If this value is odd, leave the cell black. This produces nested concentric rectangular rings (based on Chebyshev distance) radiating outward from the green cross intersection.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. The green cross remains in place. Every non-green cell is either yellow or black depending on the parity of its Chebyshev distance (max of horizontal and vertical distances) from the cross. The pattern is symmetric across both the horizontal and vertical green lines.

770cc55f.rule:
The grid is divided into two halves by a horizontal red (R) line that spans the full width. Above and below this red divider, there are two patterns of the same non-red, non-black color (e.g., blue, magenta, green, or orange) located at the top edge and bottom edge of the grid. One pattern sits in the first row (top edge) and the other in the last row (bottom edge). The rows between each colored pattern and the red line are empty (all black). Each colored pattern occupies a specific set of columns.

1. Identify the horizontal red line that spans the full grid width; this is the divider. 2. Identify the colored pattern in the top row (row 0) and note which columns it occupies. 3. Identify the colored pattern in the bottom row (last row) and note which columns it occupies. 4. Compute the intersection of these two sets of columns — the columns where both patterns have a colored cell. 5. Determine which pattern is larger (occupies more columns). 6. In the half of the grid containing the larger pattern, fill all empty rows between that pattern and the red divider with yellow (Y) in exactly the intersection columns. The other half remains unchanged. All other cells remain black.

The grid has a variable width and an odd number of conceptual sections: a top region, a single-row red divider, and a bottom region. The top and bottom regions have equal height. The background is black (.). The red divider always spans the full width. The grid dimensions vary but the structure is always: colored row, several empty rows, red divider row, several empty rows, colored row.

7953d61e.rule:
A 4×4 grid of colored cells. The grid is treated as a single rigid tile that can be rotated.

Create an 8×8 output by tiling four rotated copies of the 4×4 input into a 2×2 arrangement of quadrants: (1) Top-left quadrant: the original input, unchanged. (2) Top-right quadrant: the input rotated 90° counter-clockwise (equivalently, transpose then reverse each column). (3) Bottom-left quadrant: the input rotated 180°. (4) Bottom-right quadrant: the input rotated 90° clockwise (equivalently, transpose then reverse each row).

The input is always a 4×4 grid. The output is always an 8×8 grid composed of four 4×4 quadrants arranged in a 2×2 layout. There is no background color or border; every cell is determined by the corresponding rotation of the input.

79cce52d.rule:
The input is a 7×7 grid. The top-left cell (0,0) always contains an orange (O) marker. The remainder of row 0 and column 0 form a border. Most border cells are magenta (M), but exactly two border cells (one in row 0 and one in column 0, excluding the shared corner) contain red (R) markers. The interior of the grid (rows 1-6, columns 1-6) is a 6×6 pattern composed of various colored regions.

1. Locate the red (R) marker in the top row (row 0). Record its column index as R_col. 2. Locate the red (R) marker in the left column (column 0). Record its row index as R_row. 3. Extract the 6×6 inner grid by removing row 0 and column 0. 4. Compute the vertical shift amount: S_row = (7 − R_row) mod 6. 5. Compute the horizontal shift amount: S_col = (7 − R_col) mod 6. 6. Produce the 6×6 output by cyclically shifting the inner grid: output[i][j] = inner[(i + S_row) mod 6][(j + S_col) mod 6]. That is, rows wrap around vertically by S_row positions and columns wrap around horizontally by S_col positions.

The input grid is always 7×7. The output grid is always 6×6. The first row and first column of the input serve as a control border and are removed in the output. The interior 6×6 region uses colors from the set: blue, red, green, yellow, grey, magenta, orange, azure, maroon, and black. The cyclic shift is toroidal — rows and columns wrap around seamlessly.

7d18a6fb.rule:
The input contains three types of elements: (1) A 7×7 blue-bordered box serving as a legend. The box has a solid blue border and a blue interior, except for exactly four non-blue colored cells located at the four interior corner positions: row 1 col 1, row 1 col 5, row 5 col 1, and row 5 col 5 (relative to the box's top-left corner). Each of these four cells is a different color. (2) Five small shapes scattered outside the box, each composed of a single non-black color and fitting within a 3×3 bounding box. Four of these shapes have colors matching the four legend colors; the fifth shape has a color not present in the legend and is a distractor. (3) A black background filling the rest of the grid.

Step 1: Locate the 7×7 blue-bordered box and read the four colored cells at its interior corners. Map each color to a quadrant: top-left corner (row 1, col 1 of box) → top-left quadrant, top-right corner (row 1, col 5) → top-right quadrant, bottom-left corner (row 5, col 1) → bottom-left quadrant, bottom-right corner (row 5, col 5) → bottom-right quadrant. Step 2: Locate the five colored shapes outside the box. For each shape, determine its 3×3 bounding box and extract the pattern of colored vs black cells within it. Identify which shape color does NOT appear in the legend — discard that shape. Step 3: Construct a 7×7 output grid initialized to black. Row 3 and column 3 (0-indexed) remain black as separators, dividing the grid into four 3×3 quadrants. Step 4: For each of the four legend colors, place the corresponding shape's 3×3 pattern into the quadrant assigned to that color (top-left quadrant = rows 0-2, cols 0-2; top-right = rows 0-2, cols 4-6; bottom-left = rows 4-6, cols 0-2; bottom-right = rows 4-6, cols 4-6).

The output is always a 7×7 grid with a black background. Row 3 and column 3 (0-indexed) are entirely black, acting as separators that divide the grid into four 3×3 quadrants. Each quadrant contains exactly one colored shape pattern. No blue cells appear in the output.

7d1f7ee8.rule:
The input grid contains one or more groups of nested rectangular borders drawn on a black background. Each rectangle is a hollow frame (one cell thick) made of a single color. Rectangles nest concentrically — a smaller rectangle sits inside a larger one, which may sit inside an even larger one, and so on. At the deepest level of nesting, there may be a small solid block (e.g., 2x2) of yet another color. Each nesting group is independent and spatially separated from others. There may also be standalone colored cells (not forming rectangles) that sit outside any nested group.

For each independent group of nested rectangles: (1) Identify the outermost rectangle's border color. (2) Recolor every inner rectangle border and every inner filled block within that group to match the outermost rectangle's color. The outermost rectangle itself remains unchanged. (3) The positions, sizes, and shapes of all elements remain exactly the same — only their colors change. Any colored cells that are not part of any nested rectangle group (standalone elements) are left unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly (no resizing). The background is black (.). Rectangular borders are axis-aligned, one cell thick, and hollow. Nested rectangles share a common center region but vary in size. Groups of nested rectangles are spatially disjoint. Standalone colored cells may appear anywhere outside the rectangle groups.

7e02026e.rule:
A grid of a random cyan patterns with a black background

fill in all free (e.g exclusively black cells) cross shapes, where a cross is a 1-3-1 pattern, with green cells. Overlapping crosses are allowed and all colored in.

Output and Input grid size is the same, nothing else is changed
7e02026e.author: Claas

7e4d4f7c.rule:
The input grid has three distinct regions. Row 0 is a pattern row containing two colors: the grid's background color and an accent color arranged in a specific pattern. Row 1 has a different marker color in column 0 and the background color filling the rest. Rows 2 and beyond are filled entirely with the background color. The background color is the color that fills the bulk of the grid body (rows 2+). The accent color is the non-background color appearing in row 0. The marker color is the unique color in row 1, column 0.

1. Collapse the output to exactly 3 rows. 2. Copy row 0 unchanged. 3. Copy row 1 unchanged. 4. Generate row 2 by taking the pattern from row 0 and replacing every cell that contains the accent color with magenta (M), while leaving cells that contain the background color unchanged.

The input grid has variable width and a variable number of rows (always at least 3), but the output is always exactly 3 rows with the same width as the input. The background color is determined by what fills rows 2+ of the input. Colors 0-9 may appear, with magenta (M) reserved for the generated output row.

7ee1c6ea.rule:
The input grid contains a rectangular border made of X (grey) cells embedded within the larger grid. This X border forms a closed rectangle. Inside the X-bordered rectangle, there are exactly two non-black colors (e.g., blue and orange, or azure and magenta) intermixed with black (.) cells. Outside the X border, the same two colors and black cells appear but are not part of the transformation.

1. Locate the rectangular border of X cells within the grid. 2. Identify the interior region enclosed by the X border (excluding the X cells themselves). 3. Determine the two non-black colors present inside this interior region. 4. Swap every occurrence of these two colors within the interior: replace each cell of color A with color B, and each cell of color B with color A. 5. Leave all black (.) cells inside the rectangle unchanged. 6. Leave all cells outside the X border (and the X border itself) unchanged.

The grid is 10x10. Black (.) serves as a neutral background/filler. A rectangular frame of X (grey) cells is embedded in the grid, typically spanning most of the grid but offset from the edges. The frame is exactly one cell thick. The interior of the frame contains a mix of two non-black colors and black cells. The exterior also contains those same two colors and black cells but is not modified.

817e6c09.rule:
The input is a grid containing empty cells and 2x2 red squares. No two such squares span the same two columns.
To produce the output, first copy the input grid. Then, identify each red square by its order of appearance (counted from 1) within the grid, counted from left to right, regardless of the rows they span. Color in cyan those whose parity is the same as the parity of the number of red squares, thus squares 1, 3, 5, etc. if an odd number of red squares are present, and squares 2, 4, 6 etc. otherwise.
817e6c09.author: Adrien

833966f4.rule:
A single column of five colored cells, each cell a different color. The column can be divided into three groups: the top pair (positions 1 and 2), the middle cell (position 3), and the bottom pair (positions 4 and 5).

Swap the first and second cells. Leave the third (middle) cell unchanged. Swap the fourth and fifth cells.

A 5-row by 1-column grid. Each cell contains a distinct color. The grid dimensions remain the same after the transformation.

833dafe3.rule:
The input is an H×W grid of colored cells forming an arbitrary pattern. There is no special structure required — any arrangement of colors (including black/empty cells) can appear.

Create a 2H×2W output grid by placing four reflected copies of the input arranged in a 2×2 layout: (1) Bottom-right quadrant: place the original input as-is. (2) Bottom-left quadrant: flip the input horizontally (reverse each row left-to-right). (3) Top-right quadrant: flip the input vertically (reverse the order of rows top-to-bottom). (4) Top-left quadrant: rotate the input 180° (equivalently, flip both horizontally and vertically). The four quadrants tile together seamlessly to form the full output, which has 4-fold reflective symmetry.

The input grid has dimensions H rows by W columns. The output grid has dimensions 2H rows by 2W columns. Colors are drawn from the ARC palette (values 0–9). The output is fully determined by the input — no background fill or padding is added beyond the four reflected copies.

8597cfd7.rule:
The input grid contains a horizontal row of grey (X) cells that spans the full width, dividing the grid into a top section and a bottom section. Two vertical signals appear in fixed columns: a red (R) signal in one column and a yellow (Y) signal in another column. Each signal consists of a contiguous or non-contiguous run of colored cells in its respective column, appearing in both the top and bottom sections. The rest of the grid is black (.) background.

1. Locate the horizontal grey (X) row that divides the grid into a top section (all rows above the X row) and a bottom section (all rows below the X row). 2. Count the number of red (R) cells in the top section and the number of red cells in the bottom section. Compute the red growth: bottom R count minus top R count. 3. Count the number of yellow (Y) cells in the top section and the number of yellow cells in the bottom section. Compute the yellow growth: bottom Y count minus top Y count. 4. Whichever color has the larger growth value is the winner. 5. Output a 2×2 grid filled entirely with the winning color.

The output grid is always 2 rows by 2 columns. Every cell is filled with the same single color — whichever of red (R) or yellow (Y) had the greater growth from the top section to the bottom section.

85b81ff1.rule:
The grid is 13 rows by 14 columns. Columns 2, 5, 8, and 11 are fixed separator columns filled entirely with black (.). The remaining columns form five 2-column blocks: block 0 (cols 0-1), block 1 (cols 3-4), block 2 (cols 6-7), block 3 (cols 9-10), and block 4 (cols 12-13). Every even row (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) is fully filled with the grid's color in every block. Each odd row (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) has each block in one of two states: 'full' (both cells are the color, e.g. M M) or 'dotted' (first cell is the color, second is black, e.g. M .). This creates a 6-row by 5-column binary matrix where 1 = full and 0 = dotted.

1. Identify the five 2-column blocks and the six odd rows. 2. For each block (column of the binary matrix), compute its column sum — the number of odd rows where that block is full (1). 3. Sort the five block-columns by their column sum in ascending order (fewest full blocks on the left, most on the right). Ties may be broken by preserving relative input order. 4. Reconstruct the grid: even rows remain fully filled across all blocks, separator columns remain black, and each odd row's block values come from the rearranged column order. The content within each block-column (which specific odd rows are full vs dotted) is preserved — only the left-to-right ordering of the block-columns changes.

The grid is always 13 rows by 14 columns. A single non-black color is used throughout (blue, orange, magenta, etc.). Columns 2, 5, 8, and 11 are always black separators. The grid has a rigid alternating structure: even rows are uniform, odd rows encode binary block states. The output grid has identical dimensions and structure.

8618d23e.rule:
The input grid consists of two equally-sized rectangular blocks stacked vertically. Each block has the same number of rows and columns. The two blocks use different primary color palettes, though they may share some colors at specific positions.

1. Divide the input grid into two equal halves vertically: Block 1 (top half) and Block 2 (bottom half). Each block has r rows and c columns. 2. Create an output grid of size (2r + 1) rows by (c + 1) columns, filled entirely with maroon (W). 3. Place Block 1 in the top-left corner of the output, occupying rows 0 through r-1 and columns 0 through c-1. 4. Place Block 2 in the bottom-right area of the output, occupying rows r+1 through 2r and columns 1 through c. 5. Row r (the middle row) and the remaining edge cells stay filled with maroon (W), forming an L-shaped separator between the two blocks.
