The input grid has an even number of rows (2r) and c columns, representing two stacked blocks of size r×c. The output grid is (2r + 1) × (c + 1). Maroon (W) acts as the separator/background color, filling the diagonal gap created by shifting Block 1 to the top-left and Block 2 to the bottom-right. The two blocks are offset by exactly one row and one column from each other.

8b28cd80.rule: The input is a 3×3 grid containing one colored cell.  Create a 9×9 output containing a square spiral in the same color.  The position of the colored cell determines where the spiral starts: its row and column in the 3×3 grid are scaled to positions 0, 4, or 8 in the output. From that point, draw a clockwise square spiral starting upward, with its arms getting longer as it grows. Make sure that the is a one-cell offset between each spiral "loop". Any part of the spiral outside the 9×9 grid is simply cut off.
8b28cd80.author: Philipp

8ba14f53.rule:
Two colored shapes on a unicolored background.

count the inside cells of both respective shapes (e.g those cells which are fully contained by the colored outline). In the output grid, put one cell of the shape color for each contained cell. The count fills rows from left to right, starting with the left shape. After the count for the first shape is done, the rest of the last row is left empty and you shift to the next row for the new shape.

the output grid has the dimensions 3x3
8ba14f53.author: Claas

8cb8642d.rule:
The input grid has a black background containing one or more solid-colored rectangles. Each rectangle is completely filled with a single color (its border/fill color), except for exactly one interior pixel that is a different color — the 'marker.' The marker always sits one cell inside the rectangle's edge (adjacent to the border). Rectangles vary in size, aspect ratio, and position, and do not overlap.

For each rectangle: (1) Identify the border color and the marker pixel's color. (2) Keep the outermost ring of the rectangle (the 1-cell-thick border) unchanged in the border color. (3) Clear the entire interior (everything inside the border ring) to black. (4) Draw an X (saltire) pattern across the interior using the marker color. The X connects the four corners of the interior with diagonal lines at 45 degrees. Each diagonal proceeds from its corner toward the center one step at a time. If the interior is not square, the diagonals from opposite sides will meet before reaching the center along the longer axis; connect these meeting points with a straight line segment (vertical if the interior is taller than wide, horizontal if wider than tall) along the center axis, also in the marker color. The result is an hourglass/bowtie shape that spans the full interior, touching all four corners.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly — no resizing occurs. The background is black (.). Rectangles are axis-aligned and filled with a uniform color, always at least 4 cells in each dimension (so there is a non-trivial interior). The coordinate system is row-major, top-left origin.

8e2edd66.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid containing some cells filled with a single non-black color and some black (.) cells. The pattern forms a sparse arrangement of colored and empty positions.

1. Note the single non-black color used in the input (e.g., blue, orange, maroon). 2. Create the 'inverse' of the input: a 3×3 pattern where every colored cell becomes black (.) and every black cell becomes the color. 3. Construct a 9×9 output as a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks. For each cell in the original 3×3 input: (a) if the cell is colored, fill the corresponding 3×3 block with all black (.) cells; (b) if the cell is black (.), place the inverse pattern into the corresponding 3×3 block. 4. The block at row r, column c of the 3×3 arrangement occupies output rows 3r to 3r+2 and columns 3c to 3c+2.

The input is always a 3×3 grid with exactly one non-black color and black (.) as background. The output is always a 9×9 grid using the same single color and black. The output is tiled as a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks, so its dimensions are exactly 3× the input in each direction.

8ee62060.rule: The input grid contains multiple identical 2x2 shapes arrange in a diagonal line from one corner of the grid to the opposite corner of the grid in one of two orientations: northwest-to-southeast, or northeast-to-southwest. In the output grid, flip the orientation of the diagonal along which they are arranged by moving the shapes without rotation. Moving the shapes to their equivalent positions in the other diagonal orientation by sliding them horizontally should give the same result as by sliding them vertically.
8ee62060.author: Ryan

94414823.rule:
The input grid contains a rectangular frame made of grey (X) cells forming a 6×6 border. The interior of the frame is a 4×4 region of empty (black/dot) cells. Outside the frame, exactly two colored dots appear at positions adjacent to the frame's corners — each dot sits one cell diagonally outward from a corner of the grey frame.

Divide the 4×4 interior of the grey frame into four 2×2 quadrants (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right). For each colored dot, identify which corner of the frame it is nearest to. That dot's color fills the 2×2 quadrant on the interior side of that corner, AND the diagonally opposite 2×2 quadrant. The other dot's color fills the remaining two quadrants. The grey frame and the colored dots outside remain unchanged.

The grid is 10×10 with a black (dot) background. A 6×6 grey (X) frame occupies the center, with its outer boundary at columns 2–7 and rows 2–7. The frame's interior is a 4×4 region (rows 3–6, columns 3–6). Two colored marker dots appear outside the frame, each positioned one cell diagonally from a distinct corner of the frame.

96a8c0cd.rule:
The input grid has a black background with one red (R) cell located on or near an edge of the grid. Scattered throughout the grid are colored bars — straight segments of three or more contiguous cells of the same color, either blue (B) or green (G), oriented either horizontally or vertically. These bars act as obstacles perpendicular to the path that will be traced from the red cell.

Starting from the single red cell, trace a path heading inward (away from the nearest grid edge — e.g., rightward if R is on the left edge, downward if R is on the top edge). The path travels in a straight line until it encounters a colored bar oriented perpendicular to its current direction of travel. Upon encountering a bar, the path stops one cell before the bar and executes a detour: (1) If the bar is GREEN, turn RIGHT relative to the current travel direction; if BLUE, turn LEFT. (2) Travel in that new direction along the column or row one cell before the bar, continuing until one cell past the far end of the bar. (3) Resume the original travel direction. Repeat this process for each bar encountered. The path continues until it exits the grid or reaches the opposite edge. Mark every cell the path passes through with red (R). Do not overwrite existing colored cells (B or G) — only empty (black) cells become red.

The grid dimensions vary across instances (can be rectangular, not necessarily square). The background is black (.). The grid contains exactly one red (R) cell positioned on or adjacent to an edge, plus multiple blue (B) and green (G) bars of varying lengths arranged perpendicular to the path's travel direction. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input, with all original colored cells preserved and new red cells added along the traced path.

973e499e.rule:
The input grid is a square.
Create a square grid whose side length is equal to the number of cells in the input. Divide the output grid into the equal squares that are identical to the input grid size. In each mini-square, copy the input grid. Then, treat each mini-square as a single cell. So the number of ‘cells’ in the output would correspond to the number of cells in the input as the output size  is just a scaled up version of the input size. Keep only the color in each output cell/mini-square that corresponds to the color of that cell in the input. Consequently, the output design will resemble a scaled up version of the input design.
The number of cells in the output grid will always be the squared number of cells in the input.
973e499e.author: Navya

992798f6.rule:
The input grid has a black background with exactly two colored pixels: one red (R) and one blue (B), placed at different positions. No other non-black pixels exist.

Draw a green path connecting R and B (the endpoints themselves remain their original colors; only the intermediate cells become green). To construct the path: (1) Compute the vertical distance dy and horizontal distance dx between R and B. (2) The path is built starting from R toward B. Take exactly one diagonal step (moving one cell toward B both vertically and horizontally). (3) Next, draw a straight segment in whichever axis has the greater distance (vertical if dy > dx, horizontal if dx > dy). This straight segment has length |dy - dx| and is placed immediately after that first diagonal step (i.e., near the R end of the path). (4) Finally, continue with diagonal steps (each moving one cell toward B in both row and column) until reaching B. The total path uses min(dy, dx) diagonal steps and |dy - dx| straight steps. The straight portion always sits near R's end of the path.

Rectangular grid of arbitrary dimensions (observed up to 16x16). Background is black (.). The grid uses a standard row-column coordinate system with (0,0) at top-left. The grid dimensions and positions of R and B vary across instances. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input, with the only change being the addition of green (G) cells forming the connecting path.

9968a131.rule:
a grid with a majority background color and one to multiple outlier colors aranged in an alternating pattern.

Identify the alternating outlier pattern. The left part of this pattern is shifted to the right by one cell to turn the pattern into a straight line. All parts in the relevant row are shifted on to the right and wrap around, so the rightmost position appears at the left beginning of the row again. If there are multiple colors, choose the one with the cell that is further to the right in the first row.

The color has the same size as the input grid and the only change is the shift in rows as described above.
9968a131.author: Claas

9a4bb226.rule:
The input grid contains exactly four 3×3 blocks of non-background (non-black) cells, scattered on a black background. Three of these blocks are composed of exactly 2 distinct colors, while one block is composed of exactly 3 distinct colors.

Identify all four 3×3 non-black blocks in the input. Count the number of distinct colors in each block. Select the one block that contains exactly 3 distinct colors. Output that 3×3 block as the result.

The input is a 15×15 grid with a black (.) background. Four non-overlapping 3×3 blocks of colored cells are placed at various positions. The output is a 3×3 grid containing the selected block.

9b2a60aa.rule:
The input grid contains two key elements: (1) a small multi-cell shape (the template) made of a single color, and (2) a line of single-pixel colored dots arranged along a row or column. Exactly one dot shares the template's color — this is the anchor dot. The template is located at a specific offset from the anchor dot, perpendicular to the dot line. The remaining dots each have their own color and are spaced at varying intervals along the line.

1. Identify the multi-cell template shape and its color (the template color). 2. Identify the line of single-pixel dots (they share a row or column). 3. Find the anchor dot — the one whose color matches the template. The template is already in the output at its original position. 4. Determine the perpendicular offset from the anchor dot to the template (e.g., which rows the template occupies relative to the anchor dot's row, or which columns relative to the anchor dot's column). 5. For each non-anchor dot, place a copy of the template shape in that dot's color at the same perpendicular offset from the dot line. 6. To determine position along the dot-line axis: starting from the anchor shape's position, work outward dot by dot. The distance between the placement of each consecutive pair of shapes equals the distance between the corresponding pair of dots plus (template size along that axis minus 1). This expansion accounts for the template being wider/taller than a single pixel — effectively each 1-pixel dot is expanded into a full template, and the empty gaps between dots are preserved as empty gaps between shapes. 7. Keep all original dots and the original template in place.

The grid dimensions remain unchanged from input to output. The background is black (.). The grid is large enough to accommodate all stamped copies of the template without overlap or going out of bounds.

9c1e755f.rule:
The input grid contains one or two L-shaped structures made of grey (X) cells against a black (.) background. Each L-shape consists of two perpendicular arms meeting at a corner. One arm is a straight line of grey cells (the 'length arm'). The other arm (the 'pattern arm') sits at the end of the length arm and contains either: (a) a single column or row of colored cells adjacent to the grey arm, where each cell is a different color — this is a 1D color sequence; or (b) a small rectangular block of colored cells (2 or more rows/columns) forming a 2D tile pattern. The L-shape defines a rectangular fill region: the area swept out by extending the pattern arm along the full length of the length arm.

For each L-shaped grey structure in the grid: 1. Identify the two arms of the L. One arm is a straight bar of grey cells. The other arm meets it at a corner. 2. Determine which arm carries the pattern. The pattern arm has colored (non-black, non-grey) cells adjacent to it, either as a 1D sequence along the arm or as a 2D block at the end of the arm. The other arm (the length arm) defines how far the pattern should be replicated. 3. Count the number of cells along the length arm — this is how many times (or how far) the pattern must be extended. 4. If the pattern is 1D (one colored cell per row or column along the pattern arm): extend each color across the full span defined by the length arm. Each colored cell becomes a full row or column of that color, matching the length of the length arm. 5. If the pattern is 2D (a small rectangular tile of colored cells): tile that pattern repeatedly along the direction of the length arm to fill the rectangular region. The tile repeats cyclically until the full length is covered. 6. The grey cells and all other cells outside the fill region remain unchanged.

The grid is 10x10 with a black (.) background. Grey (X) cells form L-shaped borders that remain in place in the output. The fill regions are rectangular areas bounded by the L-shapes. Cells outside the L-shapes and their fill regions stay black. Multiple independent L-shapes may exist in the same grid, each processed separately.

9c56f360.rule:
The input grid contains three types of cells: black (.) background, azure (A) cells scattered throughout, and green (G) cells that always appear as a contiguous horizontal block of two or more cells within a row. The green block occupies a rectangular region spanning several consecutive rows, always positioned toward one side of the grid (typically the right edge). Each row either contains green cells or it does not.

For each row that contains green (G) cells: (1) Identify the contiguous horizontal block of G cells and note its width. (2) Find the rightmost azure (A) cell in that same row. (3) Remove the G cells from their current positions, replacing them with black (.). (4) Place the G block immediately to the right of that rightmost A cell, so the leftmost G occupies the column just after the rightmost A. If the row contains no A cells, place the G block flush against the left edge of the grid (starting at column 0). Rows that contain no G cells remain unchanged.

The grid is rectangular with variable dimensions. The background color is black (.). The coordinate system is row-major with row 0 at the top and column 0 at the left. The grid size and aspect ratio are preserved exactly from input to output.

9caf5b84.rule:
The input grid contains cells filled with various colors. Some colors appear much more frequently than others. Exactly two colors dominate the grid by frequency count, while the remaining colors appear less often.

Count the frequency of each color in the entire input grid. Identify the two most frequent colors. Replace every cell that is NOT one of those two most frequent colors with orange (O). Leave cells containing either of the two most frequent colors unchanged. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input.

The grid dimensions are preserved from input to output. There is no fixed size constraint — grids can be any rectangular dimensions. The grid has no special background color or boundary structure; all cells are treated equally regardless of position.

9ddd00f0.rule:
The grid is organized as a matrix of equally-sized square blocks (e.g., 2×2 or 4×4 cells each), separated by single rows and columns of black (.) cells that form a regular grid of dividers. Some block positions contain a colored block that is entirely filled with a single non-black color except for exactly one cell within the block, which remains black — this is the block's 'hole.' Other block positions are entirely black (empty). The blocks use a single color throughout the grid.

1. Identify the block size and the grid of dividers (single rows/columns of black cells) to determine the layout of block positions as an R×C matrix of blocks. 2. For each block position (i, j) in this matrix (0-indexed), the rule is: the block must be fully filled with the puzzle's color, except cell (i, j) within the block, which is black (the hole). 3. For block positions that already contain a colored block, they already follow this rule — leave them unchanged. 4. For block positions that are empty (all black), fill them in: color every cell in that block with the puzzle's color, then set the cell at local position (i, j) within the block to black. The result is that every block in the grid follows the same invariant: block at matrix position (i, j) has its single hole at internal position (i, j).

The grid dimensions accommodate an R×C arrangement of square blocks of size S×S, separated by single-width black divider rows and columns. Total grid size is (R×S + R−1) × (C×S + C−1). The background color is black (.). All colored cells use a single non-black color. The divider rows and columns remain entirely black in both input and output.

9f27f097.rule:
The input grid has a uniform background color filling most cells. Embedded in the grid are two distinct regions: (1) a small rectangular pattern made of non-background colors, bordered on all sides by background-colored cells, and (2) a rectangular hole of the same dimensions as the pattern, filled with dots (black/empty cells) instead of the background color.

1. Identify the rectangular pattern region containing non-background colors. 2. Identify the rectangular hole region filled with dots. 3. Create a horizontally reflected (mirrored left-to-right) copy of the pattern. 4. Place this reflected copy into the hole, replacing all dot cells. 5. Leave the original pattern and all other cells unchanged.

The grid is rectangular (typically 12×12) with a single background color (which varies per puzzle instance). The pattern and hole are axis-aligned rectangles of identical dimensions, positioned at different locations within the grid, each fully surrounded by background-colored cells.

9f5f939b.rule:
The input grid has an azure (A) background with blue (B) cells arranged in pairs — two adjacent B cells either horizontally or vertically. These B-pairs are scattered across the grid. Some B-pairs are arranged so that four of them form a cross or plus-sign pattern around a common center cell: one vertical pair extending above the center, one vertical pair extending below, one horizontal pair extending to the left, and one horizontal pair extending to the right. Each arm of the cross consists of a B-pair exactly 2-3 cells away from the center, with the center cell itself being azure.

For every azure cell at position (r, c), check whether it is the center of a cross formed by exactly four B-pairs at fixed offsets: (1) a vertical pair above at (r-3, c) and (r-2, c), both B; (2) a vertical pair below at (r+2, c) and (r+3, c), both B; (3) a horizontal pair to the left at (r, c-3) and (r, c-2), both B; (4) a horizontal pair to the right at (r, c+2) and (r, c+3), both B. If all four pairs are present, change that center cell from azure (A) to yellow (Y). Leave all other cells unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly — the output grid is the same size as the input. The background color is azure (A). Blue (B) cells appear in adjacent pairs (horizontal or vertical). The only change from input to output is that certain azure cells become yellow (Y) where they sit at the center of a four-armed cross of B-pairs. All B cells and other A cells remain unchanged.

a57f2f04.rule:
The input grid has an azure (A) background. Embedded within it are one or more rectangular regions filled with black (.) cells. Each rectangle has a small colored pattern occupying one corner — the pattern uses a single non-black color (e.g., blue, red, green, yellow) and sits in a corner of the rectangle, filling a sub-rectangle whose dimensions evenly divide the full rectangle's dimensions. The rest of the rectangle is black.

For each black rectangular region in the grid: (1) Identify the small colored pattern in one of its corners. Determine the pattern's bounding box — its height h and width w. (2) Treat that corner pattern as a tile. (3) Tile (repeat) the pattern across the entire rectangular region, filling it completely. The pattern repeats by copying the h×w block in a grid arrangement, covering the full rectangle exactly (the rectangle dimensions are always exact multiples of the pattern dimensions). Every black cell is replaced by the corresponding cell from the tiled pattern; the colored cells remain as they are. (4) Leave all azure background cells unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly — no resizing occurs. The background is azure (A). Rectangular sub-regions are axis-aligned and bounded by the azure border. Each rectangle's height and width are exact integer multiples of the corner pattern's height and width, ensuring seamless tiling with no partial tiles or gaps.

a59b95c0.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid containing between 2 and 9 distinct colors. Each cell holds one color value.

Count the number of distinct colors present in the input grid. Call that number N. Tile the entire 3×3 input grid N times horizontally and N times vertically to produce the output. That is, repeat the input grid in an N×N arrangement, placing identical copies side by side and top to bottom with no gaps or modifications.

The input grid is always 3×3. The output grid is (3×N) by (3×N), where N is the number of unique colors in the input. The output is composed entirely of N×N identical copies of the input grid arranged in a regular tiling pattern.

a644e277.rule:
The input grid is divided into rectangular blocks by full rows and full columns of a single divider color. The divider color forms a lattice of horizontal and vertical lines. Most intersections of divider rows and divider columns contain the divider color, but a few intersections contain the background color instead — these are 'open' intersections. The remaining cells are filled with the background color, with scattered marks in a third color.

1. Identify the three colors: the background color (most frequent non-divider cell), the divider color (forms complete rows and columns), and the mark color (sparse scattered cells). 2. Find all full divider rows and full divider columns — rows/columns composed entirely or almost entirely of the divider color. 3. Examine every intersection of a divider row and a divider column. Most intersections hold the divider color; find the ones that instead hold the background color — these are 'open' intersections. 4. The open intersections form the four corners of a rectangle. Identify the two divider rows and two divider columns that define this rectangle. 5. Extract the interior blocks enclosed within that rectangle (the cells between the bounding divider rows and between the bounding divider columns, excluding the divider lines themselves). Preserve the internal divider lines that separate blocks within the rectangle. 6. Construct the output by framing the extracted region with a one-cell-wide border of the divider color on all four sides. At the four corners of this border, place the background color instead of the divider color (mirroring the open-intersection pattern).

The input grid is a lattice of blocks separated by single-cell-wide divider rows and columns. The output grid is smaller: it contains only the blocks enclosed by the rectangle defined by the four open intersections, plus a one-cell-wide divider-color border with background-color corners. Output dimensions depend on how many blocks are enclosed and their sizes.

a8610ef7.rule:
The input grid contains cells of two types: azure (A) cells and black (.) cells. The azure cells form an irregular pattern scattered across the grid, while black cells serve as the background.

For each cell in the grid: (1) If the cell is black (.), leave it unchanged. (2) If the cell is azure (A) at position (row, col), find its vertical mirror position at (H-1-row, col), where H is the grid height. Check what occupies that mirror position in the input grid. If the mirror position also contains azure (A), replace the current cell with red (R). If the mirror position contains black (.), replace the current cell with grey (X).

The grid is 6 rows by 6 columns. Black (.) is the background color and remains unchanged throughout the transformation. The coordinate system has row 0 at the top. The vertical reflection axis is the horizontal midline of the grid, pairing row r with row H-1-r.

a934301b.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background containing several distinct rectangular objects made of blue (B) cells. Embedded within some of these blue rectangles are one or more azure (A) cells, which replace blue cells at certain positions. Each object is a contiguous rectangular blob of blue and azure cells, separated from other objects by at least one column or row of black cells.

1. Identify each distinct rectangular object composed of blue (B) and azure (A) cells. Objects are separated by black (.) background cells. 2. For each object, count the number of azure (A) cells it contains. 3. If an object contains 0 or 1 azure cells, keep it in place unchanged. 4. If an object contains 2 or more azure cells, remove it entirely by replacing all of its cells with black (.) background. 5. All kept objects remain at their original positions; the rest of the grid stays black.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. The background is black (.). The grid coordinate system is row-major with (0,0) at the top-left. Objects do not overlap and do not touch the edges of other objects.

aa18de87.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background with scattered cells of a single non-black color (the 'marker' color). These marker cells form a V-shape or chevron pattern, with lines of markers descending diagonally inward from both sides and meeting at a bottom vertex. On each row, there may be zero, one, or multiple marker cells.

For each row of the grid, identify all marker-colored cells. If a row contains two or more marker cells, fill every black cell that lies between consecutive pairs of marker cells with red (R). Specifically, for each pair of adjacent marker cells on the same row, change all black cells between them to R. Marker cells themselves remain unchanged. Rows with zero or one marker cell are left unchanged.

The grid is rectangular with a black (.) background. Dimensions vary but are typically small (under 15x15). The grid uses a single non-black color for structural markers and introduces red (R) as the fill color in the output. No wrapping or toroidal geometry applies; each row is processed independently.

aaef0977.rule:
The input is an 8×8 grid filled entirely with orange (O) cells except for exactly one cell that has a different color — the 'seed.' The seed can be any of the nine non-orange colors: black (.), blue (B), red (R), green (G), yellow (Y), grey (X), magenta (M), orange is excluded as it is the background, azure (A), or maroon (W).

1. Locate the single non-orange cell in the input. Record its color C and its position (r, c) using zero-indexed row and column coordinates.
2. Use the fixed 9-color cycle in this order: G, Y, ., X, R, A, W, M, B (indices 0 through 8).
3. Determine the index of the seed color C within this cycle. Call it i.
4. For every cell (row, col) in the output grid, compute the Manhattan distance d = |row − r| + |col − c|.
5. Assign that cell the color at position (i + d) mod 9 in the cycle.
6. Fill the entire grid this way. The result is a diamond-shaped ripple of colors radiating outward from the seed position.

The grid is always 8×8. The input uses orange (O) as the uniform background with exactly one non-orange seed cell. The output grid has the same 8×8 dimensions but contains no orange — every cell is replaced by a color from the 9-color cycle determined by its Manhattan distance from the seed.

ac0c2ac3.rule:
The input grid has an orange (O) background with several non-orange colored cells scattered across it. Each non-orange cell is a single pixel of a distinct color. The number of non-orange cells equals the number of concentric square rings needed to tile the entire output grid (including the center pixel). The cells are located at varying distances from the center of the grid.

1. Identify all non-orange cells in the input grid and record each cell's color and position. 2. Compute the center of the grid (row = (height-1)/2, col = (width-1)/2). 3. Calculate the Euclidean distance from each non-orange cell to the grid center. 4. Sort the non-orange cells by distance from the grid center, nearest first. 5. Assign each cell to a concentric square ring: the nearest cell is ring 0 (the single center pixel), the next nearest is ring 1 (the 3×3 frame around the center), the next is ring 2 (the 5×5 frame), and so on outward. The outermost cell fills the border ring. 6. Construct the output grid (same dimensions as input) by filling each ring with its assigned color. Ring 0 is one pixel at the center; ring k fills all positions whose Chebyshev distance (max of absolute row and column offsets) from the center equals k.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. The grid has odd height and odd width, ensuring a unique center pixel. The entire grid is tiled by concentric square rings emanating from the center, with no gaps or overlap. The number of rings equals the number of non-orange cells in the input, which also equals max(ceil(height/2), ceil(width/2)) for a square or near-square grid.

ac605cbb.rule:
The input grid has a black background with a small number of colored dots scattered across it. Each dot is one of four possible colors: blue (B), red (R), green (G), or magenta (M). Not all colors need to be present in every input. Each colored dot appears at most once.

Each colored dot acts as an anchor that spawns a line of grey (X) cells in a fixed direction, ending with a copy of itself. The rules per color are:

1. **Blue (B):** Extend 2 cells to the right (filling with X), then place a copy of B one cell up from that endpoint. This creates an L-shape: two X cells to the right of the original B, then one B diagonally up-right from the original.

2. **Red (R):** Extend 4 cells to the left, placing a copy of R at the far end. Fill the 3 cells between the copy and the original with X.

3. **Green (G):** Extend 3 cells downward, placing a copy of G at the far end. Fill the 2 cells between the original and the copy with X.

4. **Magenta (M):** Extend 6 cells upward, placing a copy of M at the far end. Fill the 5 cells between the original and the copy with X.

After all lines are drawn, check for intersections: if any two lines (the X-filled segments, not the anchor/copy endpoints) cross the same cell, that cell becomes yellow (Y) instead of X.

Finally, from each Y cell, draw a diagonal line extending down-left (one step at a time: row+1, col-1) until you reach the edge of the grid. Each cell along this diagonal is also colored Y (overwriting black cells only).

The grid dimensions match the input exactly (no resizing). The background is black (.). The coordinate system is row, column with (0,0) at top-left. All spawned lines, copies, and diagonals must stay within grid bounds — if a line would extend beyond the edge, it is clipped to the grid boundary. Original colored dots remain in place at their original positions.

ad38a9d0.rule:
The input grid has a background of O (orange) cells and several distinct clusters of connected M (magenta) cells. Each cluster forms a recognizable geometric shape: plus/cross shapes (5 cells), Z or S-shaped tetrominoes (4 cells), straight vertical lines of 3 cells, straight vertical lines of 2 cells, L-shaped trominoes (3 cells), and 2×3 rectangles (6 cells). Clusters are connected via orthogonal adjacency (up/down/left/right, not diagonal).

1. Identify every connected component of M cells using orthogonal (4-connected) adjacency. 2. For each connected component, classify its shape and assign a replacement color according to this mapping:
   - Plus/cross shape (5 cells: one center cell with 4 orthogonal neighbors) → G (green)
   - Z-shape or S-shape tetromino (4 cells arranged in a zigzag across two rows) → A (azure)
   - Straight vertical line of 3 cells → R (red)
   - Straight vertical line of 2 cells → W (maroon)
   - L-shaped tromino (3 cells forming an L or corner) → Y (yellow)
   - 2×3 rectangle (6 cells filling a 2-row by 3-column block) → X (grey)
3. Replace every M cell in each component with its assigned color. 4. Leave all O cells unchanged.

The grid is 9×9. The background color is O (orange). All non-background cells in the input are M (magenta). The output grid has the same dimensions; background O cells are preserved in place, and each M cluster is uniformly recolored based on its geometric shape.

ad7e01d0.rule:
The input is an N×N grid containing grey (X) cells and non-grey cells (which may be black or any other color). The grey cells form a sparse pattern within the grid, while the remaining cells contain other colors or are black. The input grid serves a dual role: it is both the tile to be copied and the map that determines where copies are placed.

Create an output grid of size (N×N) by (N×N), initialized entirely to black. Treat the output as an N×N arrangement of blocks, where each block is N×N cells. For each cell (r, c) in the input grid: if that cell is grey (X), place a full copy of the entire input grid into the block at position (r, c) in the output (i.e., fill output rows r*N through r*N+N-1 and columns c*N through c*N+N-1 with the input grid). If the cell is not grey, leave that block as all black.

The input grid is N×N (where N can vary per puzzle). The output grid is always N²×N², composed of an N×N arrangement of N×N blocks. Each block is either a complete copy of the input or entirely black, depending on whether the corresponding cell in the input is grey.

ae58858e.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background with red (R) cells scattered across it. The red cells form distinct connected clusters (using 4-connectivity: up, down, left, right). These clusters vary in size from single isolated cells to groups of 4 or more connected red cells.

1. Identify all 4-connected components of red (R) cells. Two red cells belong to the same component if they are horizontally or vertically adjacent (not diagonally). 2. Count the number of cells in each connected component. 3. If a connected component has 4 or more cells, recolor all its cells from red (R) to magenta (M). 4. If a connected component has 3 or fewer cells, leave its cells as red (R). 5. All black (.) background cells remain unchanged.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. The background is black (.). The only colors present are red (R), magenta (M), and black (.). The grid can be any rectangular size. No cells are added or removed; only the color of certain red cells changes to magenta based on the size of their connected component.

af726779.rule:
The input grid has a green (G) background with a single row containing a pattern of orange (O) cells interspersed with green (G) gaps. This seed row may appear at any vertical position in the grid. The orange cells form an irregular pattern with varying gaps between them — some consecutive orange cells are adjacent (distance 1), and some have exactly one green cell between them (distance 2). Gaps larger than 2 also occur.

1. Locate the seed row — the single row containing orange (O) cells. Record the column positions of all O cells, sorted in ascending order. 2. Examine each pair of consecutively-positioned marked cells. Identify all pairs whose column positions differ by exactly 2 (i.e., they have exactly one green gap between them). For each such pair, compute the midpoint column (average of the two positions). 3. Place marks at those midpoint columns on the row that is 2 rows below the seed row (moving away from the nearest grid edge — i.e., downward if the seed row is in the upper half, upward if in the lower half). Color these marks magenta (M). 4. Now treat the newly placed row of marks as the new seed. Repeat step 2: find all consecutive pairs with gap 2, compute midpoints, and place marks 2 rows further in the same direction. Alternate the color with each generation: first generation is magenta (M), second is orange (O), third is magenta (M), and so on. 5. Continue until a generation produces no gap-2 pairs among its marks, then stop. The original seed row and all other cells remain unchanged.

The grid is rectangular with a green (G) background. Dimensions vary across instances (e.g., 16×11, 16×13, 16×9, 15×13). The seed row of orange cells always has empty green rows on the side where marks will propagate, providing space for the cascading generations. The cascade always moves into the larger empty region adjacent to the seed row. Each new generation appears exactly 2 rows from the previous one, with a blank green row between each generation.

b1fc8b8e.rule:
The input is a 6×6 grid. The top four rows contain a connected blob of azure (A) cells against a black (.) background. The bottom two rows are entirely black (empty). The blob varies in shape but always contains either exactly 16 or exactly 12 azure cells.

1. Count the total number of azure (A) cells in the input grid. 2. If the count is 16, the quadrant tile is a full 2×2 block: A A / A A. If the count is 12, the quadrant tile is an L-triomino: . A / A A (top-left cell is black). 3. Construct a 5×5 output grid initialized to all black (.). 4. Place the 2×2 tile into four quadrant positions separated by a central cross of black cells at row 2 and column 2: top-left quadrant occupies rows 0-1, columns 0-1; top-right quadrant occupies rows 0-1, columns 3-4; bottom-left quadrant occupies rows 3-4, columns 0-1; bottom-right quadrant occupies rows 3-4, columns 3-4. 5. Row 2 and column 2 remain entirely black, forming a cross that separates the four quadrants.

The input grid is 6 rows by 6 columns with a black background. The output grid is always 5 rows by 5 columns. The output has a fixed structure: a central cross of black cells (the entire middle row and middle column) divides the grid into four 2×2 quadrants, each filled with the same tile pattern determined by the input.

b2bc3ffd.rule:
The input grid has a fixed row of azure (A) cells along the bottom. Above this azure row, one or more distinct colored shapes (connected groups of non-orange, non-azure cells) rest on or near the azure floor. The rest of the grid is filled with orange (O) background cells.

For each colored shape in the grid, count its total number of cells (its area). Then move that entire shape upward by exactly that many rows. The azure bottom row remains fixed in place. All vacated cells become orange background. Shapes maintain their exact internal arrangement — only their vertical position changes.

The grid is 8 columns wide and 8 rows tall. The bottom row is always entirely azure (A). The background color is orange (O). Shapes occupy the rows above the azure floor and are composed of non-orange, non-azure colored cells.

b745798f.rule:
The input grid has an azure (A) background. Scattered in the grid are exactly four small L-shaped figures, each made of a distinct non-azure color. Each L-shape occupies exactly 3 cells of a 2×2 block, leaving one cell of that block azure (the 'missing' cell). The four L-shapes differ in which cell of the 2×2 block is missing, giving each a distinct orientation.

1. Identify each of the four colored L-shapes and locate the 2×2 bounding box of each. Note which cell of the 2×2 block is missing (azure). 2. Compute the corner arm length: (grid_side - 1) / 2. For odd-dimension grids, this leaves one middle row and one middle column of pure azure separating the four corner regions. 3. Assign each L-shape to the corner OPPOSITE its missing cell: missing bottom-right → top-left corner; missing bottom-left → top-right corner; missing top-right → bottom-left corner; missing top-left → bottom-right corner. 4. Scale each L-shape into its assigned corner: draw the color along the full corner edge row (arm-length cells) and along the full corner edge column (arm-length cells), forming a large L of that color. The corner pixel is shared by both arms; the interior of the region stays azure. The scaled L has the same orientation (elbow position) as the original small L-shape. 5. Fill all remaining cells with azure.

The grid is always square with odd side length (e.g., 5×5, 9×9, 11×11, 15×15). The background color is azure (A). The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. A single middle row and middle column of azure divide the grid into four quadrants, one per corner L-shape.

b7fb29bc.rule:
A rectangular green (G) border encloses an interior region of empty (black) cells. Exactly one cell inside the border contains a green (G) dot — a seed point. All other interior cells are black.

For each empty interior cell, compute the Chebyshev distance to the green seed dot: max(|row_diff|, |col_diff|). Color the cell based on this distance: distance 0 remains green (G), odd distances (1, 3, 5, …) become yellow (Y), even distances (2, 4, 6, …) become red (R). This produces concentric rectangular rings alternating yellow and red radiating outward from the seed.

The grid is 15×15 with a black background. A green rectangular border (9×9 outer dimensions) is positioned within it. The interior of the border is 7×7 cells. The grid exterior remains unchanged; only the interior cells are filled.

ba9d41b8.rule:
The input grid contains one or more solid-colored rectangles placed on a black background. Each rectangle is filled entirely with a single non-black color (e.g., blue, azure, red, green, yellow, orange, magenta). The rectangles do not overlap and are separated by black cells. They can vary in size and position.

For each solid-colored rectangle in the grid: (1) Identify its bounding box — the top row, bottom row, left column, and right column. (2) Preserve the entire 1-cell-wide border of the rectangle (top row, bottom row, leftmost column, rightmost column) unchanged. (3) For every interior cell (not on the border), assign coordinates relative to the interior's top-left corner, starting at (0, 0). If the sum of the relative row and column indices is even, replace that cell with black. If the sum is odd, keep the original color. This produces a checkerboard pattern inside the rectangle where the top-left interior cell is always black.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly. The background is black (.). All cells outside the colored rectangles remain unchanged. The transformation only modifies the interior cells of each rectangle, leaving borders and background intact.

bae5c565.rule:
The input grid has two key structures: (1) a header row (row 0) containing a sequence of colored cells with one grey (X) cell among them, and (2) a vertical column of azure (A) cells extending downward from below the header. The position of the A-column corresponds to the X cell in the header row. All remaining cells are grey (X) background.

1. Identify the vertical column of azure (A) cells — this is the axis. Note its column index. 2. Read the header row (row 0). The cell at the axis column will be X (or A); split the remaining header values into a left sequence (from the axis outward to the left edge) and a right sequence (from the axis outward to the right edge). 3. Clear row 0 to all X. Keep the A-column unchanged. 4. Starting from the top of the A-column, leave the first row of A with only the A cell and X on both sides. On each subsequent row moving downward, extend one more element from each sequence: row k below the A-column top gets the first k elements of the left sequence filling leftward from the axis and the first k elements of the right sequence filling rightward from the axis. 5. If the A-column extends further than the sequences are long, repeat the final full row (with all sequence elements placed) for any remaining rows at the bottom.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. The background color is grey (X). The azure (A) column remains in place. The header row becomes all X. A triangular cascade of colors expands downward from the axis, one element per side per row, until the full header sequence is placed, then that full row repeats for any remaining rows.

bc4146bd.rule:
The input is a 4×4 grid filled with colored cells. There are no special regions, borders, or background — every cell is simply a colored tile.

Create the output by tiling the input horizontally five times, alternating between the original and its horizontal mirror. Specifically: (1) Let O be the original 4×4 grid and M be its horizontal mirror (each row reversed left-to-right). (2) Concatenate columns in this order: O | M | O | M | O. The result is a 4×20 grid — same number of rows as the input, five times as wide.

The input grid is 4 rows by 4 columns. The output grid is 4 rows by 20 columns (same height, 5× the width). Colors range over the standard ARC palette (values 0–9). There is no designated background color.

bcb3040b.rule:
The input is a square grid containing empty cells, blue cells, and two red cells. The two red cells are aligned horizontally, vertically, or diagonally, with empty and/or blue cells between them.
To produce the output, first copy the input grid. Then, color each cell along the line that joins the red cells, in red when the cell is empty, in green if the cell is blue.
bcb3040b.author: Adrien

bd283c4a.rule: The input is a 10×10 grid filled with several colors.  Count how many cells there are of each color and order the colors from most common to least common.  Refill the 10×10 grid in that order using a vertical snake pattern: fill the first column from top to bottom, the next from bottom to top, then continue alternating directions. Keep exactly the same number of cells of each color as in the input.
bd283c4a.author: Philipp

c074846d.rule:
The input grid contains exactly two non-black elements: a single grey (X) cell that serves as a pivot point, and a contiguous straight line of one or more red (R) cells extending outward from the X cell in one cardinal direction (up, down, left, or right). The R cells are directly adjacent to X and form a line along one axis.

1. Locate the grey (X) pivot cell and the line of red (R) cells attached to it. Note the direction the R line extends from X (up, down, left, or right) and the number of R cells. 2. Rotate the entire line of R cells 90 degrees clockwise around the X pivot. That is: if R extends up from X, move the R cells to extend rightward; if right, move them downward; if down, move them leftward; if left, move them upward. The R cells are placed at the same distances from X but along the new direction. 3. Replace the original R cell positions with green (G) cells. 4. The X cell remains unchanged in its original position.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly. The background is black (.). The grey pivot cell stays fixed. After transformation, the grid contains the X cell, a line of green (G) cells where the red cells originally were, and a line of red (R) cells in the clockwise-rotated direction from X.

c1990cce.rule:
a single row with a uniform colored background and a single red cell

the output shape takes the width of the input grid (w) and turns it into a wxw grid). the red cell shoots out diagonally to the left and to the right until it hits the border. There is a second component to the pattern. On every third red cell on the left arm of the shape, a blue cell shoots out diagonally to the bottom right. Importantly, if there is space, this continue even when the red cells are no longer visible on the left side (e.g when the last red cell hits the left border and a blue diagonal shoots of it, imagine the red cells continuing outside of the grid. At the third new red cell, a blue diagonal would shoot off again, and if it crosses through the visible grid, the corresponding cells are colored blue normally).

the 1xw input grid, where w is the width, turns into a wxw output grid.
c1990cce.author: Claas

c48954c1.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid of colored cells. This single tile serves as the source for a larger mosaic. The tile has no special symmetry requirements — any arrangement of colors is valid.

Create a 9×9 output by arranging a 3×3 mosaic of transformed copies of the input tile. Label the input tile as O (original). Compute three transformations: rot180 (rotate 180°), flipV (reverse the order of rows), and flipH (reverse each row left-to-right). Place them in this layout, where each entry fills one 3×3 block of the output:

  rot180  flipV  rot180
  flipH   O      flipH
  rot180  flipV  rot180

Row 0 of blocks uses rot180, flipV, rot180. Row 1 uses flipH, original, flipH. Row 2 uses rot180, flipV, rot180. Concatenate the three block-columns horizontally within each block-row, then stack the three block-rows vertically to produce the final 9×9 grid.

The input is always a 3×3 grid. The output is always a 9×9 grid (3× the input dimensions in each direction), composed of a 3×3 arrangement of transformed copies of the input tile. There is no background color — every cell is determined by the transformation applied to its block position.

c92b942c.rule: The input grid contains one or more marker cells that will anchor the pattern in the output. To construct the output grid, first copy the input grid 9 times in a 3x3 arrangement, resulting in a grid that is three times longer in both dimensions. Then, color every row containing a marker cell blue (without overwriting any of the marker cells). Finally, for each marker cell, color two of the cells it is diagonally adjacent to in green: the diagonal neighbor up and to its left, and the diagonal neighbor down and to its right.
c92b942c.author: Ryan

c97c0139.rule:
The input grid has one or more red segments that can be either horizontal or vertical.
Create an exact copy of the input grid. Then for each red segment in the output grid, populate either horizontal side (if the segment is vertical) or vertical side (if the segment is horizontal) with an identical light blue tower starting from the red segment and facing the outwards. The light blue towers on either side of the red segment should be reflections of each other and the biggest block in the light blue tower should be two cells shorter than the red segment (one cell less on either side). Every corresponding block in each tower should be two cells less (one cell less on either side) than the previous one it is stacked on and this pattern should continue such that the last block is one light blue cell.
The output grid will be the exact same size as the input.
c97c0139.author: Navya

ca8de6ea.rule:
The input is a 5x5 grid with a black (.) background. Exactly 9 non-black colored cells are arranged in an X pattern: 5 cells along the main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right) at positions (0,0), (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4), and 4 cells along the anti-diagonal at positions (0,4), (1,3), (3,1), (4,0). The center cell (2,2) is shared by both diagonals.

Compress the two diagonals of the 5x5 input into a 3x3 output grid as follows. Take the main diagonal values: d0=(0,0), d1=(1,1), d2=(2,2), d3=(3,3), d4=(4,4). Take the anti-diagonal values: a0=(0,4), a1=(1,3), a2=(2,2), a3=(3,1), a4=(4,0). Build the 3x3 output row by row: Row 0 = [d0, a1, a0]. Row 1 = [a3, d2, a1]. Row 2 = [a4, d3, d4]. Equivalently: the left column of the output is the top-left-to-bottom-left entries of the X (d0, a3, a4), the right column is the top-right-to-bottom-right entries (a0, a1 again wait—more directly: Row 0 reads the top three X-cells left to right: (0,0), (1,1), (0,4). Row 1 reads the middle three X-cells left to right: (3,1), (2,2), (1,3). Row 2 reads the bottom three X-cells left to right: (4,0), (3,3), (4,4). In other words, traverse the X-cells in three horizontal bands—top pair+center-top, center row, bottom pair+center-bottom—reading each band left to right.

Input: 5x5 grid, background is black (.). Output: 3x3 grid with no background cells—every cell is filled with a non-black color extracted from the input. The output contains exactly the 9 non-black values from the input, rearranged.

cad67732.rule:
The input is an N×N grid with a black (.) background. A diagonal band of non-black colored cells runs across the grid, typically spanning a width of a few cells. The band follows a repeating pattern that shifts one column per row, moving consistently in one diagonal direction. The non-black cells form a continuous stripe with a periodic color sequence that repeats every few rows.

Double the grid dimensions from N×N to 2N×2N. The output continues the same diagonal stripe pattern that appears in the input. Identify the direction and rate of the diagonal shift (one column per row), the width of the band, and the repeating color sequence within it. Extend the pattern by continuing the diagonal band beyond the original N×N region, filling the full 2N×2N grid with the same periodic stripe. Concretely: for each row r in the 2N×2N output, place the same repeating color pattern at the column position determined by extending the diagonal's linear shift from the input. All cells outside the band remain black.

The input grid is always square (N×N). The output grid is exactly 2N×2N. The background color is black (.). The diagonal band occupies a fixed number of columns per row (equal to the band width observed in the input) and shifts by exactly one column per row as it moves diagonally. The band wraps no edges — it simply continues until it reaches or exits the grid boundary.

cb227835.rule:
The input grid has a black (.) background containing exactly two azure (A) cells at distinct positions. These two points serve as anchor endpoints. No other non-background cells are present.

Given the two azure anchor points A1 and A2, connect them with two green (G) paths that together form a lens or parallelogram outline. Compute the displacement vector (dr, dc) from A1 to A2, using signed steps (row-sign = sign(dr), col-sign = sign(dc)). The displacement decomposes into a diagonal component of length min(|dr|, |dc|) steps (moving one step in both row and column each time) and a straight component of length abs(|dr| - |dc|) steps (moving only along the longer axis). Path 1 takes the straight component first, then the diagonal component. Path 2 takes the diagonal component first, then the straight component. Concretely, starting from A1 and stepping toward A2: For Path 1, first move abs(|dr| - |dc|) steps along the longer axis only (row-sign or col-sign), then move min(|dr|, |dc|) steps diagonally (both row-sign and col-sign each step). For Path 2, first move min(|dr|, |dc|) steps diagonally, then move abs(|dr| - |dc|) steps along the longer axis only. Mark every intermediate cell along both paths with green (G). Do not overwrite the two azure (A) endpoints. The A cells remain azure.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly. The background is black (.). The coordinate system is row-column with (0,0) at the top-left corner. The grid can be any rectangular size. Only the two azure cells and the green path cells between them are non-background; all other cells remain black.

ce8d95cc.rule:
The input grid contains a black (.) background crossed by colored lines that span the full width or full height of the grid. Some columns are filled entirely with a single non-black color (vertical lines), and some rows are filled entirely with a single non-black color (horizontal lines). These lines divide the grid into rectangular regions of background cells. At every intersection where a horizontal line crosses a vertical line, the cell takes one of the two colors (the actual value present in the input at that position).

1. Identify all vertical lines: columns where every cell is the same non-black color (ignoring intersections with horizontal lines, which may override the column color). 2. Identify all horizontal lines: rows where every cell is the same non-black color (ignoring intersections with vertical lines). 3. Collapse the grid by replacing each contiguous block of non-line columns with a single column, and each contiguous block of non-line rows with a single row. Line columns and line rows are each preserved as single columns/rows. 4. Fill the collapsed grid as follows: (a) Where a gap-row meets a gap-column, the cell is black (.). (b) Where a gap-row meets a line-column, the cell takes that column's color. (c) Where a line-row meets a gap-column, the cell takes that row's color. (d) Where a line-row meets a line-column, read the actual color from the intersection cell in the original input grid.

The output grid has (number of vertical lines + number of gaps between/around them) columns and (number of horizontal lines + number of gaps between/around them) rows. Specifically: output width = 2V + 1 where V is the number of vertical lines (one gap before, between each pair, and after), and output height = 2H + 1 where H is the number of horizontal lines. The background color is black (.).

cf133acc.rule:
The input grid contains two types of colored elements on a black background: (1) Horizontal bars — rows that are mostly filled with a single color but contain exactly one gap (a black cell). Multiple horizontal bars appear at various rows, each a different color. (2) Vertical seeds — short vertical columns of a single color at the bottom of the grid, each occupying one column. Each vertical seed sits in a column that corresponds to the gap position of one of the horizontal bars. The horizontal bars and vertical seeds together form two independent vertical chains (one per gap column), where the bars are like rungs and the seeds are starting points at the bottom.

For each vertical seed at the bottom of the grid: (1) Identify which column the seed occupies. (2) Trace upward from the seed through that column. The seed's own color fills the cells from the seed's position downward to the bottom edge. (3) Moving upward from the seed, find the nearest horizontal bar that has its gap in this column. Fill the gap cell in that bar with the bar's own color (completing the bar). Fill all black cells in this column between the seed and this bar with the color of the bar directly below (the seed's color for the first segment). (4) Now treat this bar's color as the new propagating color. Continue upward from this bar to find the next horizontal bar with its gap in this column. Fill all cells in this column between the two bars with the current propagating color. Fill the gap in the newly reached bar with that bar's own color. (5) Repeat: adopt the latest bar's color and continue upward. When no more horizontal bars remain above, fill the remaining cells in this column up to the top edge with the color of the last bar encountered. (6) All cells outside these gap columns remain unchanged.

The grid is 15 rows by 15 columns. The background is black (.). The grid dimensions remain the same between input and output. Horizontal bars span most or all of a row and always contain exactly one black gap cell. Vertical seeds are short contiguous columns of a single color positioned at the bottom of the grid. Each gap column is shared by multiple horizontal bars, creating a vertical chain.

cf5fd0ad.rule:
The input is a 3×3 grid with azure (A) as the background color and one or more non-background colored cells placed at various positions.

1. Compute four rotations of the 3×3 input grid: (a) 180° rotation, (b) 90° clockwise rotation, (c) 90° counter-clockwise rotation, (d) the original unrotated grid. 2. Construct a 12×12 output grid divided into four 6×6 quadrants arranged in a 2×2 layout. 3. Fill the top-left quadrant (rows 0-5, columns 0-5) by tiling the 180° rotation in a 2×2 arrangement (the 3×3 block repeated twice across and twice down). 4. Fill the top-right quadrant (rows 0-5, columns 6-11) by tiling the 90° clockwise rotation in the same 2×2 arrangement. 5. Fill the bottom-left quadrant (rows 6-11, columns 0-5) by tiling the 90° counter-clockwise rotation in a 2×2 arrangement. 6. Fill the bottom-right quadrant (rows 6-11, columns 6-11) by tiling the original input in a 2×2 arrangement.

The input grid is always 3×3. The output grid is always 12×12, composed of a 2×2 arrangement of quadrants, each quadrant being a 2×2 tiling of a 3×3 block (one of the four rotations of the input). The background color is azure (A).

d19f7514.rule:
The input consists of two equally-sized grids stacked vertically. The top half is a grid containing green (G) cells and black (.) cells. The bottom half is a grid containing grey (X) cells and black (.) cells. Each half has the same dimensions.

Overlay the two halves by combining them with a logical OR operation. For each cell position, if the top grid has G OR the bottom grid has X (or both), place a yellow (Y) cell in the output. If neither grid has a filled cell at that position, place a black (.) cell. The output is a single grid with the same dimensions as each half.

The input grid has twice as many rows as columns (e.g., 12 rows by 4 columns), representing two stacked sub-grids of equal size (e.g., 6 rows by 4 columns each). The output grid matches the dimensions of one sub-grid. Background color is black (.).

d282b262.rule:
A grid with a majority background color and a couple of objects with two colors each.

The objects "fall" to the right edge, meaning they are shifted as far as they can until they touch the edge, or they are stopped by another object. Objects cannot break, they always stay in their original shape and composition, so even if only part of them are stopped by another shape, the rest of the shape cannot move further either.

Grid dimensions stay the same, including everything else instead of the right shift.
d282b262.author: Claas

d2acf2cb.rule:
The input grid contains cells of black (.), maroon (M), and yellow (Y). Yellow cells appear in pairs that share either the same row or the same column. Between each Y pair, the intervening cells are composed of M and . values. No orange (O) or azure (A) cells appear in the input.

1. Locate all yellow (Y) cells in the grid. 2. Match each Y cell with its partner: the other Y cell that lies in the same row or same column. Each Y belongs to exactly one pair. 3. For each Y pair, identify every cell strictly between them along their shared row or column. 4. Transform each intervening cell: replace maroon (M) with orange (O), and replace black (.) with azure (A). 5. Leave all other cells unchanged, including the Y cells themselves.

The grid dimensions vary across instances. The grid uses a sparse palette: black (.) as background, maroon (M) as structural fill, and yellow (Y) as boundary markers. Y cells always occur in pairs aligned along a single row or column. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input, with orange (O) and azure (A) appearing only in the segments between Y pairs.

d304284e.rule:
The input is a 28-column by 23-row grid with a black background. Somewhere on the grid there is a single small shape made of orange (O) cells. The shape occupies a rectangular bounding box and may have internal black cells (holes). The shape's bounding box width and height, along with its position, define the tiling parameters.

1. Identify the orange shape's bounding box (width W, height H) and its top-left corner position (r, c).
2. Tile the shape horizontally to the right edge of the grid. Each copy is placed with a 1-cell gap between bounding boxes (horizontal period = W + 1). The first copy is the original. Color the copies in a repeating cycle of period 3: copy 1 = orange (O), copy 2 = orange (O), copy 3 = magenta (M), copy 4 = orange, copy 5 = orange, copy 6 = magenta, and so on. Each copy reproduces the exact shape pattern but with its assigned color replacing orange.
3. Tile the shape vertically downward from the horizontal band. Each copy is placed with a 1-cell gap between bounding boxes (vertical period = H + 1). However, only the horizontal positions where magenta (M) copies appeared in step 2 receive downward copies. All downward copies are colored magenta (M). The non-magenta horizontal positions do NOT get any vertical copies below the first row of shapes.
4. Continue both horizontal and vertical tiling until copies would extend beyond the grid boundary. Partial copies that fit within the grid are included; cells that would fall outside are simply omitted.

The grid is 28 columns wide and 23 rows tall. The background is black (.). The output grid has the same dimensions as the input. The coordinate system is row-major with (0,0) at top-left. All shape copies preserve the internal structure (holes remain black) and only differ in color assignment (orange or magenta).

d47aa2ff.rule:
The input is a 10x21 grid containing a vertical column of grey (X) cells at column 10, dividing the grid into two 10x10 subgrids: the Left grid (columns 0-9) and the Right grid (columns 11-20). Both subgrids contain scattered colored cells (such as Y, W, O, A, G, M) on a black (.) background. The two subgrids are nearly identical, but they differ at a small number of positions: some colored cells appear in the Left grid but not the Right, and some appear in the Right grid but not the Left.

1. Separate the input into the Left grid (columns 0-9) and the Right grid (columns 11-20), discarding the grey divider column. 2. Compare the two grids cell by cell. 3. Start with a copy of the Left grid as the output. 4. For each position where the grids differ: (a) If the Left grid has a colored cell and the Right grid has black at that position, replace that cell in the output with red (R). (b) If the Left grid has black and the Right grid has a colored cell at that position, replace that cell in the output with blue (B). 5. All positions where the Left and Right grids match remain unchanged in the output.

The input grid is 10 rows by 21 columns. A vertical grey (X) divider at column 10 splits it into two 10x10 subgrids. The output grid is 10x10, the same dimensions as each subgrid. The background color is black (.).

da2b0fe3.rule:
The input grid contains a single colored shape (made of one non-black color) arranged symmetrically around an axis. The shape has a gap — a line of empty (black) cells running through its center along its axis of symmetry. This gap divides the shape into two mirror-image halves. The gap may be a vertical column or a horizontal row of black cells that passes through the interior of the shape.

1. Identify the colored shape in the grid and determine its axis of symmetry. 2. Find the row or column of empty (black) cells that runs through the center of the shape along that axis, splitting it into two symmetric halves. 3. Fill that entire row or column — edge to edge across the full grid — with green (G). All other cells remain unchanged.

The grid is 10x10 with a black (.) background. It contains one connected symmetric shape made of a single non-black color. The output grid has the same dimensions, with the original shape preserved and one full row or column replaced by green.

dc2aa30b.rule:
The input is an 11×11 grid divided by dot-filled rows and columns into a 3×3 arrangement of nine 3×3 subgrids. Each subgrid contains only red (R) and blue (B) cells. The dot separators appear at row indices 3 and 7 and column indices 3 and 7, creating a tic-tac-toe-like layout of subgrids.

1. Extract the nine 3×3 subgrids from their positions in the 3×3 arrangement (row 0–2, col 0–2). 2. Count the number of red (R) cells in each subgrid (each subgrid has 9 cells total). 3. Sort the nine subgrids in ascending order by their red-cell count (fewest R first, most R last). 4. Place the sorted subgrids into the output grid in right-to-left, top-to-bottom order. That is, the subgrid with the fewest R cells goes to position (row 0, col 2), the next to (row 0, col 1), then (row 0, col 0), then (row 1, col 2), (row 1, col 1), (row 1, col 0), then (row 2, col 2), (row 2, col 1), and the subgrid with the most R cells goes to (row 2, col 0). 5. Reconstruct the full 11×11 output grid with dot separators in the same positions as the input.

The grid is 11 rows by 11 columns. Rows 3 and 7 and columns 3 and 7 are filled entirely with dots (.) and serve as separators. The remaining cells form nine 3×3 subgrids arranged in a 3×3 layout. Each cell in a subgrid is either R (red) or B (blue). The dot-separator structure is preserved identically in the output.

df9fd884.rule:
The input is a grid with mostly orange cells that act as background, two yellow U-shapes, one touching the upper side of the grid, the other touching the upper side of it (and being turned downward), and another shape acting as an object that can be moved, of a different color. That shape spans the same column(s) as the open part of the lower U-shape.
To produce the output grid, first copy the input grid. Then, move the object such that it touches the lower side of the grid and spans the same column(s) as the open part of the upper U-shape. The initial position of the object becomes orange.
df9fd884.author: Adrien

e133d23d.rule:
The input grid is a rectangular grid with a single vertical column of yellow (Y) cells that divides it into two equally-sized regions: a left half and a right half. The left half contains magenta (M) cells and black (.) cells. The right half contains azure (A) cells and black (.) cells.

Remove the yellow divider column to isolate the left and right halves. Create an output grid with the same dimensions as each half. For each cell position, if the left half has a non-black cell (M) OR the right half has a non-black cell (A), place a red (R) cell in the output. If both halves have black (.) at that position, place black (.) in the output.

The input grid is N rows by (2K+1) columns, where the middle column is always yellow. The output grid is N rows by K columns. The background color is black (.).

e1baa8a4.rule:
The input grid is entirely tiled by rectangular blocks of uniform color. Each block is filled with a single color, and the blocks fit together edge-to-edge with no gaps or overlaps, forming a coarser grid of colored rectangles that partitions the entire input.

Identify the tiling of the input grid into maximal rectangular blocks of uniform color. Determine the number of block rows and block columns by finding the distinct horizontal and vertical boundary positions where colors change. Replace each rectangular block with a single cell containing that block's color, producing a smaller output grid with one cell per block.

The input grid has dimensions that factor into a grid of rectangular blocks, where blocks in the same column share the same horizontal span and blocks in the same row share the same vertical span, but different rows and columns may have different heights and widths. The output grid has as many rows and columns as there are block rows and block columns in the input, with each cell holding the color of the corresponding block.

e345f17b.rule:
The input is a 4×8 grid containing three colors: black (.), magenta (M), and grey (X). The grid naturally divides into a left 4×4 half and a right 4×4 half. The left half contains a pattern of magenta cells on a black background, and the right half contains a pattern of grey cells on a black background. In each half, the black cells represent gaps or empty spaces.

1. Split the input grid vertically into two equal halves: a left half and a right half, each 4×4. 2. Create an output grid of the same dimensions as each half (4×4), filled with black (.). 3. For each cell position (row, col) in the output grid, check the corresponding cell in the left half and the corresponding cell in the right half. 4. If BOTH the left-half cell and the right-half cell are black (.), place a yellow (Y) in the output at that position. 5. Otherwise, leave the output cell as black (.).

The input grid is always 4 rows by 8 columns. The output grid is always 4 rows by 4 columns — exactly half the width of the input. The background color of the output is black (.). Yellow (Y) is the only non-background color in the output.

e4075551.rule: The input contains a red cell and four other colored cells positioned above, below, left, and right of it.  The output grid size stays the same size.  Use the four outer colored cells to define the edges of a rectangle. Draw the top and bottom sides using the colors of the top and bottom cells, and the left and right sides using the colors of the left and right cells. Then draw a gray vertical and horizontal line through the red cell inside the rectangle. Keep the red cell at the intersection of these lines.
e4075551.author: Philipp

e45ef808.rule:
a bicolored pattern where one color inhabits the bottom, and one black row at the very top.

a brown (or dark red) line extends from the black top row in the relevant column until it meets the lowest point of the color (e.g the column where there are fewest cells of the color that lives at the bottom of the grid). Also, a yellow line extends from the black top row in the relevant column until it meets the highest point of the color (e.g the column where there are most cells of the color that lives at the bottom).

Same size and shape as the input grid.
e45ef808.author: Claas

e57337a4.rule:
The input is a 15×15 grid filled almost entirely with a single background color. Scattered within the grid are one or more black dots (.) that replace the background color at specific positions. The grid can be conceptually divided into a 3×3 arrangement of 5×5 blocks.

Divide the 15×15 input grid into a 3×3 arrangement of 5×5 blocks (rows 0-4 / columns 0-4 form block (0,0), rows 0-4 / columns 5-9 form block (0,1), etc.). Create a 3×3 output grid. For each of the nine 5×5 blocks, check whether it contains a black dot (.). If it does, place a black dot (.) in the corresponding cell of the 3×3 output. If it does not, place the background color in that cell.

The input grid is always 15×15, filled with a uniform background color (which varies per puzzle instance) and a small number of black dot markers. The output grid is always 3×3, using the same background color as the input, with black dots indicating which 5×5 blocks contained markers.

e5790162.rule:
The input grid contains a black background with three types of colored cells: exactly one green (G) cell, and one or more magenta (M) and azure (A) cells scattered across the grid. These colored cells act as a source and deflectors for a path that will be drawn.

Starting from the green (G) cell, emit a path of green cells moving RIGHT. The path travels one cell at a time in its current direction. When the path reaches the cell that is exactly one step before a magenta (M) or azure (A) cell (i.e., adjacent to it along the direction of travel), it stops and makes a turn: if the deflector is magenta (M), turn CLOCKWISE 90 degrees (right becomes down, down becomes left, left becomes up, up becomes right); if the deflector is azure (A), turn COUNTER-CLOCKWISE 90 degrees (right becomes up, up becomes left, left becomes down, down becomes right). After turning, the path continues in the new direction from the cell where it stopped. The deflector cells themselves are NOT overwritten — the path stops one cell before each deflector. This process repeats, bouncing off deflectors in sequence, until the path exits the grid boundary. All cells the path passes through are colored green. The original G, M, and A cells remain unchanged.

The grid has a black (.) background. Dimensions vary across instances. The coordinate system is row-column with (0,0) at the top-left corner. The grid boundaries act as the termination condition for the path — once the path would move outside the grid, it stops. The original colored cells (G, M, A) are preserved in place; only the path cells are added as green.

e5c44e8f.rule: The input grid contains a green cell, marking the origin of a green spiral in the output, and potentially red "blocker" cells. In the output, starting from the green origin, begin drawing a green spiral by extending two cells upwards, then two cells to the right, then five cells down, and so on, always leaving one layer of background black cells between the layers of the spiral and drawing clockwise as the spiral grows outwards. Continue even if the spiral leaves the edge of the grid, continuing the line in green wherever the spiral re-enters the grid (if it ever does). Only stop once all new green cells will always be off the edge of the grid, or if the spiral would overwrite a red cell, which instead acts as a "blocker" and stops the spiral from extending.
e5c44e8f.author: Ryan

e633a9e5.rule:
A 3x3 grid of colored cells. Each cell contains one of several possible colors. The grid has three rows and three columns, with no special background color or distinguished elements — every cell is equally significant.

Expand the 3x3 input grid into a 5x5 output grid by duplicating the border rows and columns while keeping the center row and column single. Specifically: (1) Duplicate each column: the first column appears twice, the middle column appears once, and the last column appears twice, producing 5 columns per row. (2) Duplicate each row: the first row appears twice, the middle row appears once, and the last row appears twice, producing 5 rows total. In index terms, output row i maps to input row [0,0,1,2,2][i], and output column j maps to input column [0,0,1,2,2][j].

Input is always a 3x3 grid. Output is always a 5x5 grid. There is no background color; all cells carry meaningful color values. The transformation preserves all original colors and spatial relationships, only scaling the grid by stretching the border rows and columns.

e681b708.rule:
