The input grid has a framework of blue (B) lines running horizontally and vertically, dividing the space into rectangular cells. At certain intersections and endpoints of these grid lines, there are colored corner markers — non-blue, non-black symbols such as R (red), G (green), A (azure), Y (yellow), M (magenta), etc. These colored markers always sit on the grid lines themselves, typically at corners where lines meet or at the ends of lines along the grid border. Inside the rectangular cells formed by the grid lines, there are scattered blue (B) pixels on an otherwise black (.) background. These scattered B's are distinct from the structural B's that form the grid lines.

1. Identify all grid lines: continuous horizontal and vertical runs of B's (and colored markers) that span the width or height of a cell region. Colored markers embedded in these lines are part of the framework. 2. Identify the rectangular cells formed by adjacent grid lines. 3. For each cell, find the colored (non-B) corner markers at the intersections or endpoints of the grid lines that bound that cell. Collect all such corner colors. 4. Determine the majority color among those corners (the color that appears most frequently). 5. Replace every scattered B inside that cell (i.e., B's that are NOT part of the grid lines) with the majority corner color. 6. Leave all grid-line B's, corner markers, and black background pixels unchanged.

Grids vary in size (roughly 20-26 rows/columns). The background is black (.). Blue (B) lines form a rectangular partition of the grid into cells of varying sizes. Colored markers at grid-line intersections and endpoints use colors from the ARC palette (R, G, A, Y, M, etc.). The grid lines, corner markers, and black cells are invariant; only the scattered non-grid-line B's within cells change color.

e69241bd.rule:
The input grid contains three types of cells: wall cells marked X, empty cells marked . (black), and a small number of colored marker cells (each a distinct non-X, non-. color). The colored markers are scattered individually across the grid, each occupying exactly one cell. The X cells form an irregular barrier network that partitions the empty space into connected regions.

For each colored marker cell in the grid, perform an orthogonal flood fill starting from that marker's position. The fill spreads to all adjacent cells (up, down, left, right) that are empty (. cells), continuing recursively through connected empty cells. X cells act as impassable walls that block the spread. Every empty cell reached by the flood fill is recolored to match the marker's color. The marker cell itself retains its color. X cells and other marker cells are never overwritten. If two markers' flood regions would never overlap (because X walls separate them), each simply fills its own connected region independently.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly (no resizing). The grid uses a standard row-column coordinate system. The background is . (black), walls are X, and colored markers are any other character. Output preserves all X cells and marker cells in their original positions; only . cells change, becoming the color of whichever marker can reach them via orthogonal connectivity through . cells.

e6de6e8f.rule:
The input is a 12*2 grid with 5 red shapes arranged horizontally in a line.
Create a 7*8 grid. Starting from the center of the top row in the grid, start creating the same red shapes down the grid as seen in the input grid . Every next red shape should start from the end of the previous shape and include the last red cell from the previous shape such that shapes share cells. The resulting shape would be a large red shape that spans the entire height of the output grid. Then color the topmost red cell of that shape green.
The output grid is 7 columns by 8 rows. It is fully filled with no background color — every cell is determined by the stacking red shapes rule outlined above.
e6de6e8f.author: Navya

e74e1818.rule:
The input grid contains several colored shapes arranged as vertically stacked blocks against a black background. Each distinct non-black color occupies a contiguous band of consecutive rows, forming a group. These color groups are stacked on top of each other with no vertical gaps between them (though they may not span the full width of the grid). Within each color group, the rows may differ in width and pixel pattern, giving each group an asymmetric top-to-bottom profile.

For each color group (a set of consecutive rows sharing the same non-black color), reverse the vertical order of its rows in place. That is, the first row of the group swaps with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on. Each group stays in the same vertical position within the grid — only the internal ordering of its rows is flipped. The horizontal positions of all pixels remain unchanged. Repeat this for every color group independently.

The grid has a black (.) background. Its dimensions vary but include a border of black cells around the colored content. The colored regions collectively tile a vertical band of rows in the interior of the grid without overlap or gaps between adjacent color groups. Each color appears in exactly one contiguous vertical band of rows.

e7639916.rule:
The input grid contains exactly three azure (A) pixels on a black (.) background. These three points define the corners and edge midpoints of an axis-aligned rectangle. Each A pixel sits on a different edge of the bounding rectangle formed by the three points.

1. Identify the three azure (A) pixels and note their (row, column) coordinates. 2. Compute the bounding rectangle of these three points: top edge = minimum row, bottom edge = maximum row, left edge = minimum column, right edge = maximum column. 3. Draw the entire border (perimeter) of this bounding rectangle using blue (B) pixels. This means fill every cell along the top row, bottom row, left column, and right column of the rectangle with B. 4. Restore each of the three original azure (A) pixels to their original positions on the border, overwriting the blue at those locations. The interior of the rectangle and all cells outside the rectangle remain black.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly (no resizing). The background is black (.). The only non-background colors are azure (A) for the three anchor points and blue (B) for the rectangle border. The coordinate system is row-major with (0,0) at the top-left corner.

e7b06bea.rule:
The input grid has a black (dot) background. In the leftmost column, some number of rows starting from the top contain a grey (X) marker; the remaining rows in that column are black. On the right edge of the grid, there is a vertical stripe of two or more adjacent colored columns that span the full height of the grid. Each of these colored columns is a single solid color, and together they form an ordered sequence of distinct colors read left to right. The region between the X column and the colored stripe is entirely black.

1. Count the number of rows that contain an X marker. Call this the GROUP SIZE. 2. Read the colors of the rightmost colored columns from left to right. This gives an ordered COLOR SEQUENCE of length N (where N is the number of colored columns). 3. Replace all N colored columns with black (dots). 4. Create a single output column positioned one cell to the left of where the leftmost colored column was (i.e., immediately adjacent to where the stripe began). 5. Fill this output column by cycling through the COLOR SEQUENCE, repeating each color for exactly GROUP SIZE consecutive rows before moving to the next color in the sequence. When the sequence is exhausted, wrap back to the first color and continue. Fill until all rows of the grid are covered (truncating the last group if the grid runs out of rows). 6. The X markers and all black cells outside the old stripe region remain unchanged.

The output grid has the same dimensions as the input grid. The background color is black (dot). The leftmost column retains its X markers in the same rows as the input. The N rightmost columns that held colors in the input are now black. A single non-black column appears one position to the left of where the colored stripe started, containing the cycled color pattern.

e84fef15.rule:
The input is a large grid divided into a 5×5 arrangement of identical 5×5 tiles, separated by green (G) lines. The green lines form a regular grid of separators: full rows of G and full columns of G every 6th position (every 5 content cells plus 1 separator). All tiles are copies of a single base pattern — except exactly one tile, which has been altered by replacing some of its non-azure (non-A) cells with azure (A).

1. Parse the green (G) separator rows and columns to extract the 5×5 arrangement of 5×5 tiles. 2. Determine the base tile: the tile pattern shared by the majority of tiles (all but one). 3. Find the single anomalous tile that differs from the base pattern. 4. Compare the anomalous tile to the base tile cell by cell. Every position where the base tile has a non-azure value but the anomalous tile has azure (A) is a 'erased' position. 5. Produce the output by copying the base tile, then replacing each erased position with blue (B).

The input grid is 29×29 (five 5×5 tiles separated by single-cell-wide green lines in both dimensions). The output grid is 5×5, matching the dimensions of a single tile. Azure (A) serves as the background/default color within tiles. Green (G) is used exclusively as a separator and does not appear in the output.

e99362f0.rule:
The input is a rectangular grid divided into four quadrants by a yellow cross — a horizontal row of all yellow cells and a vertical column of all yellow cells that intersect at one point. This cross splits the grid into four equally-sized rectangular regions. Each quadrant contains a pattern made from one signature color on a black background: the top-left quadrant uses orange (O), the top-right uses white (W), the bottom-left uses red (R), and the bottom-right uses azure (A). Each quadrant has the same dimensions.

1. Identify the yellow cross (one full yellow row and one full yellow column) and extract the four quadrants, ignoring the yellow dividers. All four quadrants share the same dimensions — this will be the output size. 2. For each cell position in the output grid, examine the corresponding cell in all four quadrants. Each quadrant cell is either its signature color or black. 3. Determine which quadrants have a non-black (colored) value at that position. If none do, the output cell is black. 4. If one or more quadrants are non-black at that position, select the winner using the fixed priority order: azure (A) > orange (O) > white (W) > red (R). The highest-priority non-black color wins and is placed in the output cell.

The input grid is 11 rows by 9 columns, with a yellow row (row 5) and a yellow column (column 4) forming a cross that divides the grid into four 5×4 quadrants. The output grid matches the quadrant dimensions: 5 rows by 4 columns. The background color is black (.). The four signature colors — orange, white, red, azure — each appear exclusively in their respective quadrant in the input but may all appear in the output.

e9c9d9a1.rule:
The input grid is divided into rectangular regions by continuous green (G) lines that span the full width (horizontal) or full height (vertical) of the grid. These green lines form a grid-of-regions, like a table or window pane. All non-green cells are black (.). Each region can be classified by its position within this grid-of-regions: corner regions (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right), edge regions (on the top/bottom/left/right border but not a corner), and interior regions (not touching any border of the grid-of-regions).

1. Identify all full-spanning green lines: horizontal lines where every cell in that row is G, and vertical lines where every cell in that column is G. These divide the grid into a matrix of rectangular regions. 2. Determine the position of each region within this matrix of regions (its row index and column index among the regions). 3. Classify each region: (a) Top-left corner region (first row of regions, first column of regions) → fill all its black cells with Red (R). (b) Top-right corner region (first row of regions, last column of regions) → fill all its black cells with Yellow (Y). (c) Bottom-left corner region (last row of regions, first column of regions) → fill all its black cells with Blue (B). (d) Bottom-right corner region (last row of regions, last column of regions) → fill all its black cells with Azure (A). (e) Interior regions (not in the first or last row of regions, and not in the first or last column of regions) → fill all their black cells with Orange (O). (f) Edge regions that are not corners (on the border of the region matrix but not at a corner) → leave unchanged (black). 4. All green lines remain unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly. The background color is black (.). Green (G) lines act as structural dividers, forming complete horizontal and vertical partitions across the full grid. The grid can be any size, with any number of green dividing lines, producing a variable-sized matrix of rectangular regions.

ea9794b1.rule:
The input is a 10x10 grid divided into four 5x5 quadrants. Each quadrant uses exactly one non-black color paired with black (.) cells: Top-Left uses Yellow (Y), Top-Right uses Green (G), Bottom-Left uses Maroon (W), and Bottom-Right uses Azure (A). Each quadrant forms a sparse pattern of its color against a black background.

To produce the 5x5 output grid, overlay all four quadrants cell by cell. For each position (r, c) where r ranges 0-4 and c ranges 0-4, examine the corresponding cell in each quadrant: Top-Left at (r, c), Top-Right at (r, c+5), Bottom-Left at (r+5, c), Bottom-Right at (r+5, c+5). Each quadrant cell is either its designated color or black. Assign the output cell using this strict priority order from highest to lowest: Green (G) > Maroon (W) > Azure (A) > Yellow (Y) > black (.). That is, if Green is present in any quadrant at that position, output Green. Otherwise if Maroon is present, output Maroon. Otherwise if Azure is present, output Azure. Otherwise if Yellow is present, output Yellow. Otherwise output black (.).

The input grid is always 10x10, composed of four non-overlapping 5x5 quadrants arranged in a 2x2 layout. The output grid is always 5x5. Each input quadrant contains exactly one chromatic color (Yellow, Green, Maroon, or Azure) plus black cells. The output uses all four colors plus black.

ed98d772.rule:
A 3×3 grid containing colored cells and black (.) cells forming a pattern.

Construct a 6×6 output grid by arranging four rotations of the 3×3 input in a 2×2 layout: place the original (0°) in the top-left quadrant, the 90° counter-clockwise rotation in the top-right quadrant, the 180° rotation in the bottom-left quadrant, and the 90° clockwise rotation in the bottom-right quadrant.

The input is a 3×3 grid with cells valued from the color palette. The output is a 6×6 grid composed of four 3×3 quadrants, each a rotation of the input. There is no overlap or gap between quadrants.

edcc2ff0.rule:
The grid is divided into two regions by a solid horizontal row of a single color at row 7. Above that divider (rows 0–6) is a mostly black section with exactly three single-pixel colored indicators placed in column 0 at rows 1, 3, and 5. Below (rows 7–19) is a rectangular grid whose background color matches the divider row; scattered across this lower grid are small connected shapes in various colors, some matching the indicator colors and some not.

1. Identify the three indicator colors from column 0 at rows 1, 3, and 5 in the top section. These are the 'kept' colors. 2. Identify the background color of the lower grid (the color filling the solid divider at row 7). 3. In the lower grid (rows 7–19), find all connected components of each kept color (4-connected adjacency). Count how many distinct components exist for each kept color. 4. Update the top section: for each indicator at row r, extend that color rightward from column 0 so the total number of filled cells in that row equals the component count for that color. If the count is 0, clear the indicator entirely (replace with black). All other cells in the top section remain black. 5. In the lower grid, remove every shape whose color is NOT one of the three kept colors by replacing those cells with the background color. Shapes in kept colors remain unchanged.

The grid is always 10 columns wide and 20 rows tall. Row 7 is a solid horizontal divider whose color defines the background of the lower 13-row region (rows 7–19). The upper 7 rows (0–6) use black as background, with indicator pixels only at (row 1, col 0), (row 3, col 0), and (row 5, col 0). Odd rows in the top section hold indicators; even rows are entirely black.

ef26cbf6.rule:
The grid is divided into rectangular sections by solid yellow (Y) lines — both horizontal and vertical — forming a matrix of sub-grids. Each sub-grid contains either: (1) a single non-black, non-blue, non-yellow colored pixel on an otherwise black background (a 'key' section), or (2) a pattern made of blue (B) pixels on a black background (a 'template' section). Each horizontal band of sections (row of sub-grids between horizontal yellow dividers) contains exactly one key section and one or more template sections.

For each horizontal band of sub-grids (separated by horizontal yellow lines): 1. Identify the key section — the sub-grid containing a single uniquely-colored pixel (not blue, black, or yellow). Note its color. 2. Identify the template section(s) — sub-grids containing blue (B) pixel patterns. 3. Replace every blue (B) pixel in the template section(s) with the key color from that same horizontal band. 4. Leave all other pixels unchanged: the key sections remain as-is, yellow dividers remain, and black background pixels remain black.

The grid is rectangular, with solid yellow (Y) rows and columns acting as dividers that partition it into a matrix of equally-sized sub-grids (typically 3x3 cells each). The background color is black (.). Yellow dividers span the full width (horizontal) or full height (vertical) of the grid. The grid dimensions vary but maintain this regular partitioned structure.

f0afb749.rule:
The input is a grid with a black (.) background containing one or more colored cells (any non-black color). These colored cells are sparsely placed and act as anchor points. Each colored cell sits on a diagonal line defined by the constant (row minus column).

1. Create an output grid with double the height and double the width of the input, filled with black (.). 2. For each cell in the input, map it to a 2×2 block in the output at position (2*row, 2*col) through (2*row+1, 2*col+1). 3. For each colored (non-black) cell in the input, fill its corresponding 2×2 block entirely with that color. 4. For each colored cell, compute its diagonal index d = row − col. Find all other cells in the input grid that share the same diagonal index (i.e., where their row − col also equals d) and that are empty (black). 5. For each such empty cell on the diagonal, place a blue diagonal stroke in its 2×2 output block: set the top-left pixel (2*row, 2*col) and bottom-right pixel (2*row+1, 2*col+1) to blue (B), leaving the other two pixels black.

The output grid is exactly twice the height and twice the width of the input grid. The background is black (.). Each input cell maps to a 2×2 block in the output. Colored cells become solid 2×2 blocks; empty cells on a colored cell's top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal become 2×2 blocks with blue pixels at top-left and bottom-right corners only.

f21745ec.rule:
The input grid has a black background with several colored rectangles scattered across it. Each rectangle is a hollow border (one cell thick) drawn in a single color, enclosing an interior region. Exactly one rectangle has a non-trivial pattern inside it — some of its interior cells are filled with the border color while others remain black, forming an asymmetric design. All other rectangles have completely empty (all-black) interiors. The rectangles vary in size (exterior dimensions). Some rectangles share the same exterior dimensions as the patterned rectangle, while others have different dimensions.

1. Identify the one rectangle whose interior contains a pattern (some interior cells filled with the border color, not all black). This is the SOURCE rectangle. Record its exterior dimensions (height × width) and extract its interior pattern as a grid of filled/unfilled cells. 2. Find all other rectangles that have exactly the same exterior dimensions as the source. These are TARGET rectangles. For each target, copy the source's interior pattern into the target's interior, using the target's own border color for filled cells and black for unfilled cells. The border of each target remains unchanged. 3. Leave the source rectangle completely unchanged (border and interior pattern preserved). 4. Erase (replace with black) every rectangle whose exterior dimensions differ from the source's dimensions — remove both border and interior entirely. 5. Leave the black background unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input (variable size, typically around 19-23 rows and columns). The background is black (.). Rectangles are axis-aligned with single-cell-thick borders. No rectangles overlap or touch. The output grid has the same dimensions as the input.

f3cdc58f.rule:
The input is a 10×10 grid with a black (.) background. Scattered across the grid are cells of exactly four colors: Blue (B), Red (R), Green (G), and Yellow (Y). Each color appears some number of times at various positions throughout the grid.

1. Count the total number of occurrences of each of the four colors in the input grid: Blue (B), Red (R), Green (G), and Yellow (Y). 2. Construct the output as a 10×10 grid initialized entirely to black (.). 3. Assign each color to a fixed column: B → column 0, R → column 1, G → column 2, Y → column 3. 4. For each color, draw a vertical bar in its assigned column, bottom-aligned to row 9, with height equal to that color's count. That is, fill the cells from row (10 − count) through row 9 in that column with the color. 5. All other cells remain black.

Both input and output grids are 10×10. The background color is black (.). The output uses only columns 0–3 for the bar chart; columns 4–9 are entirely black. The bars are bottom-aligned (anchored to row 9) and grow upward.

f45f5ca7.rule:
The input is a 10x10 grid with a black background. Column 0 contains a sequence of colored pixels — each is one of four colors: azure (A), red (R), yellow (Y), or green (G). Some rows in column 0 are black (empty). All other cells in the grid are black.

Each color has a fixed destination column: azure goes to column 1, red goes to column 2, yellow goes to column 3, and green goes to column 4. For each row, take the colored pixel in column 0 and move it to the column assigned to its color, keeping it in the same row. Remove the pixel from column 0 (set it to black). Rows that are already black in column 0 remain entirely black.

The grid is 10 rows by 10 columns. The background is black. Only one pixel per row is non-black, and it always appears in column 0 in the input or in its color-assigned column (1–4) in the output.

f9a67cb5.rule:
The grid contains a set of either gapped cyan columns or rows. There is also one single grid cell

The red cell is extended to try and reach the other end (e.g left to right, right to left, top to bottom, bottom to top), when it reaches a column or row, it extends in both directions in parallel to it (e.g when meeting a column it extends to top and bottom). This extension continues until it hits the relevant border, or a gap in the cyan, upon which it continues through the gap and takes the primary direction from the start again. This continues until the red reaches the opposite border (e.g if the start was at the top, it has to reach the bottom-most row). It is possible for the red to divide into several distinct streams, which all have to be completed, but this depends on the gap arangement and does not always happen.

Output grid size does not change, the only transformation is the red extension.
f9a67cb5.author: Claas

fd02da9e.rule:
An 8x8 grid with an orange (O) background. Up to four non-orange colored pixels may appear, each located at one of the four corners of the grid: top-left (row 0, col 0), top-right (row 0, col 7), bottom-left (row 7, col 0), or bottom-right (row 7, col 7). Each corner either holds a single colored pixel or is orange (empty).

Start with an entirely orange 8x8 grid. For each corner that contains a non-orange pixel, remove it from the corner and stamp a small shape in a fixed interior position using that pixel's color. The four corners map to these fixed shapes (row, col coordinates, 0-indexed): Top-left corner → a 2x2 block at (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2). Top-right corner → a 2x2 block at (1,5), (1,6), (2,5), (2,6). Bottom-left corner → three cells in a descending-then-diagonal pattern at (4,2), (5,2), (6,3). Bottom-right corner → three cells in a descending-then-diagonal pattern (mirrored) at (4,5), (5,5), (6,4). Each corner is processed independently. If a corner is orange, no shape is produced for that corner. Multiple corners can be active simultaneously without overlap.

The grid is always 8x8. The background color is orange (O). The output grid has the same 8x8 dimensions. The coordinate system is 0-indexed with (0,0) at the top-left. The interior shapes are symmetric about the vertical center line of the grid: top-left mirrors top-right, and bottom-left mirrors bottom-right.

fe9372f3.rule:
The input is a grid with empty cells and a plus-shaped red object made of five cells (a central one and one per cardinal direction).
To produce the output grid, first copy the input grid. Then, for each of the four diagonal directions stemming from the central cell of the red shape, color all the cells in blue until reaching a side of the grid. Similarly, expand the shape in its cardinal directions with the repeating pattern « cyan – cyan – yellow » until reaching the boundaries of the grid.
fe9372f3.author: Adrien

ff72ca3e.rule: The input contains yellow cells and several gray cells on a black background.  For each yellow cell, find the nearest gray cell. Use its distance to determine the size of a red square centered on the yellow cell: the square grows equally in every direction but stops one cell short of the nearest gray cell.  Fill that square red while keeping the yellow center and the gray cells unchanged. The output grid size stays the same.
ff72ca3e.author: Philipp

test2_t3.rule: A rectangular box is placed so that it runs off one edge of the grid and continues on the opposite edge, offset along that edge; the two halves may carry different outline colours. Reassemble the box across the wrap and output only its interior — the cells inside the outline, with the outline itself removed.

test2_t4.rule: A small framed key sits in one corner of the grid holding a 3x3 pattern. Divide the whole grid into a 3x3 arrangement of equal blocks. Each coloured group in the key corresponds to a single rectangle of blocks in the output: draw it scaled up as a hollow outline one cell thick, in that colour (multiple adjacent rectangles of one cell are merged, they do not have internal separators). Inside each of these outlines fill one quadrant solid red — the specific quadrant corresponds to the corner the key itself occupies in the input grid, so a key in the top-left fills each rectangle's top-left quadrant.

test2_t5.rule: Orange cells are fixed walls. Cyan behaves like a liquid inside whatever region the walls leave open. In each region the same number of cyan cells settles at the bottom under gravity: rows fill from the bottom upward, each row is filling outward from the middle of the row (rows end at the border or an orange wall). Orange keeps its position.

test2_t6.rule: A grey rectangle encloses an area split into separate compartments, where each compartment has a single set of colored cells. In the grid, there is exactly one cell that is green (it can be in one of the compartments, or outside). Rank the compartments by how close their content cells (the colored cell) lie to the green cell, measured as the shortest Manhattan distance from the green cell to one of the object cell in that compartment. Fill each compartment solid: green for the nearest, yellow for the second, red for the third. The grey rectangle stays as it is and everything outside it becomes black.

test2_t7.rule: A single cyan cell and one or more solid single-coloured objects sit on a black background. Trace the four diagonals out from the cyan cell and take the object it reaches first. Fill the black cells along that diagonal with cyan, stopping at the object. Then outline that object in cyan: every black cell orthogonally adjacent to one of its cells becomes cyan. All other objects and every remaining cell are unchanged.

test2_t8.rule: There is a large body of blue cells in the grid ("water"). In this body, there are red cells ("fish") and a connected grey line, 8-connected ("the net"). The grey closed boundary encloses a body made of blue and red cells. Imagine extracting the contents of that enclosed body. Inside it let the red cells fall: in each column every enclosed red cell stacks at the bottom, keeping its column. The output is a box with these contents, which has the dimensions of the maximal vertical and horizontal stretch of the enclosed blue and red cells (e.g largest y position minus smallest y-position and same for x). The box has red where it settled and black everywhere else — the blue body and the boundary are discarded.

test2_t9.rule: Several coloured pieces lie scattered on the grid. Exactly one subset of them fits together, by translation only, into a solid rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps. Output that assembled rectangle, each piece keeping its own colour. Where more than one subset could work it is the one covering the largest area; pieces not needed for the assembly are left out.

test2_t14.rule: A red cell sits on the bottom row and travels right along it. It steps forward as long as it can. The red block can cross empty cells always and when a green block stands directly ahead it jumps over (landing to the right of it) but only if that block's column is one or two cells tall and the landing cell is empty; anything taller stops it. Output the grid with the red cell moved to where it came to rest and everything else unchanged. If it reached the last column, also draw a five-cell yellow plus with its center at the top right (a 3 cell-column at the second position from the right in the top row and a 3 cell row from the right in the second row from the top).

test2_t15.rule: In the grid, there is a pattern. The pattern has four-fold rotational symmetry about a centre, except for a single cell that breaks it. Move that one cell a quarter turn clockwise about the centre, into the position its rotation would occupy, leaving black behind where it was. Every other cell is unchanged.

test2_t33.rule: Several coloured pieces lie on the grid. Removing exactly one of them leaves a set that fits together into a solid rectangle; that removed piece is the odd one out. Output only the odd piece, cropped to its own bounding box.

test2_t1.rule: The grid is square with an even side n. Up to four coloured components sit in the corners, each inside a corner window of side n/2 − 2. Every component slides inward until the group packs against the middle. The top-left and top-right components move down together by the amount that brings their lowest occupied row onto row n/2 − 1; the bottom pair move up so their highest occupied row lands on row n/2. Horizontally the same: the left pair shift right so their rightmost column lands on column n/2 − 1, the right pair shift left onto column n/2. The shift is shared within each pair, so two components on the same side move by the same amount and keep their relative positions.

test2_t2.rule: Find the 8-connected objects of non-black cells; their leftmost cells all sit in different columns. Order the objects by that leftmost cell (by column). Rotate the colours one step along that order with wrap-around: each object takes the colour of the object before it, and the first takes the colour of the last. Shapes and positions are unchanged.

test2_t10.rule: Every cell has a 180-degree partner: the cell at the opposite position through the grid's centre. For each cell, keep its own colour if it is non-black, otherwise take the colour of its partner. In these puzzles at most one of any partner pair is non-black to begin with, so each pair ends up filled with that single colour on both sides.

test2_t13.rule: The pattern is a set of concentric rectangular rings around a red center, each ring a single colour, with one green cell somewhere among them. Peel inward from the outermost ring, counting a new layer each time the ring colour changes. Stop at the ring the green cell lies on: replace that green cell with the ring's own colour. Then record the depth reached by stacking that many 9s (brown) in the last column — a green cell on the outermost layer scores one, the next layer in scores two, and so on.

test2_t16.rule: Exactly one colour other than grey appears, in small fragments, alongside several grey shapes. Treat the coloured fragments as pieces, where fragments touching only at a diagonal count as one piece. Work out which shapes can be built by fitting those pieces together without overlaps. In the output the original colored fragments are erased, and any grey shape whose form matches one of those assemblies is recoloured in the fragment colour. Grey shapes that cannot be built from the pieces stay grey.

test2_t17.rule: The foreground is a single colour and consists of repeated copies of one shape, some of them clipped by the grid edge. Every copy falls straight down by exactly the height of that shape. The output shows only the fallen copies, on an otherwise empty grid. Note that partially shown patterns fall into the grid in full (e.g their previously cut off parts are shown when pushed into the visible grid) and copies at the bottom can fall out of the visual grid.

test2_t18.rule: A horizontally periodic motif occupies one half of the grid, with its axis row reaching one side edge (left or right) and not touching the opposite edge. The motif wraps into the other half on the same side as that wrap edge, shifted vertically into the other half, and from there continues across that half all the way to the opposite grid edge. The period and the motif are the same in both halves, and the axis row sits at the same relative position within each half.

test2_t19.rule: Two grey cells sit on two different edges of the grid; imagine a straight line (can be diagonal) between them that divides the grid into two sides. No shape touches that line. Each side is handled on its own, using only the cells on it, and grey cells never count as part of a shape.  If a side holds more than one shape, take the bounding box of all of them together and fill it solid grey. If a side holds exactly one shape, replace it with a solid square in that shape's own colour, with side equal to the longer side of the shape's bounding box. The square must contain the whole shape and stay on its own side of the line; where several placements would, take the one furthest down and to the right. The output keeps the two grey cells and shows only these filled regions. Everything else, the original shapes included, is cleared.

test2_t20.rule: The rule is an adaption of the game space invaders. Alien ships are the foreground components that are neither grey nor pink. Pink cells are shots, fired vertically upward. Shots are resolved by shooter row, from the top row down, and each shot destroys ("deletes/makes black") the whole connected component of the first ship it reaches. Where several shots share a row, they are ordered so that as many ships as possible are destroyed overall. The grey cannon along the bottom is unchanged.

test2_t21.rule: Four square patches, one at each corner, are cut from the input. Their side length k is the side of the bounding box of the largest corner shape, where cells touching diagonally count as joined. The patches are then swapped diagonally: top-left with bottom-right, and top-right with bottom-left. The output is the 2k by 2k grid assembled from the four patches in their new positions.

test2_t22.rule: Every colour has an anchor: its cell lying closest to the centre of the grid, measured by straight-line distance. No colour has two cells tied for closest, and no two colours have their anchors on the same row. Work through the colours in order of anchor row, top to bottom. For each colour, connect its anchor to each of its cells in turn with an L-shaped path in that colour: first straight down or up the anchor's own column to the target's row, then straight across that row to the target. A path overwrites whatever it crosses, with one exception — it never writes over a cell belonging to a colour that has not had its turn yet. Those cells are protected until their own colour is processed, after which they can be overwritten like anything else. The output is the input with these paths drawn on top; nothing is cleared.

test2_t23.rule: Cells of the same colour that touch, including diagonally, form one shape. Take every pair of shapes that share a colour. If the two shapes share a row, they can be joined straight across it; if they share a column, straight down it. Where both are possible, use the shorter join, and where those tie, the horizontal one. Each join is drawn in grey, filling only the gap between the two shapes — the cells strictly between them, none of the shapes' own cells. The output shows only these grey connectors. Every original coloured shape is gone.

test2_t24.rule: A single red cell is an infection's starting point. Every other coloured region — cells of one colour joined edge to edge — is a shape that can catch it. The infection reaches from any infected cell to any cell of a shape that is next to it, either orthogonally or diagonally, or two steps away in a straight line with a single black cell in between. Once any cell of a shape is reached, the whole shape is infected and spreads onward from all of its cells, so the infection travels shape to shape until nothing further is in reach. In the output every infected shape is recoloured red, and the original red cell becomes black. Shapes the infection never reached keep their own colour, and the rest of the grid is unchanged.

test2_t25.rule: The grid holds one foreground colour split into several 4-connected shapes. One of them is the prototype: the shape that cannot be composed from copies of any other shape present, but can itself compose at least one other. Where more than one qualifies it is the largest, and it is unique. Any shape that can be built exactly from one or more non-overlapping copies of the prototype, allowing translation, rotation and reflection, is kept. Every other shape is removed.

test2_t26.rule: The input shows a hollow coloured outline together with one or two cyan lines. Each cyan line is an axis of symmetry, running vertically, horizontally, or along either diagonal. Reflecting a position across those axes gives a set of matching positions. Fill any empty position whose matching set already holds a coloured cell, using that colour. Where every position in a matching set is empty, they all stay empty.

test2_t27.rule: Several shapes lie on the grid, all of different shape. They divide into groups such that the shapes within a group can be fitted together, by translation, into a solid rectangle. For each group, take each of its shapes in turn as an anchor and lay the assembled rectangle down so that the anchor covers the cells it already occupies. Every shape keeps its own colour, and the result is drawn on an empty grid.

test2_t28.rule: The input contains several obstacles, a single coloured cell near the bottom, and a two-cell grey pointer extending from it diagonally. The pointer gives that cell's starting direction. The cell moves one step at a time along the diagonal, bouncing off the grid walls at forty-five degrees. It stops when the next step after any bounce would land on an obstacle. The output shows the cell at its last empty position, with the original cell and the grey pointer removed.

test2_t29.rule: Each connected block of a single colour slides diagonally in a direction fixed by that colour: magenta up and right, green up and left, yellow down and left, cyan down and right. Every block travels as far as it can, stopping when one more step would push any part of it off the grid. Blocks are never rotated or reshaped.

test2_t30.rule: The grid is a vertical stack of equal-sized frames, and some of the frames are blank. The filled frames show a step-by-step progression — a shape growing, a ring expanding outward, a line sweeping across, a border travelling round, or a figure translating. Work out which progression the filled frames follow and continue it into every blank frame. Frames that already had content stay exactly as they were.

test2_t31.rule: A full-height green line divides the grid into equal left and right halves. Every other object is a solid two-by-two block. Each block has a destination in the opposite half, on the same rows and at the same position within that half — a block sitting three columns from the left edge of its own half moves to three columns from the left edge of the other half. It crosses straight over; it is not reflected. A block stays where it is if its destination would overlap the starting cells of any block, or if two blocks are aiming at destinations that overlap — in which case every block involved stays. All other blocks move, leaving their starting positions empty. The output shows the green divider and the blocks in their final positions, on an otherwise empty grid.

test2_t32.rule:
A full grey row divides the grid. Above it, each row is a colour pairing: a run of one colour on the left and a run of another on the right, and those two colours correspond. The pairing works in both directions.
Below the grey row the area is split into two halves by a black column down the middle. Coloured blocks sit wholly in one half or the other. Every block is also drawn into the other half, at the same rows and the same position within that half, recoloured to its partner — a block on the left takes its right-hand partner colour, one on the right takes its left-hand partner colour. Each block also stays where it is, in its original colour.

test2_t34.rule: The input contains a cyan square occluder with exactly one red cell at one of its corners. The output is the pattern hidden beneath that square, rotated so that the red corner would end up at the top-left: no rotation if the red corner is already top-left, a quarter turn anticlockwise if it is top-right, a quarter turn clockwise if it is bottom-left, and a half turn if it is bottom-right.

test2_t35.rule: The input is a horizontal row of equally sized frames separated by vertical cyan lines, shown out of order. In the correct order the content drifts steadily across the sequence: frames are ordered by the natural movement progression, and where that ties, by how many cells are filled. The output shows the same frames rearranged into that order, separated as before.

test2_t36.rule: The top row carries the directions: a yellow start marker, then alternating pairs of a place colour and a turn colour, ending with a cyan destination marker. Below sits a lattice of grey three-by-three tiles separated by blank rows and columns, each tile holding a coloured centre. Begin at the yellow centre and move to a neighbouring tile whose centre matches the first place colour — the start has no turn attached to it. At every tile after that, the paired turn colour says where to go relative to the way you were already heading: blue carries straight on, red turns right, green turns left. Move one tile that way, and its centre must match the next place colour. After the last pair, the final turn must bring you onto the cyan destination. In the output the top row of instructions is gone and the route is drawn in yellow, a line one cell thick running through the tiles visited and the corridors between them. The destination centre stays cyan.

test2_t37.rule: The input contains one large single-colour shape, clear of the top row and the left column. Cells in the left column mark rows: red means shift that row's shape cells one step right, green means one step left. Cells in the top row mark colours for columns. In each marked row, every shape cell moves one step in the marked direction, and before moving, a cell whose column carries a top-row marker takes that marker's colour. Shape cells in unmarked rows neither move nor change colour. All the markers in the top row and left column are removed from the output.

test2_t38.rule: The input is a self-similar fractal built from a small template. Starting from a single filled cell, each round replaces every filled cell with a copy of the whole template, so the grid grows by the template's height and width each time. Most filled cells share a base colour and a few carry a distinct highlight colour. The output is the template itself, drawn in the base colour, except that a template cell takes the highlight colour if any highlighted cell in the input sits at a matching position — the same coordinates once row and column are reduced modulo the template's height and width.

test2_t39.rule: The input contains several three-by-three hollow square islands, their borders sharing one colour. A red cell at the midpoint of an island's side is a one-way gate, allowing movement from that island to the neighbouring island in that direction. One island's centre holds a yellow cell, the source; another holds a cyan cell, the target. Follow the shortest path of gates from source to target, which is unique. In the output every gate used along that path turns grey, the source centre is cleared, and the target centre turns yellow.

test2_t40.rule: The input contains several hollow rectangular blocks. Some are marked by having their whole interior filled with red. Every marked block is removed. Any remaining block then left unsupported is removed as well, and this repeats until nothing more falls. A block is supported if its bottom edge rests on the bottom row of the grid, or if another surviving block sits directly beneath it, its top edge exactly one row below, with their horizontal spans overlapping.

test2_t41.rule: The input contains a dotted vertical grey line and a single coloured cell to its left. The cell travels horizontally right, passing through the line and continuing to the far-right edge on the same row. From the point where it crosses the line, a second copy sets off diagonally up and to the right until it reaches the top edge or the right edge. The output keeps the dotted line and shows just those two cells where they came to rest; the original cell on the left is gone.

test2_t42.rule: The grid is split down the middle into a left and a right half. The left half is unchanged. Both halves are divided into the same stack of boxes, one above the other, each box using two colours. Every box on the right is adjusted to show the same pattern as the box beside it on the left. Only the two colours already present in that right-hand box are used — cells switch between them, and no new colour appears. Of the two ways those colours can be assigned to the pattern, take the one needing fewer changes.

test2_t43.rule: Several objects overlap, each hiding part of those behind it. Every object's full shape can be worked out from the parts that stay visible, and the front-to-back order is unambiguous. Rebuild each object complete, then redraw them all with that order reversed, so what was in front is now furthest back and what was most hidden is now on top.

test2_t44.rule:
A nest of concentric square outlines surrounds a single marked centre cell, and a second cell of that same marker colour sits on the grid edge, lined up with the centre either horizontally or vertically. The side of the nest that this edge marker faces is the target side. Every outline is missing exactly one cell, at the midpoint of one of its four sides — that is its gap.
For each outline, count how many quarter turns clockwise would carry its gap round to the target side. The count is 0 if the gap already faces that side, and otherwise 1, 2 or 3.
The output is a new grid, not the input modified. It is three cells wide, with one row for each outline, ordered innermost at the top and outermost at the bottom. In an outline's row, the first n cells from the left are filled with that outline's own colour and the rest are black, where n is its count. A count of 0 leaves the row entirely black; a count of 3 fills it.

test2_t45.rule: A yellow marker sits at a corner of the grid or at the midpoint of one edge, and the grid has a single background colour. Every cell that is neither background nor yellow casts a black shadow directly away from the marker — along rows and columns when the marker is on an edge, along diagonals when it is at a corner. Yellow cells cast no shadow. Where a yellow cell falls inside another object's shadow it shines instead: the cells beyond it along that same direction are restored to the background colour, until the ray meets another object.

test2_t46.rule: The grid is five by five, with a grey middle row and middle column dividing it into four two-by-two quadrants. Four colours fill the sixteen non-grey cells so that no row, no column and no quadrant holds the same colour twice. The input reveals four cells, one of each colour, and the output is the single completion those constraints allow.

test2_t47.rule: Two equal halves are separated by a full grey line, and both share one background colour. Each half carries a single other colour as its foreground. Compare the halves position by position: where only the first half has foreground, the output takes the first half's colour; where only the second does, it takes the second half's colour; where both have foreground, or neither does, the output is black.

test2_t48.rule: The last row begins with four palette colours. Above it lies a map whose walls are drawn in a colour that is not in the palette, dividing the area into regions. Some regions already carry a palette colour and at least one is still empty. Fill every empty region so that no two regions sharing a border end up the same colour.

test2_t49.rule: Several two-by-two nodes sit on the grid, all in one colour. Two nodes can be joined only where their blocks line up, sharing a top row or a left column. The cost of a join is the gap between the facing edges of the two blocks, counted in cells. Connect every node using the cheapest set of joins that leaves them all linked, drawing the corridors in grey, two cells wide to match the nodes.

test2_t50.rule: Grey cells are nodes, and one node carries a different colour, marking the start. Beside each node sits a single orange cell, which points in one of the four directions. From a node, travel in its indicated direction until the next node is met; this gives every node exactly one successor. Follow successors from the highlighted start until reaching a node already visited — the loop from that node onward is the cycle. In the output, return the start node to grey and draw the cycle as a closed polygon, joining consecutive nodes with straight horizontal or vertical lines in the highlight colour.

test2_t11.rule:
Diagonal rays with wall bounces.

Rule:
- Input has exactly one non-zero start cell (source color).
- From start, shoot along all 4 diagonal directions.
- For each direction:
  1) March to the first wall (boundary cell), coloring visited cells with source color.
  2) Bounce off that wall and move the same number of steps again, with reflective
     boundary behavior (can bounce multiple times while consuming remaining steps).
  3) Mark the final cell blue (1).
- Finally, color each final cell's 4 diagonal neighbors green (3), potentially
  overwriting existing colors.

test2_t12.rule: The input contains a straight full-length line of 9s and, touching it, a hollow shape open on one side — a C, a V, a diagonal cup, or a ring with one gap. Other coloured cells lie scattered around. In the output, the shape has slid in the direction of its opening, one cell at a time, pushing along every coloured cell it ran into (and everything those pushed cells ran into), until the shape or something it was pushing would have left the grid or hit the line of 9s. Cells it never reached, and the line of 9s, are unchanged.

abovebelow/abovebelow1.rule: Remove all objects or pixels below horizontal line

abovebelow/abovebelow10.rule: Fill in pixels below the line with the same color as that line.

abovebelow/abovebelow11.rule: Recolor the selected object group after selecting the objects above the horizontal reference line from path-trace objects split by a horizontal reference line.

abovebelow/abovebelow12.rule: Translate the selected object just below the horizontal reference line after selecting the bottommost object from path-trace objects split by a horizontal reference line.

abovebelow/abovebelow13.rule: Recolor the selected object group after selecting the objects below the horizontal reference line from path-trace objects split by a horizontal reference line.

abovebelow/abovebelow14.rule: Keep only the selected object group on the same canvas after selecting the objects below the reference-colored object from objects split by a colored reference object.

abovebelow/abovebelow15.rule: Keep only the selected object group on the same canvas after selecting the objects below the horizontal reference line from path-trace objects split by a horizontal reference line.

abovebelow/abovebelow2.rule: Remove all objects or pixels above green square

abovebelow/abovebelow3.rule: Move horizontal line above square down vertically to rest on top of square

abovebelow/abovebelow4.rule: Color leftmost pixel of shorter lines above longest horizontal line with color of longest horizontal line. Color rightmost pixel of shorter lines below longest horizontal line with color of longest horizontal line.

abovebelow/abovebelow5.rule: In each vertical line, take color of different colored pixel, and color all pixels above that pixel with that color.

abovebelow/abovebelow6.rule: In each rectangular object, take color of differently colored lines and color rows in the object below those differently colored plines with that color.

abovebelow/abovebelow7.rule: Move object that is on top of any rectangle to bottom of that rectangle.

abovebelow/abovebelow8.rule: Remove all colored rows of rectangles, as well as any part of the "snake-like" cyan object inside the green rows.

abovebelow/abovebelow9.rule: Remove pixels below solid horizontal line.

center/center1.rule: Put single pixel of the same color in center of each object

center/center10.rule: For each pair of gray objects, place single blue pixel at the center of the space between them.

center/center11.rule: Move the selected object to the grid center after selecting the unique-color marker from parallel lines with an off-center marker.

center/center12.rule: Mark the selected object's center after selecting the object nearest the grid center from scattered objects.

center/center13.rule: Move the selected object to the grid center after selecting the largest container object from an off-center object with a marker.

center/center14.rule: Mark the selected object's center after selecting the object closest to the grid center from scattered objects.

center/center15.rule: Mark the selected object's center after selecting the largest object from a large object with an external marker.

center/center2.rule: Extract center pixel in each line

center/center3.rule: Extract center object from each large unfilled object

center/center4.rule: Delete pixel or object that is in the center of the grid

center/center5.rule: Move horizonal or vertical pair of pixels to center of horizontal or vertical line

center/center6.rule: Move single pixel or group of pixels to center of larger object

center/center7.rule: Extract center row from set of horizontal lines

center/center8.rule: For each line , move single (differently colored) pixel to center of line and extend that single pixel by two pixels in direction perpendicular to line.

center/center9.rule: For each pair of parallel lines of the same color, move single pixel in direction perpendicular to the lines to the space at the center (horizontal or vertical) of the pair of lines

cleanup/cleanup1.rule: Recolor noise pixels to fit striped pattern

cleanup/cleanup10.rule: Remove noise pixels so that only shapes are two intersecting or T-shaped lines, each of which span the grid either horizontally, vertically, or diagonally

cleanup/cleanup11.rule: Erase selected objects to the dominant canvas color after selecting the detached single-cell objects from diagonal symmetric shapes with detached noise.

cleanup/cleanup12.rule: Erase selected cells to the dominant canvas color after selecting the non-dominant non-background color cells from crossing lines with detached differently colored noise.

cleanup/cleanup13.rule: Overwrite inferred replacement cells at their original positions after selecting the cells disagreeing with dominant solid rectangle regions from solid rectangles with detached background noise.

cleanup/cleanup14.rule: Overwrite inferred replacement cells at their original positions after selecting the cells disagreeing with dominant hollow rectangle regions from hollow rectangles with detached background noise.

cleanup/cleanup15.rule: Erase selected cells to the dominant canvas color after selecting the non-dominant non-background color cells from same-color filled triangles with detached color noise.

cleanup/cleanup2.rule: Recolor noise pixels so that filled rectangle is a uniform color

cleanup/cleanup3.rule: Remove noise pixels so that all filled objects are a uniform color

cleanup/cleanup4.rule: Remove noise pixels so that all unfilled rectangles have a uniform color boundary and the pixels inside these rectangles are all the background color

cleanup/cleanup5.rule: Remove noise pixels from background and repeating shape

cleanup/cleanup6.rule: Remove noise pixels from background and symmetric shapes

cleanup/cleanup7.rule: Remove cyan rectangle from grid, and complete copied shapes that were "beneath" the cyan rectangle

cleanup/cleanup8.rule: Remove noise pixels from grid, revealing diagonal arrangement of squares

cleanup/cleanup9.rule: Remove noise pixels from background and from sides of unfilled squares, so that sides of unfilled squares have a uniform color

completeshape/completeshape1.rule: Fill in missing pixels to complete the shape

completeshape/completeshape10.rule: Fill in missing pixels on "bottom" (longest h orizontal or vertical) row of pyramid.

completeshape/completeshape11.rule: Render a colored cell patch alone at its original position after selecting the full cells of a color-matched translated template from a complete pattern with a partial translated copy to its side.

completeshape/completeshape12.rule: Render a colored cell patch alone at its original position after selecting the full cells of each selected enclosed region from a hollow object with distractors.

completeshape/completeshape13.rule: Overlay a colored cell patch at its original position after selecting the missing cells of each selected enclosed region from filled objects together with one unfilled object.

completeshape/completeshape14.rule: Render a colored cell patch alone at its original position after selecting the full cells after isolated diagonal gap repair from a sloped regular shape with isolated interior gaps.

completeshape/completeshape15.rule: Render a colored cell patch alone at its original position after selecting the full cells of a color-matched translated template from paired objects where the lower counterpart is missing a part.

completeshape/completeshape2.rule: Fill in missing pixels to make each of the intersecting lines solid. At the intersection keep the row.

completeshape/completeshape3.rule: Fill in missing pixels to complete the sides of the unfilled rectangles

completeshape/completeshape4.rule: In the input, two sides of a rectangle are drawn; draw the other (missing) sides.

completeshape/completeshape5.rule: For each yellow shape, add single green pixel to make it a square.  For each green shape, add single yellow pixel to make it a square.

completeshape/completeshape6.rule: For each shape of a uniform color, add pixels to make it a complete filled rectangle.

completeshape/completeshape7.rule: Add pixels of the same color as the existing pixels to create a filled-in square.

completeshape/completeshape8.rule: For the pixels of non-gray colors, fill in pixels of the same color to make the same shape as the gray shape in the top right corner, then delete that gray shape.

completeshape/completeshape9.rule: Fill in single pixel of same color as other pixels to complete shape.

copy/copy1.rule: Append a copy of the grid to the left (horizontally) of the original grid.

copy/copy10.rule: Copy the outer object (that encloses an inner object) on the left or top side of the grid, and place it so that it encloses the other object on the right or bottom of the grid.

copy/copy11.rule: Copy selected cells to a side location indicated by a partial copy after selecting the complete source cells before a translated side target from paired objects where the side counterpart is missing a part.

copy/copy12.rule: Copy selected cells to a side location indicated by a partial copy after selecting the complete source cells before a translated side target from matching side objects where one is missing outer context.

copy/copy13.rule: Copy selected cells to a side location indicated by a partial copy after selecting the complete source cells before a translated side target from a complete pattern with a partial translated copy to its side.

copy/copy14.rule: Copy selected outside objects into the largest container after selecting the objects outside the largest container object from a container with an external source object to copy.

copy/copy15.rule: Copy the selected cells into three horizontal slots after selecting the all cells in the input canvas from a whole input canvas to copy.

copy/copy2.rule: Put a copy of the smaller shape inside the larger unfilled rectangle. Keep the original smaller shape where it was.

copy/copy3.rule: Add pixels to the right part of the grid so that the right part is identical to the left part.

copy/copy4.rule: For each of the single pixels, copy the filled square with the same outer color, and put each copy with its top left corner in the position of one of the single pixels.

copy/copy5.rule: The single blue pixels indicate how many copies to make of the adjacent object, and which direction to extend the grid so those copies can be placed.  For each single blue pixel, make a copy of the object and place it in extended grid in the direction of the single pixel, deleting the single pixel but leaving the row or column of that pixel as all black.

copy/copy6.rule: If objects on input grid are arrayed horizontally, append copy of grid to bottom of original grid, with a horizontal line of all black pixels separating the original grid from the copy.  If objects on input grid are arrayed vertically, then append copy of grid to right of original grid, with a vertical line of all black pixels separating the original grid from the copy.

copy/copy7.rule: The left object in the input is identical to the right object except the left one has a different colored line on it.  Copy that line to corresponding location on the right object, keeping the original left object and its line intact.

copy/copy8.rule: The left object in the input is identical to the right object except that it has another object or pattern of pixels "attached to it on the top, bottom, right, or left.  Copy the attachment to the corresponding position in the right object, keeping the left object and its attachment intact.

copy/copy9.rule: For each single (isolated) pixel in the grid, copy the larger object of the same color and place the copy centered on that pixel.

count/count1.rule: Count the number of objects in the input and output a 1x6 grid with yellow pixels filled in from left to right, where the number of yellow pixels is equal to the count.

count/count10.rule: Count the number n of levels in each object.  Output a 1xn grid filled with black pixels.

count/count11.rule: Render the selected count as fixed stripes after selecting the objects inside the largest container object from a hollow container with inside and outside objects.

count/count12.rule: Render the selected count as a bar after selecting the the number of background cells inside the largest container from an object centered inside a frame.

count/count13.rule: Render the selected count as cells on a centered line after selecting the connected objects from one or more hollow objects.

count/count14.rule: Render the selected count as stripes after selecting the connected objects from one or more hollow objects.

count/count15.rule: Render the selected count as cells on a centered line after selecting the connected objects from nested containers with inside, between, and outside objects.

count/count2.rule: Count the number n of sides on the object, and output a 1xn dimensional grid filled in by orange pixels.

count/count3.rule: Count the number n of lines in the input, and output a 1xn grid filled with green pixels

count/count4.rule: Count the number n of colors in the input, and output a 1xn grid filled with black pixels.

count/count5.rule: Count the numbern  of grid cells inside the green rectangles.  Output a 1xn grid filled with black pixels.

count/count6.rule: Count the number n of non-black pixels inside the unfilled rectangle in the input.  Output a 7x1 grid, filled in order of top to bottom with n yellow pixels.

count/count7.rule: Count the number n of pixels on the border of the unfilled object whose color is different from the rest of the border.  Output an nx1 grid filled with red pixels.

count/count8.rule: Count the number n of pixels in the filled object, whose color is different from the rest of the filled object.  Output an nx1 grid filled with red pixels.

count/count9.rule: Count the number n of differnet objects in the input.  Output a 1xn grid filled with black pixels.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary1.rule: Extend a line from the side of the object to the boundary of the grid, in the direction in which has the most empty space in the grid.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary10.rule: Extend the orange pixels towards the direction of the yellow shape until it touches the inner boundary of the yellow shape.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary11.rule: Extend a selected object's centerline in a fixed direction until before another object after selecting the largest object from separated varied lines with repeated and singleton directions.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary12.rule: Extend a selected object's centerline to a fixed boundary after selecting the longest line object from scattered straight-line objects.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary13.rule: Extend a selected object's facing contour to a fixed boundary after selecting the longest line object from separated varied lines with repeated and singleton directions.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary14.rule: Extend each marker by ray until it reaches a projected line after selecting the marker cells away from a projected line from a solid projected line boundary with off-line markers.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary15.rule: Extend each selected marker toward the nearest aligned wall after selecting the same-color singleton marker cells from one enclosing frame with outside markers aligned to openings.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary2.rule: From the isloated pixel, extend a line out in both vertical directions until the top and bottom of the line collide with an object boundary.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary3.rule: From the isolated pixel, extend an unbroken line of pixels ending at (but not intersecting with) the dotted line.  The unbroken line of pixels is perpendicular to the dotted line.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary4.rule: Extend the colored shape or pixel until it touches the other colored shape in a perpendicular manner (choose the pixel or shape that will touch the other one for elongation)

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary5.rule: Extend the (orange) pixel to all four directions in a diagonal manner (top right, top left, bottom right, bottom left) until it touches the grid boundary.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary6.rule: Extend the blue pixel or pixels in a diagonal way to the top right direction until the red shape or the grid boundary is touched.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary7.rule: Extend the colored (non-grey and non-black) pixels in a horizontal or vertical manner towards the grey line until it is touched.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary8.rule: Extend the pixel inside the rectangle shape horizontally and vertically until it touches the surrounding rectangle in the extension direction.

extendtoboundary/extendtoboundary9.rule: Extend the shape inside the other shape in a horizontal and vertical manner until it touches the surrounding shape in extension direction.

extract/extract1.rule: Extract the biggest single-colored connected component with a minimal bounding box by cropping everything around it and no other cells inside the box.

extract/extract10.rule: Extract a single example of the repeating rectangle shape that is made up by two colors in a minimal bounding box. Without these shapes the rest of the grid must be a single color.

extract/extract11.rule: Keep only the selected object on the same canvas after selecting the largest object from scattered objects.

extract/extract12.rule: Keep only the selected object group on the same canvas after selecting the one fixed-background foreground object from each of two panels behind an inferred solid separator from two black-background panels containing equal-dimension objects behind a variable-color, variable-width full-span separator.

extract/extract13.rule: Keep only the selected object on the same canvas after selecting the the sole object whose color has no other object instance from a repeated lattice of same-color hollow objects with one differently colored hollow object drawn over or around it.

extract/extract14.rule: Render only the selected object group in a sampled corner of a blank input-sized canvas after selecting the the largest repeated equal square objects amid cell noise from equal filled or hollow square objects with potentially touching single-cell noise.

extract/extract15.rule: Keep only the selected object on the same canvas after selecting the the unique unfilled object from filled objects together with one unfilled object.

extract/extract2.rule: Extract the biggest single-colored connected component that is not part of a background pattern with a minimal bounding box by setting all other contained colors to black.

extract/extract3.rule: Extract the rectangle that is in the foreground. Alternatively, extract the shape that is not being overlapped or repeated.

extract/extract4.rule: Extract the biggest shown rectangle without background.

extract/extract5.rule: Extract the repeating rectangle shape and align its instances horizontally in the order of their appearance from left to right in a minimal bounding box.

extract/extract6.rule: Extract the shape on the left and the shape on the right or the top and the bottom of the yellow line without a colored background, by aligning them horizontally for a vertical yellow line and vertically for a horizontal yellow line in a minimal bounding box.

extract/extract7.rule: Extract the shape on the left and the shape on the right of the separation line which spans one grid length, without a colored background, by aligning them horizontally for a vertical separation line and vertically for a horizontal separation line in a minimal bounding box.

extract/extract8.rule: Extract the shapes which are surrounded by black pixels and arrange them in the order of appearance from left to right in a minimal bounding box.

extract/extract9.rule: Extract the shape contained in a rectangle of another color in a minimal bounding box. Replace all colors that are not the color of the extracted shape with black.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled1.rule: Produce a single pixel of the color of the shape that is not filled, meaning that there are black pixels fully surrounded by coloured ones.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled10.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while completing the pattern that alternates between yellow and black pixels inside of the green shape.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled11.rule: Recolor the selected object after selecting the the unique filled object from one filled object together with unfilled objects.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled12.rule: Recolor the selected fill-state group after selecting the all unfilled objects from multiple filled objects together with multiple unfilled objects.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled13.rule: Remove the selected object after selecting the the unique unfilled object from filled objects together with one unfilled object.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled14.rule: Fill selected enclosed regions in place after selecting the enclosed background cells of the unfilled objects from one filled object together with unfilled objects.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled15.rule: Toggle every selected object between solid and hollow after selecting the all filled objects from multiple filled objects together with multiple unfilled objects.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled2.rule: Produce a completely black grid with the dimensions of the filled shape (meaning the shape that does not enclose any black pixels).

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled3.rule: Produce a grid displaying the shape that is enclosed fully in another colored shape in a minimal bounding box. The inner shape may also be black.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled4.rule: Reproduce the input grid completely, while filling the contained shape with the color of the shape if it is not filled.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled5.rule: Reproduce the input grid completely, while filling the contained shape with the color of the shape if it is not filled, and removing the body leaving only a one-pixel outer boundary for shapes that are filled.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled6.rule: Reproduce the input grid completely, while filling the contained shapes with the color of the respective shape if they are not filled, and removing the body leaving only a one-pixel outer boundary for shapes that are filled.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled7.rule: Reproduce the input grid completely, while filling the gap between two parallel colored lines with the color of the respective lines, or replacing the body of a rectangle with black pixels leaving only two parallel colored lines, one at the top and one at the bottom.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled8.rule: Reproduce the input grid completely, while filling the gap between two parallel colored lines with the respective color, producing a rectangle.

fillednotfilled/fillednotfilled9.rule: Fill the area inside of the blue shape with red pixels up to the top, meaning the highest point where blue pixels are still on the right and the left side.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical1.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while replacing the black pixels inside of rectangles with a longer vertical axis with green pixels and the black pixels inside of of rectangles with a longer horizontal axis with orange pixels.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical10.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while adding a cyan continuous vertical line at the right edge of the grid if the contained lines are horizontal, or adding a continuous cyan line at the top edge of the grid if the contained lines are vertical.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical11.rule: Render a colored cell patch alone at its original position after selecting the interior cells colored by each hollow object's aspect ratio from wide and tall closed hollow rectangles.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical12.rule: Keep only the selected object group on the same canvas after selecting the horizontal objects of the marker color from varied closed outlines containing oriented line objects.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical13.rule: Mark an edge chosen from selected color-band orientation using one-cell dashes and 1-cell black gaps after selecting the all visible cells in color-banded regions from one multicolor region with horizontal or vertical bands.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical14.rule: Keep only the selected object group on the same canvas after selecting the objects left and right of the colored reference from a reference with aligned, symmetric cardinal appendage pairs.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical15.rule: Mark an orientation-mapped edge in the selection color using one-cell dashes and 1-cell black gaps after selecting the the uniquely colored aligned marker cells from a large filled silhouette with an aligned marked-cell pair.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical2.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while replacing shapes that include continuous vertical lines that span the entire shape height in a single color with black pixels.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical3.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while adding a continuous blue line at the left grid border in a vertical manner for shapes that are repeated in a vertical manner (meaning the shapes are at the same horizontal position but a varying vertical one), or a continuous horizontal blue line at the top for shapes that are repeated in a horizontal manner.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical4.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while coloring horizontal red lines with green pixels.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical5.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while adding a continuous horizontal green line at the top of the grid, if the two outer lines of the yellow shape are oriented in a horizontal manner, or a continuous vertical green line at the right border if the two outer lines are oriented in a vertical manner.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical6.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while adding a continuous vertical green line at the right border of the grid if the blue shape is longer in a vertical manner than in a horizontal one, or adding a continuous horizontal green line at the top of the grid if the blue shape is longer horizontally than vertically.

horizontalvertical/horizontalvertical7.rule: Reproduce the grid completely, while adding a vertical continuous line in the color of the two pixels inside or adjacent to the larger shape with another color at the right edge of the grid, if the two pixels are aligned in vertical manner, or adding a horizontal continuous line at the top of the grid in the pixel color if the two pixels are aligned in a vertical manner.
